en: Preface to the Two Commentaries on the *Nyāyapraveśaka-śāstra-vṛtti*.
Now, as for the *Nyāyapraveśaka-śāstra*, it was composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
Master Kuiji wrote a commentary (*vṛtti*) upon it; although Master Xuanzong of Zizhou produced an abridged compilation, he thoroughly elucidated the essential tenets of its eight sections.
Is it not because scholars have labored in vain over the detailed commentaries on the *Vyākhyāyukti*, finding it difficult to achieve mastery?
Therefore, I, Pu, have brought forth my own disciple; he has applied his thoughts with refined precision to examine and resolve the lineage of the former sages.

Having elucidated what was obscure, he has once again opened up the two records and clarified the profound and subtle principles of the two causes. Alas! This shall bring benefit to both oneself and others.
Ah! On the day I traveled to the Southern Capital to listen [to his teachings], I received [his instructions] from Xun and took as my model the lofty standards of the Western Capital.
I have cherished and admired them for years. As for his writings, their principles are profound and subtle; they are vast enough to dispel ignorance and expansive enough to encompass the great.

Moreover, throughout successive dynasties, texts have been revered yet have become fragmented and exhausted; even great scholars have harbored lingering doubts, and the matter remains vast and unresolved.

There are many instances where that which should be harmonious becomes impaired; yet now, having selected a few from the fundamental scales to rectify them, I shall circulate this work alongside the *Fengyīng* for the world.
I also beg the discerning scholars of the realm to revise it once more.
It is like fish dwelling on land, moistening one another with their saliva; were they to reach the Great Perfection, they would surely become a single stream.

In the third month of spring in the third year of the Kyōhō era, the śramaṇa Kenkō of the Eastern Province’s Takanawa Monastery recorded this at Chishaku Jūsya in the eastern part of Kyoto as a preface to the first volume of the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra-ṭīkā* (The Commentary on the Entrance to Logic). (Also styled Jiheng) Puyang Zhizhou composed this [text]. "Kongsang" refers to the name of a mountain;
it is the place where Confucius was born, and because this mountain exists there, he cites the mountain.
This is to clarify the person [who spoke]. A questioner asks: "The six positions (liu wei) were developed by Fuxi; they were not taught by the Master (Confucius).

How can it be said that 'Kongsang opened the way for sagehood and provided the six positions'? Answer: Since the text uses the term "provided" (zi), it is clearly known that this was not spoken by the Master himself.
However, because he assisted those six names, it is called "providing" (zi). Therefore, there are six. The fact that Fuxi was born from a *kongsang* tree is a meaning established in both traditions.

The details are not clear; however, according to this text, it is understood that the Master [Confucius] favored [the study of the *Yi*], and thus produced the *Ten Wings* (*Shiyi*) and drew upon the "Six Positions" (*liuwei*).
The "Six Positions" are the same as the "Six Lines" (*liuyao*).
Regarding the commentary on returning to true quiescence at the two rivers, there are briefly two interpretations: the first states that Ānanda departed from the territory of King Ajātaśatru.

As he was crossing the Ganges intending to enter parinirvāṇa in another kingdom, King Ajātaśatru, looking up with longing and attachment, raised an army, desiring to attack that kingdom and seize Ānanda.
Ānanda, knowing his own situation and having no recourse for advancing or retreating, feared that both kings might be harmed;
thus, by means of his supernormal power, he caused the river to split into two streams, and in the middle, he manifested fire and entered parinirvāṇa, leaving behind all his relics.
It was divided into two portions so that the two kings might each take one half.

Second, regarding the statement that the Ganges and the Bahudā are called "the two rivers," although there are two interpretations of the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa at these two rivers, both are difficult to reconcile.
Now, concerning the account of the Buddha’s previous life, it is logically untenable for the first interpretation to assign the two rivers to Nanda; the Blessed One resided only by the Bahudā River.
Yet, returning to the silence [of nirvana], the subsequent explanation of the two rivers is also untenable; observing the flow of the text, the subsequent explanation is the primary one.
In reality, it was simply at Bāḍarī that he attained parinirvāṇa, and it is only in contrast to the twin trees (śāla-drumas) that the term "two rivers" is used.

There are many such examples in the Master’s writings, such as when he says "the golden tablet praises the south," which belongs to this same category. This is especially so regarding the two matters of teacher and disciple.
Taken together as a single phrase, the initial explanation is also acceptable.
Regarding "Mount Qiao," *qiao* means "high.
Regarding "the sages of yore," the meaning of the transformation [of the characters] can be understood.
In the first section of the Commentary, regarding the "Exposition of Causes," there are two parts: the extensive and the concise.

The extensive account is as clarified in the biographies of Vasubandhu, Dignāga, and others, which explain that the refutation of the Sāṃkhya school, the bellowing of the stone, and the sounding of the mountain all originated from the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) treatises;

fearing prolixity, these are not recorded here. The concise account is as presented in this commentary, wherein there are five masters, as can be understood from the text. Question: The original *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of causes...
Question: Why is the *hetuvidyā* (science of logic) not mentioned as being established by him? Answer: For now, we shall cite that it was separately composed by him;

however, since the *yogācāra* treatises provide a general exposition [of it], we have omitted it here. All other cases should be understood accordingly. Nevertheless, although the Buddha did not separately compose a *hetuvidyā*, he is the original Teacher, and therefore it is merely recounted [as his teaching].

Regarding the statement that "the cultivation of commentaries exists within the various sūtras," a question is raised: "Is it the case that every sūtra is itself *hetuvidyā* (logic), or are there some that are not? The answer is:
"Wherever the principles of *hetuvidyā* are present, that is *hetuvidyā*; it does not mean that everything [in the sūtras] constitutes *hetuvidyā*."
Regarding the phrase "Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* says... and so forth, this citation is intended to prove that the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) was taught by the Buddha.
For a bodhisattva seeking the Dharma, all bodhisattvas prior to their attainment of Buddhahood must seek it within these five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

Regarding the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthānāni*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* (Chapter 38) states: first, the field of inner knowledge (*adhyātma-vidyā-sthāna*); second, the field of logic (*hetu-vidyā-sthāna*); third, the field of grammar (*śabda-vidyā-sthāna*);
fourth, the field of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā-sthāna*); and fifth, the field of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā-sthāna*).

The speech of all Buddhas is called the field of inner knowledge, and so on, up to all worldly arts and crafts, which are called the field of arts and crafts. How many characteristics does each of these five possess?
The tradition states that the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā-sthāna*) briefly has two characteristics: first, it reveals the characteristics of correct cause and effect;

second, it reveals the characteristic of the non-arising of what has already been done and the non-attainment of what has not been done. The science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*) also has two characteristics: first, it reveals the excellence of defeating and subduing the arguments of others;
second, it reveals the excellence of escaping and avoiding the arguments of others. The science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) also has two characteristics: first...

The characteristics of the excellence of linguistic expression are twofold: the manifestation of established meanings and the manifestation of newly formulated characteristics. Regarding the medical science (*cikitsā-vidyā*), it possesses four characteristics:

first, the manifestation of the nature of diseases; second, the manifestation of the causes of diseases; third, the manifestation of the recurrence of disease after it has been cured; and fourth, the manifestation of the non-recurrence of disease once it has been cured.
As for the science of crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), it manifests the various distinct fields of craft and industry.

Regarding the question of how the term "Inner Science" (adhyātma-vidyā) is established based on the Buddha’s words concerning the various distinct characteristics of the sciences, how do the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim there are five sciences?

There are two explanations. The first says: The non-Buddhists claim there are five sciences because they possess the other four, and since those four are also divisions of the five sciences, they obtain the name "five sciences.
This is like saying "burning clothes," where the term is applied by extension to a specific instance; or as it is said:
The six kinds of quaking do not necessarily require all six to move simultaneously to be designated as "sixfold quaking";

rather, within the context of the sixfold quaking, even if only one or two types occur, it may still be termed "sixfold quaking. This is also like the statement in the second [chapter] regarding how non-Buddhists possess the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Question: As for those such as the *svabhāvavāda* (Naturalist) non-Buddhists, they fundamentally do not admit the existence of [these things]. How is this so?
Regarding the meaning of cause and effect, since those schools lack these two internal characteristics, how could they possibly possess the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic)? Answer:
To say that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) possess the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) does not mean that all of them must necessarily possess all five.

For instance, even the Vaiśeṣikas and others speak of the principle of cause and effect. Now, let me provide an alternative explanation: all non-Buddhists possess the *Adhyātma-vidyā* (Inner Science).

Those non-Buddhists each take the teachings expounded by their own respective schools as "inner science" (*adhyātma-vidyā*), and thus regard them as authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*) in relation to their own traditions;
this case should be understood in the same way. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The words of the Buddhas possess both characteristics [of an authoritative scripture]"—this is said with reference to the inner science within one's own tradition, and it is not permissible to use one's own criteria to challenge those of others.

Some say it is called "Inner Science" (*adhyātma-vidyā*) because it establishes the internal body; this interpretation contradicts both the scriptures and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the explanation of Inner Science.
While there may be some slight logic in explaining it according to its meaning, it lacks scriptural authority.

Regarding the tradition concerning the "One with Eyes on His Feet" (Pādamūlaka), there are two interpretations among the Śākya masters. First, it is said that "feet" (*pāda*) means "many" and "eyes" (*mūla*) means "wisdom" (*prajñā*); thus, one who possesses abundant wisdom is named "One with Eyes on His Feet. Second, it is said that "feet" refers to the feet themselves; because there are eyes beneath his feet, he is named "One with Eyes on His Feet," similar to how the monk Kuṭīka is described as having hair beneath his feet. Question: Regarding the initial statement, "The source of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) was taught solely by the Buddha," what is its meaning? Answer: It means that the Buddha alone is the source of all treatises on logic. This is because the Buddha is the sovereign of all phenomena and the ultimate authority regarding all things. Furthermore, it is because the Buddha is the teacher of the world and the one who has realized the truth through direct perception. Therefore, the source of this science is exclusively the Buddha’s teaching. As for the term "source" (*yuan*), it signifies the origin from which all other treatises derive their principles. Because the Buddha is the supreme teacher, he is the primary source of all such works. Consequently, it is said that the source of the *Hetuvidyā* is the Buddha alone. This is because the Buddha is the master of all dharmas and the one who has attained the ultimate realization. Thus, the source of this science is exclusively the Buddha’s teaching. As for the term "source," it denotes the origin from which all other treatises draw their fundamental principles. Since the Buddha is the supreme teacher, he is the primary source of all such works.
