Why is it that the current discourse on the "Feet and Eyes" (Pādapāṇi) being first presented is said to be a general treatise on the three times? This is because the source of *hetuvidyā* (logic) has already been taught by Buddhas of the distant past;
it is only in reference to the beginning of this present kalpa that the "Feet and Eyes" are said to have first presented the categories of the true and the false.

Thus, there is no contradiction. Alternatively, it may be that the Tathāgata merely taught the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) without detailing the true and the false, whereas Pādapāṇi provided a comprehensive exposition.

Second, regarding the "true and the counterfeit": one might consider this to be included within the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), as it was originally taught by the Buddha; however, the teachings of non-Buddhist schools also address it, and the tradition holds that *Pīlu* (Sanskrit:

*Bhavya*) was the first to clarify it. As for the tradition concerning *Pīlu*: it is said that there were markings on the soles of his feet, and because these resembled eyes, he was named accordingly. Question:

Since *Pīlu* already established the categories of the true and the counterfeit, is the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic) not redundant at the present time? Answer: Although *Pīlu* [established these],...
The previous summary of the true and the similar was concise and could not yet provide a detailed differentiation;

therefore, I have now composed this essential treatise on the true and the similar, investigating each point one by one so that both principle and phenomena may be fully understood—this is why it is being written anew.
"Profound refinement" refers to the locus and the principle.
This is called the "mandate of the age," which corresponds to the mandate [of Heaven]. The *Book of the Former Han* states that Sima Qian said:

"Confucius spoke of a cycle of five hundred years as one epoch, during which a worthy person ought to appear; a thousand years constitute a period, during which a sage ought to appear. This applies to the present.
I consider that if Dignāga had appeared five hundred years after me, he would have been a *bhadra*;
if he had appeared a thousand years after me, he would have been a *ārya*.
To examine the merits and defects of his compositions is not the same as the *hetuvidyā* (logic) that examines the causal principles of the original sūtras of previous Buddhas.
Question: When intending to explain the Buddha’s sūtras, one contemplates their benefits and disadvantages as well as their extensiveness or brevity.

How is this known? Is it not by observing the preceding *Pramāṇaviniścaya* (Treatise on Valid Cognition)? Answer: The commentary below states: "When about to explain the profound sūtra," which refers to that very passage.
Prior to this point, he intended only to explain the sūtras and had not yet intended to compose a treatise (*śāstra*). It was only after being instructed by the Bodhisattva Śrīmat that [he began].
When he composed the *Pramāṇavārttika*, he questioned the mountain deity as well, yet why did he speak only of Mañjuśrī?

The answer is that although the mountain deity had requested it, his request was not earnest; therefore, [the Buddha] did not immediately grant it. "Now, by good fortune" means "by virtue of a prayer."
The phrase "Mañjuśrī and others" does not refer exclusively to the master Dignāga; rather, it serves as a general admonition for all those who might abandon the Mahāyāna to return to the Hīnayāna.

For example, when the Bodhisattva Vasumitra wished to collaborate with the Arhats in composing the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, he was excluded by them because he had not yet realized the fruit of Aśaikṣa. Vasumitra then said, "I have realized [the state of] no-learning..."
"Learning is not difficult; if you do not believe me, I shall now cast this thread-knot into the air.

Before it reaches the ground, you will surely realize the state of no-more-learning. Mañjuśrī, fearing that he might abandon his great resolve, withdrew the thread from mid-air so that it would not fall.

Regarding the meaning of the essence of original reality (*benzhen*): the essence of all forms is its meaning; that is to say, these aforementioned [categories] such as permanence and impermanence, substantiality and non-substantiality, and so forth.
As for the Master Guigu, there are two interpretations: first, that "Guigu" is a personal name; second, that "Gui... [the text here is incomplete].

In the valley of Zhizhou, there was the Ghost Valley Cave (Guigu Ku) in Xian County; a man lived within this cave and studied his books there, taking the cave as his name and becoming known as Master Guigu.
Su Qin and Zhang Yi both studied the two doctrines of "conjunction" (cong) and "separation" (heng), as well as the arts of statecraft, under this Master Guigu, and none in the world surpassed them.
The second [section], the explanation of the title, consists of five interpretations. Within each interpretation, there are three parts:
first, entering the name through the correct principles of *hetuvidyā* (logic) and connecting it to the teaching; second, analyzing the names such as *hetuvidyā* individually;

and third, providing a combined explanation based on those six types of etymological analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-nirukti*). Furthermore, these five interpretations proceed from the broadest to the narrowest; since they are fully present in the text, one should reflect upon them.
It is taken up.
By clarifying these two causes, one immediately gives rise to the two conditions for production.

Although the principle of the two conditions is clearly evident through scripture, it is said that they "enter into the correct principle" because they are understood by an opposing cognition. What follows below states: "This is simply the entry into the correct principle."
Regarding the "cognition arising from the statement" (*vāda-ja-jñāna*), it is also said that both the opponent and the proponent take [the statement] as their object.
It is called "cognition arising from the statement" because the cognition of the one who understands and attains comprehension arises based on the words of the proponent's thesis;

thus, it is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Alternatively, it may be understood that "statement" refers to the words of the proponent's thesis, and "cognition" refers to [the resulting understanding].
This is precisely the cognition of the opponent; such an explanation is not good. The proponent’s statement cannot be called a "thorough understanding of the thesis" (siddhānta).
Since both the reason (*hetu*) and the illumination (*prakāśana*) are distinct yet share the name "reason," the proponent’s statement serves as the reason for the opponent’s cognition.
The fact that cognition serves as the essential substance of the cause for the thesis being established is precisely what constitutes *hetuvidyā* (the science of logic).

All these serve as effects for others; that is, the arising of cognition and speech is taken as the effect, and the establishment of the thesis is taken as the effect for the cognition of the opponent;
thus, they are said to "enter" [into each other] differently.

Regarding the phrase "Although the establishment of the thesis relies on words such as 'arising' and so forth," there are two sections below this that respond to anticipated objections (*vādanigraha*).

In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), there are two instances of the character *sui* (although), which constitute these two sections. The intent of the anticipated objections can be understood by careful examination.
"One must rely on reasoned speech (*yukti-vākya*) to achieve understanding" means that the opponent must understand what is established;
when the opponent understands the speech that establishes [the position], they possess understanding. That is, the opponent's own reasoned speech constitutes the two types of understanding.
Regarding "the forty treatises composed by Dignāga," this refers to the forty works he produced on the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).

Regarding "purifying the thesis and its fruit": "purifying" (*viśuddha*) means clarity; it signifies that the proponent of the argument is able to clarify and purify the thesis (*pakṣa*) being established so that it is free from all faults, and thus is called "clarified."

The "yoga" (application) that reaches [the goal] is precisely the *hetuvidyā* (science of reasons). It is established through the eight branches, such as the thesis (*pakṣa*), which are specific designations for its own nature;
these are called "capable of conforming" because they accord with that which is to be established. Thus, it is said that "all matters" constitute the *hetuvidyā*.

Since the *hetuvidyā* resides within those matters, it is clearly understood that the essence of the reason (*hetu*) itself receives the name "vidyā" (science); this is an example of a *karmadhāraya* compound (an appositional determinative compound).

Question: Regarding that which is stated as "the cause for illumination," if this causal essence refers only to the production of words (*śabda*), then those two causes therein would be the object expressed by words (*vācya*) and the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Since the subject and object are thus distinct, how can they serve as proof? Answer: In that context, the two causes are the thesis (*pakṣa*) and are exclusively objects.
The general statement of the cause contains both its production and its manifestation; within that text, these two causes [function as such].

Within this, taking one portion—the cognition that takes the expressive verbal teaching as its object—as the proof, and not taking the two entities of the expressed meaning and the objective referent, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, the explanation that the eight "establishers" (*sādhana*) within the *Yogācārabhūmi* are [treated] as *hetuvidyā* (logic) by way of a *karmadhāraya* compound is because they possess three meanings:
first, they can conform to the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, they can serve as the reason (*hetu*); and third, they can illuminate. Thus they are complete.

These three meanings are designated by the function of their objects; in this treatise, the statement that "arising wisdom and comprehension" also possesses these three meanings thus receives the designation of a "function-of-object" compound (*karmadhāraya*).

Therefore, the citation of the *Gāthā* as proof refers to the similarity of these three meanings. That which serves as the preliminary stage for *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) is precisely Buddhism as *Hetuvidyā*.
Regarding "the two teachings," these refer to the Buddhist sūtras and the treatises composed by Dignāga; hence, they are called the "two teachings.

Alternatively, as for the statement that "the cause is itself the clear understanding," this refers exclusively to the "entry" (*praveśa*) and "correct understanding" (*yukti*) among the three explanations.
"Cause" is itself "clear understanding"; "entry" is "correct understanding. "Correct" means entering the correct principle (*samyak-naya*). Correctly entering the heavenly [truth] is what is meant.
The *Nyāyamukha* belongs to Dignāga.

Regarding the fifth [work], as for the question of to which teaching it belongs: "belongs" (*shǔ*) here means "follows. Since both the original Buddhist sūtras and Dignāga—the Lord of Heaven—both designate this field as *hetuvidyā* (logic), the question is raised as to which teaching it follows.

Regarding the statement that "correct reasoning (*yukti*) is also fivefold," the question is: what is the distinction between the first three? The answer is that there is indeed a distinction in their meaning.
First, grasping the true nature and specific characteristics of all phenomena is called correct reasoning; second, grasping the subtle principles of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*);
and third, grasping the thesis (*pakṣa*) one has established oneself—thus there are three distinctions.

Regarding the fifth point, "comprehensively encompassing the preceding four": it refers to the fact that by simply stating "correct principle" (*nyāya*), one does not call it anything else; since it is precisely the correct principle, it is said to comprehensively encompass the preceding four.

As for "the teaching is its equipment": *hetuvidyā* (logic) is that which is explained (*lakṣya*), while the teaching is that which explains (*lakṣaṇa*); thus, this very teaching functions as the reason (*hetu*) for the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because it possesses [these qualities], it is called "possessing that.

According to the latter four explanations, since the teaching (*śāsana*) is the object to be explained (*abhidheya*), this treatise is named *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic) based on its reliance upon logic (*hetuvidyā*).
Furthermore, the principle itself is the object to be explained. Moreover, there is another explanation regarding the object to be explained; this refers to the latter four [explanations].

Regarding the five explanations for "Understanding Hetuvidyā as Entering into Principle" (*Hetuvidyā-praveśa-tattvārtha*), they all rely on the signified (*abhidheya*) rather than the signifier (*abhidhāna*).

Thus, "Hetuvidyā is the treatise that enters into correct principle" is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. If one adopts the first explanation—that the teaching itself is Hetuvidyā—then "Hetuvidyā is the treatise" is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound.
As for the term "treatise" (*śāstra*), its phonetic measure is pronounced with a level tone (*ping shen*).
In order to cause the intelligence of the proponent and the opponent to arise following the words, so that they may clearly understand the thesis established below,
this very intelligence of the opponent— which is the illumination arising from the words— is called "the illumination produced by the reason" (*hetu-janya-prakāśa*).
Regarding the phrase "such as the Madhyamaka-śāstra and others": the correct wisdom of the Middle Way is called Madhyamaka;
because one desires to cause sentient beings to attain this correct wisdom and realize the principles of the observed theory, it is named after its intended purpose.

It is the same with Hetuvidyā (Logic), which is established by its name based on what is explained in the sūtras—namely, the rules for entering the ten stages. This present work is also like that: it relies upon the flowers.
When water arises, it is called "water-flower"; the same applies to land. A flower is named according to its support;
this teaching is likewise so called because it arises based on those who are well-versed in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*). Thus, it is named "Hetuvidyā."
Regarding the statement that "there are a thousand names," it means that at the beginning of the kalpa, all sentient beings possessing form had a thousand names, not only Brahmā.
To clarify the refutations, there are seven difficulties in total, which constitute seven pairs; the names established for them now are as follows: first, the three branches... [incomplete].

1. The objection regarding the two truths; 2. The objection regarding the contradiction between the real and the apparent; 3. The objection regarding the distinction between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*);

4. The objection regarding the existence or non-existence of speech and cognition; 5. The objection regarding the difference between cognition and non-cognition; 6. The objection regarding the capacity or incapacity to establish [a thesis]; 7. The objection regarding the mutual dependence of cause and effect.
Regarding these responses, there are two different interpretations for each objection; here, we shall adopt the first interpretation for each to establish their names.
1. Answering by way of the difference between breadth and narrowness; 2. Answering by citing the real to subsume the semblance; 3. Answering by showing that both equally produce wisdom;
4. Answering by inferring and verifying through the cause; 5. Answering by following the cause from the fruit; 6. Answering by distinguishing between the indeterminate and the determinate;
7. Answering by eliminating the confused and retaining the real. The remaining explanations follow the text.

Regarding the statement "because the scope of the name and its referent is broad": Question: If it is said that the reason (*hetu*) is called *hetuvidyā* (the science of reasons) because its scope is broad, then since the nature of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is also broad in its name and referent—pervading all three [members of the syllogism]—why is it not also called *hetuvidyā*? Answer: Because the opponent does not clearly understand the property (*dharma*) being established;

whereas the property is narrow in relation to the locus (*dharmin*), it is [narrower still] in relation to the reason (*hetu*). Therefore, it is not *hetuvidyā*. Furthermore, because the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also narrow, it is not [called *hetuvidyā*]. Thus, there is no [contradiction].
For three reasons, it is not *hetuvidyā* (logic). In the subsequent explanation, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also not *hetuvidyā*, and only the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not *hetuvidyā*.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that because it is clarified through others, it is also called *hetuvidyā*; since the name is established based on the cause, there is no fault.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the various *sādhana*s do not consist of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*)," the intended meaning is that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also called a "reason" (*hetu*) because it is a *sādhana*;
since it is not only the reason itself that is termed a *sādhana*, it is said that they do not possess a single characteristic.
Regarding "citing the real to include the semblance": since those who argue by contrasting the real and the semblance cite the real cause and clarify the real, they thereby include the semblance.

Alternatively, it is because [the semblance] has already been included; for the term *hetuvidyā* (logic) is comprehensive, and thus the word "cause" (*hetu*) already refers to the semblance—this is what is meant by the character "already" (*ji*).

It should be stated that "the correct [reasoning] subsumes the pseudo-reasoning. If one were to state the true *hetuvidyā* (logic) correctly, then the pseudo would indeed be subsumed within it; this is what constitutes *hetuvidyā*. Now, I say this is not so.
Since it is said that "by citing the true, the pseudo is subsumed," how can one then say that "the correct subsumes the pseudo"?

Therefore, this is untenable. It should follow the original commentary; there is no need for the word "hence" (*gu*), for if this were the text, there would be no other record stating that there is a reason.

Regarding "clarifying for others" (*parārthānumāna*), it refers to being able to act as a cause for others to achieve clear understanding; thus it is called *hetuvidyā* (Logic), not merely that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To examine this specifically as *pramāṇa*, there is a supplementary record in the commentary that is not present [in other versions].

The proponent of the proof establishes a proof to establish their own position; the proponent of the refutation establishes a proof to refute the opponent's thesis; the one who points out faults exposes flaws in the opponent's argument;
and the one who presents fallacious refutations employs types of pseudo-faults and the like.
The answer is: "Because this belongs to the category of *hetuvidyā* (logic), whereas this commentary contains supplementary records that [other versions] lack.

This response sets forth a refutation by stating that true refutation is itself free from fault and can produce the two types of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*)—namely, proof and establishment—and is therefore *hetuvidyā*.
Alternatively, when responding to one who appears to be a true *hetuvidyā* (logician) by using a pseudo-refutation, the name "*hetuvidyā*" applies to both the true and the pseudo;
thus, because the preceding term refers to the category of *hetuvidyā*, both types of refutation are answered together.

A "true refutation" (*bhūta-dūṣaṇa*) is so named because it can act as a cause to produce the clear knowledge of another, whereas a "pseudo-refutation" (*abhūta-dūṣaṇa*) can only produce a cognition that counters the opponent's proof.
Thus, both types of refutation are either *hetuvidyā* (logic) or pseudo-*hetuvidyā*; as before, it should be understood that they are identical.

Regarding the term "lack of knowledge regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*"): its essence is not speech, hence it is called "speechless" (*avākya*); because it cannot directly produce the knowledge of the opponent or the witness, it is called "lack of knowledge" (*ajñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the seeing cause is also luminous" (*dṛg-hetuś cāpi prakāśakaḥ*), there are two explanations. First, regarding the analysis according to the three parts: the "seeing" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).

It is called the "cause" because it is able to draw forth the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) by serving as its object. The essence of seeing is that which is capable of discerning; thus it is called "luminous.
Since the cause is itself luminous, this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. The word "also" (*api*) in the text is intended to indicate that it is a *karmadhāraya*.

Regarding "the proof of seeing the cause" (*hetu-pramāṇa*): the "seer" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), which draws forth and gives rise to what is called the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti*).

This is termed the "proof of seeing the cause" because the self-cognizing portion itself is clearly manifest; it is called "proof" (*pramāṇa*) because it is the clarity (*pramā*) of the cause (*hetu*). Thus, it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound), meaning "the clarity of the cause."
If self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is also the cause, then because the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) is able to produce the seeing and appearing portions, it is termed the "cause.

Because it manifests itself, it is termed "illumination" (*prakāśa*). This is thus a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). In the text, the word "also" (*api*) indicates this *karmadhāraya*. Now, let us provide another interpretation:

it is also a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), where "cause" belongs to self-cognition and "illumination" belongs to the seeing portion. The seeing portion is so called because it performs discernment (*vikalpa*).
This is called "illumination" (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of illumination; thus, it is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (dependent compound). This point answers the question as a whole:

since "seeing" (*darśana*) includes both inference (*anumāna*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is collectively termed *hetuvidyā* (the science of reasons). Self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is exclusively direct perception, yet it is also considered *hetuvidyā*.

As for the statement that "seeing the reason is also illumination," it means that inferential cognition arises through understanding by seeing its cause; therefore, this meaning is designated as such.
"Clarifying the reason" (*hetu-prakāśana*) is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) because it clarifies [the object] by means of the reason.

For example, when one infers that sound is impermanent based on a reason that possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa-hetu*), such as being produced (*kṛtaka*). This refers to the "clarification" (*prakāśana*) which is the realization through seeing the reason.

As for "the clarification of the reason" (*hetu-prakāśana*), it is so called because the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) arises upon seeing its reason; thus, the understanding that realizes the reason is termed "clarification. Therefore, it is a *tatpuruṣa*.

The explanation is as follows: it is like seeing smoke and knowing it is caused by fire; because one perceives this through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and thereby cognizes it to be smoke, it is called "seeing the cause" (*hetu-darśana*), which constitutes proof (*sādhana*).
This also relies on one's own realization (*svasaṃvedana*). Other points are as explained previously and shall be further discussed in the section on the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is also a cause; because one attains direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) through self-cognition, these two serve as causes for indirectly awakening others.
Since it not only clarifies [the truth] for oneself but can also serve as a cause for indirectly awakening others, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also called a "cause" (*hetu*).
Regarding the "causes for illumination" (*prakāśana-hetu*): these refer to both the words and the arising of meaning, which together constitute the opponent's cause.

That is to say, because the proponent’s words clarify the meaning and the opponent’s intelligence is able to comprehend them, they are termed "illuminating. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

if all [factors] are in accord with the illumination that establishes the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*), then these words, the arising of meaning, and so forth, are all capable of being mutually concordant. How so? [As follows:]...

Because the proponent possesses the thesis (*pakṣa*), they are able to utter words; since the meaning expressed by those words conforms to the [thesis], it is called a "thesis. Thus, the words accord with and illuminate the establishment of the thesis.
The answer states that these are the causes for clarification: both the two types of arising and the two types of cognition are known to function as the cause for the wisdom of realization (*jñāna*).
This is examined in detail.
Because it is not established with certainty, that which is posited as "not so" is a thesis not accepted by both parties; this is called an "uncertain reason" (*anaikāntika-hetu*).
Since it is a property accepted by both parties, it can be termed "certain" and "examined.

That which is named from its certainty—namely, the two types, the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—is able to establish the thesis only when they are certain; otherwise, the uncertain reason and example fail to establish it.

The "extreme" (*anta*) refers to that which is to be established (*sādhya*). If the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established as having that nature and those specific qualities, then [the reason] is the means of establishment (*sādhana*).

Regarding the resolution of contradictions below, the first commentary cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, stating: "Just as it is established by means of the reason and the example. Since it says "established by the example," why would it not be that which is to be established?
If it were that which is to be established, it would likewise be identical to the thesis, because it would remain indeterminate (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, it is not [the case].

Regarding the response concerning the name *Hetuvidyā* (Logic): although it is established by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is not what [the proponent] themselves accepts as the thesis (*sādhya*);

therefore, it is not called the "probandum" (*sādhya*) and thus cannot serve as a parallel case. Furthermore, another explanation states that the Lord Dignāga, considering the thesis (*pakṣa*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and the proof (*sādhana*) as being indeterminate with respect to these two masters, held that the thesis could no longer be termed *Hetuvidyā*.
Prior to this, the various masters of *Hetuvidyā* regarded the thesis solely as a member of the proof (*sādhana*).
If one follows the ancient masters and takes "establishment" (*sādhana*) as the primary term, there is no fault; the previous interpretation remains the basis.

Regarding the phrase "the illumination that is the fruit of the fruit," there are three kinds of fruits: first, the illumination that is the fruit; second, the illumination of the fruit; third, the non-illumination of the fruit.
When the cognizing wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) realizes this, it is said that the essence of the produced fruit is illumination; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Thus it is established.
The treatise states that "clarification" (*vibhāṣā*) refers to the meaning; it is the capacity to clarify and purify the establishment of a thesis, and thus it is termed "clarification.
Because it does not arise from another, it is not called a "result" (*phala*). Therefore, following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, it is called the "clarification of the result.

Although this statement regarding "arising" and so forth relies upon the cognition of the meaning, because that cognition of the meaning is not something other [than the thesis], the cause of its arising cannot be called a "result"; rather, it clarifies that the thesis being established is [the result].
The term "result" (*phala*) is not explicitly stated in the text; rather, its meaning is implied by the phrase "possessing the result" (*phalavat*). It is said that there are two kinds of results:

first, the "produced result" (*utpatti-phala*), and second, the "manifested result" (*vyañjana-phala*). Regarding the "produced result," it refers to the fact that the "knowledge of the adversary's proof" (*parapramāṇa-jñāna*) arises from the "knowledge of the cause of realization" (*sādhanajñāna*); thus, it is called the produced result.

Regarding the "manifested result," it refers to the fact that the "proposition to be established" (*pakṣa*) is illuminated and made manifest by the adversary's proof; thus, it is called the manifested result. Furthermore, the produced result may also be considered a cause.

The name "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*) is explained through two interpretations: as that which possesses it (*āśrayin*) and as the agent of the action (*kāraka*). These clarify that the result alone cannot be called the cause, nor can it be called clear knowledge.
If one were to adopt this interpretation, what would constitute the clear knowledge of the result? The former explanation is taken as the primary one.
Regarding the phrase "the light that has a cause" (*sahetu-prakāśa*) and so forth: "the light that has a cause" refers to the light that possesses a cause;
"the light that is the cause" (*hetu-prakāśa*) refers to the opponent's cognition, which is the cause for the production of that [cognition]. This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound).

"The light that is the cause" means that the cause for the production of the statement is able to purify and establish the thesis; therefore, it is also called "light. Other causes should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) nature of the "resultant illumination" (*phala-prakāśa*): because this thesis is a result but not an illumination, it is termed "inconclusive. Some versions of the text lack the character *you* (有);
when one speaks of "resultant illumination," it is confused with the "result" of this thesis, and thus it is called "confused" (*sāṃkaryam*).
Regarding the term "Hetuvidyā" (Logic) as referring to both types of certainty: since all such reasons are indeed "vidyā" (knowledge), there are instances where the word "vidyā" is originally absent.

"Vidyā" is designated as the two certainties, or alternatively, that which reveals the two is called "hetu" (reason), and thus it is named "Hetuvidyā," while the two certainties are named "dviniścaya" (the two certainties).

Because the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are fully present, this establishes the proof (*sādhana*) as understood by both ancient and modern scholars; thus it is said that "the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*) is perfectly accomplished.

The remaining seven [members] are to be understood accordingly (as noted in the sub-commentary on the second section). Regarding the statement that "both the dependent (*āśrita*) and the basis (*āśraya*) are complete": the property (*dharma*) is the dependent, and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) is the basis.
One defeats that [opponent] by means of words; one defeats him, one defeats him. Because what is established by another necessarily relies upon words, it is said to be "by means of words.
(The above two sections have no further commentary.)

Regarding the establishment of realization and proof, as well as the proponent of the thesis: one must ask whether this opponent first understood [the position] and is now pointing out a fault, or whether they did not previously understand and are now able to point out a fault.
If it is said that they did not previously understand, then how can there be a mutual confrontation between the proponent and the opponent?

If it is said that they do not understand, how could they point out a fault or produce a response for another? Thus, in the mutual confrontation of proponent and opponent, the opponent must have possessed the meaning [of the position] beforehand.

When one who establishes a formal argument (sādhana) refutes the opponent’s own argument, even if that argument carries a fault, it is not a fault for the proponent because they have realized the principle themselves.

This is like the Vaiśeṣika establishing to a Śabdika that sound is impermanent. Although the Śabdika initially did not understand the meaning of the impermanence of sound, he incurred a definitive defeat by taking the very nature of sound as he heard it to be the basis of the argument; this was made manifest by the Śabdika himself.
Since the "self-defeating argument" (*svavacanavirodha*) also arises from one's own [contradictory] explanations, it is established as a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "according to the majority" in this verse, the intended meaning is as follows: in the first half-verse, the fruit (*phala*) reveals the internal true *sādhanas* (means of proof) and refutations that fully awaken others;
furthermore, among the two types of pseudo-reasons, there are those that also awaken and realize [the truth] for the proponent himself. Therefore, it is said to be "by the majority. Question: Why?

The statement that "consciousness exists" refers only to mind (*citta*); it does not apply to objects. If one asks for the reason why "only" (*mātra*) is established, [the answer is] "only self," "only other," and "not self-aware.

This is as explained in the commentary regarding the response concerning the "majority portion" (*bahubhāga*). Although this response is given, the objection is still not fully resolved. "Only" (*mātra*) implies determination;

if it were said to refer to a "minor portion," how could it be called "determined"? The term "only" (*mātra*) in the expression "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is not based on a minor portion, for it is called "only" precisely because it excludes everything else.

Now, the commentary explains: The fundamental intent of establishing [a position] and refuting [an opponent] is solely to awaken others; since the two types of fallacious [reasoning] can also partially awaken others, the word "only" (*eva*) is employed.
Although one's own words are not originally intended for this purpose, because they do lead to self-awakening, they are likewise not termed "awakening [others]."

Regarding the statement that "inference (*anumāna*) is so called because it is a definitive cognition of a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)," some say that [cognitions] such as "impermanence" are common-characteristic cognitions, and that the cognition of sound as impermanent is a common-characteristic cognition.

This interpretation is incorrect; for how could the properties to be established (*sādhyadharma*) be limited to these four alone? Furthermore, since the scripture does not explain them as being common characteristics, one should rather say:
"The opponent previously did not accept this; now, having refuted that which was not yet accepted, one causes them to accept a conceptualized cognition that is identical [to the object]."

Regarding the "common characteristics" (as noted in the detailed sub-commentary on the lower three sections): when one establishes a thesis such as "it is established," there is a definitive contradiction.
Although the three marks [of a valid reason] may be present, the fact that the proponent and opponent each hold different interpretations based on their own tenets is termed "discordance" (*viṣama*).

If, among the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the principle is profound while the phenomenon is manifest— such as when the principle of "abiding in space" and so forth regarding form and so on is called "profound," whereas form and so on themselves are called "manifest" phenomena.

Regarding the question: "If the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) of the causal stage perceive objects clearly whether they are subtle or manifest, how can it be said that they do not perceive the principles (*dharma*) inherent within those objects?
Answer: This is explained by combining the discussion of both the causal and resultant stages.

If one speaks of the various consciousnesses at the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), as well as the five consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness associated with them during the fixed state of the causal stage, they all clearly perceive these principles.

If, in the state of distraction, the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) take objects clearly while their principles remain obscure—or if, in that distracted state, the five sense-consciousnesses directly perceive objects such that although they do not take principles as their object, the objects are nonetheless non-erroneous—then the principle and the object naturally become clear; one should reflect further on this.

Since there is neither separation nor conjunction between the general and the specific regarding the reason (*hetu*), the term "reason" alone refers to the general reason, while the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) of the reason are its specific names.

Furthermore, some assert that the four [members of the syllogism] constitute the proof (*sādhana*); the intention of this master is that the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), are not themselves directly capable [of establishing the conclusion].

The two members of the *upanaya* (application) and *nigamana* (conclusion) are excluded together because they do not exist externally; since the *dṛṣṭānta* (example) and *upanaya* are distinct, they are divided into two types, thus [the syllogism] consists of only four members.

Regarding the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, there are pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) consisting of pseudo-direct perception and pseudo-scriptural authority (*āgama*).

Regarding the two [types] that are both universally established (*prasiddha*), one may take either the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and its differentiation as the two, or the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) as the two.
Now, in this case, the proponent utters the word "Pāda"; however, it is feared that there may be an error here. The *Nyāyamukha* states:
"Furthermore, by means of a single word, one expresses the proof (*sādhana*). The intention of that treatise is to say that one expresses the proof within the sound of a single word.

Regarding this *sādhana* (probans), why is it now said to reside in the word "one" (*eka*)? Furthermore, within the commentary on this *sādhana*, the Master of the Commentary (*Ṭīkākāra*) also cites a single phrase from the *Nyāyamukha* to prove the meaning of *sādhana*;
thus, we know that the current [reading] is an error. Moreover, upon examining the intent of the commentary, it should not be mistaken;
for he states that the *sādhana* resides in the word "one," while the three—reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and [thesis]—together constitute a single *sādhana*.
Because the thesis has been established, we now rely on the actual capacity for proof (*sādhana*). There are many instances where [the reason] is included within *pudgala* and *pudgala*.

If it did not include the capacity for proof, then *pudgala* would fail to encompass the full extent of the multiple statements. If one provides this interpretation, there should likewise be no contradiction; reflect further on this.
Since those who speak excessively are all called by the sound "Pāṭa," it is said that they appear to be speaking excessively.

Regarding the phrase "that which is established is not fixed, for that which is established can establish the meaning": the words "can establish the meaning" explain that [the subject] is not fixedly established.
That which is established by means of the thesis (*pakṣa*) as being able to accomplish its own nature and specific qualities is called the "prover" (*sādhana*).

Since the meaning expressed by the thesis is definitively only that which is to be established (*sādhya*), there should be two sets of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on this. Taking what is to be established as the thesis-meaning, there is [the case where] it is only the prover;
the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the thesis-statement (*pakṣavākya*), and the reason (*hetu*) constitute the combined categories. The fourth [alternative] can be understood by careful examination.
The distinction of natures is established as a thesis by means of the upper half [of the syllogism], like water; the latter part is explained in detail as previously stated.

Second, regarding the phrase "the proof of the collection of dharmas in general," it is asked: If a general aggregate is established by means of individual dharmas, then whichever school one follows, there are two faults.
For instance, in the Buddha-dharma, if one attempts to establish a general aggregate by means of a portion of sound, it will certainly result in error.

There are two faults: first, it contradicts the scriptures; second, it contradicts your own tenets. Although you maintain that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entity is permanent and, while not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), is nonetheless subsumed under the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), you nevertheless assert that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) as a whole are impermanent because the unconditioned is permanent.
To establish [the eighteen elements] as impermanent in this way contradicts the scriptures, for any school would likewise admit that things such as jars and basins are impermanent. Now...

If it were established as that [other], there would be the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*). The answer-text states that one should exclude the first two faults according to what is appropriate, because sound is established in accordance with what is being disputed.

Thus, if it refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), then for those who falsely imagine it to be permanent, the thesis (*sādhya*) is free from faults.

If this were so, then one thing would be established by means of another distinct thing, rather than a distinct thing being established by a general category. To illustrate, consider the case of the five [aggregates].

The "aggregates" (*skandha*) are called a "total collection," and this total collection is what is to be established. Within this total collection, taking one part—namely, the specific nature and distinction of sound—is called the "establishing factor" (*sādhana*).

First, having established against an opponent that this sound is impermanent, one then cites this sound to establish that whatever is subject to dispute within the total collection is likewise definitively impermanent;
thus, both the general and the particular possess the property of being produced (*kṛtaka*).
Because it is the nature [of the subject], and because there exists a primary reason (hetu), it is termed "establishing the general by means of the particular.

Although this [particular] is also something to be established (sādhya) in relation to the thesis (pakṣa), when one portion of that [particular] is presented to the opponent, its own nature and specific qualities (viśeṣa)—in contrast to its own nature as the thesis—are likewise things to be established. The rest is clear from the text.

Regarding the meaning of "conjunction with the basis" (*āśraya-saṃyoga*): "conjunction" means not being separated. The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*) are conjoined with this thesis;

they are not the sense of the "basis" itself. Alternatively, both the intrinsic nature and the specific qualities of the sense may be called the "basis," and their being so termed is what constitutes "conjunction."

Regarding the statement, "The nature of non-separation between that which can rely [the dependent] and the thesis (pakṣa) constitutes the thesis; thus, this thesis is called 'that which can rely'": Question:
What is the difference between the first and the second of these two explanations? Answer: The first is explained by correlating the means of proof (sādhana) and the object of proof (sādhya);

the latter is distinguished by correlating that which can rely (the dependent) and that upon which it relies (the basis). The second explanation concerns the correlation between the general and the specific names.
Regarding "because of establishing the particular through the general": this nature of inseparability is called "establishing the particular through the general";

that is, the specific differentiation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-viśeṣa) is called "particular," and because it is established by means of the nature of inseparability, it is termed "establishing the particular through the general."
Regarding the statement "there are twenty-eight [factors] when two are omitted," this merely refers generally to the method of performance (*vidhi*).
If one discusses their actual substance (*tattva*) according to the eight [categories] of Yoga, it is impossible for there to be twenty-eight by combining omissions; why is this so?

When citing Yoga as a general category, since both the commonalities and the differences are also omitted during that citation, it is not possible. If one follows this principle, then regarding the omissions...

The first [alternative] is likewise not established; since the eightfold formulation is deficient, the citation of the reason and the example is also deficient because of the lack of identity and difference.

Therefore, according to the Abhidharma, this too cannot exist without deficiency. When the eightfold formulation is combined and concluded, if the essence is lacking, the reason and the example are also deficient at that time.

If a proponent of the Science of Sound (Śabdika) asks: "When all three characteristics [of a valid reason] are absent, how can the third characteristic be missing when the substratum of the quality (*guṇa*)—the cause—is not admitted by either the Śabdika or the Buddhist, such that both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) lack two characteristics, and even in the case of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) consisting of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the reason does not apply?
Answer: This text is erroneous; it should read "śabda-viśeṣau" (sound and particularity).

Regarding the relative cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) as it pertains to the three characteristics of a reason according to the *Vaiśeṣika* school, all three are deficient. Their system asserts that qualities (*guṇa*) depend upon substances (*dravya*), and that sound (*śabda*) does not depend on qualities;

therefore, because sound is a quality, the reason "that which is the substratum of a quality" does not apply to sound, thus lacking the first characteristic (*pakṣadharmatva*). Furthermore, since they do not admit the existence of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as a quality, the reason "being the substratum of a quality" also lacks the second characteristic (*anvaya*).

Finally, because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are subsumed under the category of substance, the reason "being the substratum of a quality" [is absent from them]. Thus, the reason is deficient in its application to the subject.
This also transforms the deficiency into the third characteristic.
Regarding the phrase "the *Nyāyamukha* and so forth," the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used because it includes the remaining thirty-nine treatises; thus, these are the forty treatises of Dignāga.

Regarding the faults such as the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), the non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), and so forth: Question: If the example lacks a qualifier, it is called "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).
As stated, if the thesis (*pakṣa*) commits the fault of lacking a qualifier, it becomes an uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇahetu*). Since both examples lack a qualifier, they are called "uncommon.

Why is it that the term "qualifier" is missing [from the definition], and why is it said that the fault of the qualifier constitutes an uncommon reason? Answer: It is not the case that the unestablished qualifier is simply that [fault].

In the context of the reason (*hetu*), "non-common" (*asādhāraṇa*) does not apply in this way; rather, it is because of that reason that the reason is established as non-common. For example, when addressing the Sāṃkhya school, one might establish the argument:
"Sound is subject to destruction," using "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) as the differentiating reason. This reason is "non-common" and "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, if the reason of being a product (*kṛtakatva*) were partially subject to destruction, and if the Sāṃkhya school did not accept such a reason within the similar or dissimilar instances (*sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*), it would likewise be called "non-common."

This is stated based on a partial interpretation and is not the commentary of the author of the *Vyākhyā*. It recounts the explanation of an ancient master regarding the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) and so forth:
that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property itself constitutes a fault of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-doṣa*).

Thus, for example, the statement "the eye and so forth must be for my use" is a fault of the qualifier when considered from the perspective of a Mahāyāna teacher. Furthermore, the reason of being an "accumulation" (*saṃcita*) is also a fault with respect to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
The fault of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dharma is explained as one of the four types of contradiction.

As for the claim that the reason already possesses the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its occurrence throughout the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), this is an objection raised by way of illustration.

The other objections are the same as those previously mentioned; here too there is a lack of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), yet it differs from the previous case because it is similar to the "lack of an example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) pointed out when refuting the proof (*sādhana*).

As for the objection based on "conformity" (*pratibādhita*), since this section follows the opponent’s intention by citing an example, the difficulty regarding both [the proof and the counter-proof] being absent is not raised.
If [the reason] is established, it is called "mutual non-establishment" because the reasons for both the proponent's and the opponent's positions are unestablished;
if it is mutually unestablished, then the similar example (*sapakṣa*) is unestablished, and that which is not excluded by both is the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*).
Regarding the explanation of the reason for this, it says: "By means of the application of the example (*upanaya*), it is shown that [the reason] does not apply to all.

This statement regarding the application of the example is intended to clarify and state that the teacher Dignāga refuted the heterodox outsiders' faulty establishment of "difference" (*anyatva*) as the logical reason (*hetu*). The intention of the outsiders was as follows:
by saying "all," they meant to show that sound is not included in "all"; by saying "impermanent," they meant to show that sound is permanent and distinct [from impermanent things].
This sets forth the reason by abandoning the formal expression (*pramāṇa*) in order to reveal the intended thesis (*siddhānta*) through its inversion. How can it reveal [the meaning]?

Since it is stated that "all things are impermanent," it conversely causes the analogical statement—"whatever is not all is permanent"—to be understood: because sound is not "all," it is known to be permanent.
This is the intention of the non-Buddhist. Regarding the explanation of the "reason" (*hetu*), this refers to the words of the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*).
Regarding the phrase "because this cause does not exist, yet there is existence in that which has come to be," the meaning of the commentary (*ṭīkā*) is as follows:
"This" refers to the fact that all these [phenomena] are impermanent. Because of this cause of impermanence, the absence of existence within phenomena is termed "non-existence.
The intended meaning here is that while all causes are not subsumed within the thesis (*pakṣa*), the term "all" within the statement "the cause can be the thesis" does indeed include them.

If the thesis (*pakṣa*) has already been subsumed within the reason (*hetu*), upon what further basis could the two parties—the proponent and the opponent—establish their respective theses? Since both parties admit that the subject of the thesis (*dharmin*) is included within the reason, neither would admit a separate thesis;

thus, based on the name "thesis," both [types of] "unestablished" (*asiddha*) would apply. Question: Since the subject is already included within the reason, the reason would have nothing upon which to rely.
Why, then, is it not called "unestablished due to lack of a substratum" (*āśrayāsiddha*)? Answer: If the subject lacked an entity (*svabhāva*), then it would simply be the reason itself.
Regarding the point that the locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished: the subject (*dharmin*) "sound" currently exists; it is not a non-entity and thus cannot be the fault of lacking a locus.

However, because the reason (*hetu*) is broad in its application, it necessarily encompasses the subject of the thesis (*pakṣadharmin*). One must not, on account of the reason, rely upon the reason itself [as the locus]. Therefore, this is an "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*).
As for those who claim that this reason is not existent and so forth, they are mistaken; it is not the case that all reasons lack an existent subject for both the proponent and the opponent.
When it is mutually agreed that a reason does not apply to the sound in question, this is called "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*).

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because it is a part of the probandum (*sādhyāṃśa*)," the meaning of the commentary is as follows: when a reason exists in one part of the probandum while being absent in another, it is called a "part.
Although it is not non-separable from the whole, it is nonetheless designated as "a property of the probandum" because it belongs to one portion of that which is to be proven.
The "part" (*ekadeśa*) is also called the "probandum" (*sādhya*). Some claim that the non-Buddhists offer this defense: "Our school accepts that sound is not 'all' (i.e., not omnipresent);

therefore, there is no fault of the reason being unestablished for both parties. To refute them once more, [the author] states that this is the meaning of "one part of the probandum. The actual refutation states:
"In your school, it is said that sound is not 'all,' because you use the term 'all' as a designation (*saṃjñā*). How could you then possibly [use that same term] to..."

Since one part of the thesis (*pakṣa*), namely the property-bearer (*dharmin*), is used as the reason (*hetu*), and because that which is a part of the thesis does not reach the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is the fallacy of the reason being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the thesis. Question:

The intent of that objection is to say that sound is not "all," yet the property-bearer is merely stated as "sound," and the property (*dharma*) is stated to be "permanent"; it does not take "not being all" as the property.
How can it be said that a portion of the *dharmin* (the subject) is taken as the reason (*hetu*)?
If one were to take a portion existing upon the entire *dharmin* as the reason, then one would be saying that a portion of the *dharma* (the property) is the reason.

Since the nature of the *sādhya* (the probandum) must also be taken as the reason in relation to sound (*śabda*), it too would have to be a portion of the *dharmin*. But since this is not the case, how could that [other position] be so? Therefore, it is not tenable.
The resolution of these difficulties should be further examined with care.

Therefore, both of these schools are not at fault regarding the thesis; for all that the ancient masters cited is "because everything is impermanent," whereas the reason established by Dignāga is not called "the reason of everything" by the two schools.

Regarding the statement, "One who posits a fallacious alternative is called 'one who posits the fallacious' (dūṣaṇābhimānin) because they explain by way of an analogy," this summarizes the first clause.
It restates the opponent's citation and concludes that the latter clause is incorrect, as it contradicts their own tenet rather than being a fault of the tenet itself.

If it is argued that because the fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) is not established within the thesis (*pakṣa*), this is merely citing an example to rescue [the position] by claiming that the thesis contradicts the reason;
such an objection is not permitted, for it is a case where the reason contradicts the thesis, rather than the thesis contradicting the reason.

Regarding the phrase "this is not a valid reason because it reaches what is unestablished," this further explains why the basis for doubt is not established as being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) in two ways:

either for both the proponent and the opponent, or for one or the other. The term "this" refers to the aforementioned expression "the basis for doubt," which applies to both parties—the proponent and the opponent—or to either one individually.
The term "unestablished" encompasses both of these positions: that which is unestablished for both, or that which is unestablished for either one. Thus, it refers to them collectively.
The meaning is as follows: that which is based on hesitation is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*) because it cannot establish itself, nor can it establish another.

Within this, there are two types: the "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*) and the "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*). Since these do not differ from the original categories of "unestablished for both" and "unestablished for one," they are distinguished separately by stating:
"either that which is certain is unestablished for the opponent, or that which is doubtful is hesitant."
Regarding what is called the Mṛgāramātṛ-vihāra: in Sanskrit it is called Vaiśākhamātṛ, which in Chinese means "Mother of the Deer. Here, the mother is named after her son;
thus she is called Mṛgāramātṛ (Mother of the Deer). This Mother of the Deer built a hall for the Saṃgha within the Jeta Grove;
as the name was established based on the person, it is called the Mṛgāramātṛ-vihāra.

Regarding the statement that "there is this establishment [of a position] up to its refutation," which refers to one who engages with another's school: among these three phrases, they are mutually contradictory.
Within the first phrase, there is an interpretation that does not permit it to be merely an establishment (*sādhana*) rather than a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, within the third phrase, there is again an interpretation that does not permit it to be both an establishment and a refutation. The answer states: "Refutation means..."

Regarding the second point of the opponent's position: why is it that some explanations do not admit that what is capable of refuting (*dūṣaka*) is necessarily what establishes (*sādhaka*)? The answer is:

within the category of what establishes, there is that which merely presents one's own [position] without refuting the other; there is also that which establishes one's own [position] while refuting the other. The same applies to what is capable of refuting.
If one were to say that all that establishes is not capable of refuting, this would contradict the principle that what establishes is indeed capable of refuting.
If one says that the "establisher" (*sādhana*) is itself the "refuter" (*dūṣaṇa*), then it would contradict the subsequent statement that the refuter is not the establisher.
Now, it is shown that the establisher establishes for oneself while the refuter refutes others; yet both the refutation of others and the establishment for oneself are non-conclusive (*aniyata*).

Therefore, the term "existent" (*sat*) is placed as an explanation to distinguish and exclude fixed attachment. Regarding the first phrase, there is an explanation based on its own establishment while simultaneously refuting others; regarding the third, there is an explanation.

In brief, when one employs autonomous (*svatantra*) reasoning without refuting the assertions of others, yet refutes what others do not establish while not establishing one's own position, these mutually cited arguments are not contradictory as a whole.

For example, within the Buddha’s teaching, when refuting the non-Buddhist *ātman* (self) as being permanent and so forth, one merely refutes the notion that "the self is permanent" and does not intend to establish that "the self is impermanent.
This is thus purely a negation (*pratiṣedha*) rather than an affirmation (*vidhi*). As it is said:

Regarding the critique of the theory that sound is eternal: if one simultaneously establishes that sound is eternal while also asserting that it is impermanent, this constitutes both affirmation and negation.
However, if one merely establishes one's own position without refuting the tenets of others, this is simply establishing one’s own view rather than refuting another’s.

It is said that when the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths for Kauṇḍinya and others in the Deer Park, he established only his own doctrine without refuting others; this refers to the aforementioned [case].
The various categories are paired with one another according to this principle, each taking slight variations to constitute the number of propositions.

Regarding the phrase "there is inference and non-valid cognition up to all non-valid cognitions," etc.: this takes inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) as the primary terms to be contrasted with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to form the propositions;
it does not mean that the essence of inference is itself called "inference-as-non-valid-cognition. Question: [Why is this so?]
Question: Why are the *sādhana* (proof) and so forth not paired with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others as categories? Answer:

Because the *sādhana*, *dūṣaṇa* (refutation), and so forth differ from the verbal cognitions of direct perception, inference, and so forth; and because the distinctions between self-awakening and awakening of others constitute entirely different entities, they are not paired.

Although, according to the systems of others, one may arrive at a distinct manifestation of what appears to be a refutation, this explains away the anticipated objection. An external objection states: "If it were truly..."
If the *sādhana* (proof) is authentic, then the *dūṣaṇa* (refutation) should simply be the negation of that proof; why then establish a separate branch for refutation?
One might ask: "The case of the pseudo-proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) should also be understood by this same principle. It is precisely because of this question that the following answer is given.
Regarding the phrase "because they are realized by the two cognitions of the real and the manifest": direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) are termed the "two cognitions.

These two cognitions are called "realization" (*jñāna-pariccheda*). Since the term "realization" encompasses both the real and the semblance, these four [types of cognition] are subsumed within the cause of realization (*pariccheda-hetu*).
The semblance of direct perception and the semblance of inference are both non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); therefore, based on these eight meanings, their essence consists of only seven.

Question: Since pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) and pseudo-inference (*anumānābhāsa*) possess a distinct ontological nature from true perception and true inference, how can the two valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) encompass all cognitions exhaustively?
Answer: The two valid cognitions—perception and inference—encompass all cognitions exhaustively because pseudo-perception and pseudo-inference do not possess the nature of valid cognition;

they are termed "invalid cognition" (*apramāṇa*). Therefore, what contradiction is there in the principle that these two [valid] cognitions do not include them? Some say that both types of pseudo-cognition are subsumed under invalid cognition. If this were the case...
It is unreasonable to provide this interpretation regarding the distinction between the categories of the real (*tattva*) and the semblance (*pratirūpaka*).
First, concerning the essence of the treatise (*śāstra-tattva*), the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), fascicle 15, states that there are six essences of a treatise.
Those that differ from the *Abhidharma* are appended here according to the text: first, "discourse" (*vāda*) refers to all speech, sounds, and expressions; second, "superior discourse" (*pravāda*).
This refers to all the discourses heard by people in the world as appropriate to them, which are of three kinds of pure discourse. The intent of that discourse is as follows:

whether one's own objects of the five senses and so forth are seized by another, or another's property is seized by oneself, or even regarding ownerless objects of the five senses and so forth, one should not mutually seize them; furthermore, this extends to the five [views] such as eternalism and nihilism.
Seeing causes such as these, the arising of various disputes is called "disputatious discourse" (*vivāda*). Fourth, "slanderous discourse" (*apavāda*):
it refers simply to slander; that is, when, with a defiled mind, one incites resentment and mutually reviles another, the speech thus produced is called "slanderous discourse.

Fifth, "discourse in accordance with correctness" (*anuvāda*): it refers simply to discourse in accordance with correctness, which is the proclamation of the correct [Dharma] for the sake of all sentient beings.

The investigation of the Dharma, the definitive analysis of the teachings, the instructions, and the precepts are for the purpose of severing all doubts of sentient beings, for the purpose of realizing the profound meaning of various phrases, and for the purpose of bringing about the ultimate purity of knowledge and vision;

because they accord with right practice and accord with liberation, this treatise is called the *Anupūrva-śāstra* (Treatise in Accordance with Rightness). Sixth is the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (Instructional Treatise); regarding that, it says: "The instructional treatise refers to instruction."

For those individuals who are training in the higher training of mind and the higher training of wisdom, this discourse causes those whose minds are not yet concentrated to attain concentration, and those who are not yet liberated to attain liberation;

it causes them to train in and understand true knowledge, and it causes them to open up to and comprehend true knowledge. Therefore, among these six types of discourse, this is called the "Discourse of Instruction."
The causes for the arising of objects such as sensory dust are not the essence of the treatise (*śāstra*); rather, the verbal discourse that arises [therefrom] is the true essence of the treatise.
Therefore, it is said in general that the "generative cause" is the essence of the treatise.
Regarding the "locus of treatises," there are six such loci; here we cite only two, while the remaining four are as listed below. That text states:
"The locus of treatises refers to the royal court, those who uphold principles, virtuous associates, and those well-versed in the meaning of the Dharma—such as the Brahmins of your gate.
As for the "basis for the preceding commentaries and treatises," that text contains eighteen items, namely the eight means of proof (*sādhana*) and the two objects of proof (*sādhya*).
The *Vyākhyā* states that "the means of proof" (*sādhana*) refers to the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding the phrase "the true and pseudo [means] of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), etc.," the word "pseudo" (*sadṛśa*) should be understood as applying to the scriptures (*āgama*) as well; this is because that treatise does not take pseudo-direct perception and so forth as its basis.

There is a manuscript reading "byi" (with the character *yi*), which should be corrected accordingly. That treatise states: "There are two kinds of bases for the treatise: first, that which is to be established (*sādhya*)."

There are two types of means of proof (*sādhana*) and two types of objects to be proven (*sādhya*); that is, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its specific attributes (*viśeṣa*). There are eight means of proof:

the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), the conclusion (*nigamana*), and the three measures of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the "ornament of the treatise" (*śāstrālaṃkāra*), there are five qualities of such a treatise: first, being skilled in one's own and others' tenets; second, possessing perfection in speech.
Regarding "endowed with perfection," all that is spoken is done with sound and not with non-sound. What is meant by "sound"?
It refers to being endowed with five virtues: first, not vulgar, meaning it is free from the coarse and colloquial language of various regions;
second, easy to understand, meaning all that is said employs terminology commonly used in the world; third, majestic and clear, meaning...

1. Establishing words based on meaning (*arthapratiṣṭhāpana*): being skillful and eloquent in establishing that meaning. 2. Being majestic (*vīryavat*) and dignified (*prabhāvavat*): [the fourth quality]. 3. Correspondence (*sānubandha*):

meaning that the preceding and succeeding meanings of the dharma accord with one another without distraction. 4. Excellence of meaning (*svartha*): meaning that it leads to superior rebirths, brings about meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and is free from error.
5. Fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*): meaning that when in the midst of a great assembly and so forth, one’s mind is free from inferiority, anxiety, or fear.
First, his body is free from perspiration, his face shows no sign of fear, his voice is free from stammering, and his mind is free from timidity—these are the four.

Fourth, he is dignified and waits for the proper time before speaking, neither too slowly nor too hastily. Fifth, being by nature fit for offerings, he is well-disciplined and does not afflict others;
he never transgresses the grounds of discipline, and he utters speech in accordance with the minds of others at the appropriate time.
Speech that is able to lead toward benefit as it truly is is gentle and soft, like that of a virtuous friend.
If one relies on these five treatises to adorn their discourse, one should know that there are twenty-seven kinds of praiseworthy qualities, as explained at length in those commentaries.
Those commentaries provide extensive analysis, stating: "It is like a person seeking sensual pleasures who adorns themselves with mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and so forth."

Just as one adorns oneself with precious ornaments such as girdles and bracelets, whose majestic power is intense and whose radiance shines everywhere, so too does this proponent adorn themselves with these twenty-seven praised qualities as ornaments of the treatise;
their majestic power is intense and their radiance shines everywhere. For this reason, it is called the "Ornament of the Treatise."

Regarding the *Abhidharma*, there are six [qualities], four of which constitute eloquence (*pratibhāna*): fifth is being an adversary (*prativādin*), and sixth is being one worthy of offerings (*arhat*). The rest are all the same as this.

However, that treatise explains that "one worthy of offerings" refers to a noble person (*ārya*) established in their nature; "speaking words" refers to skillful means (*upāya*) that accord with the mind of the opposing debater.
The treatise states that there are three ways of losing an argument (*parājaya*). First, abandoning the discussion (*vāk-tyāga*), which consists of thirteen items;
that is, the proponent addresses the opponent, saying: "My argument is not good, while yours is good. The rest is as explained therein.
Second, being defeated in speech (*vacana-parājita*), which also consists of thirteen items; that is, the proponent being overcome or subdued by the opponent. The rest is as explained.
Furthermore, regarding the three types of "faults of speech" mentioned therein, these refer to the nine kinds of defiled faults of speech committed by the proponent.
First is "confusion," which refers to abandoning the subject under discussion and speaking of irrelevant matters; the rest is as explained in that [text].

However, according to that treatise, it speaks only of fallacious proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*) and not of fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*); yet, by citing the fallacious proof, the fallacious refutation is implied through logical necessity.

Because they exist, the *Vyākhyā* explains them in detail; it also states that "speaking of abandonment" refers to speaking for oneself, saying, "I [abandon] the treatise," while "speaking of yielding" refers to retreating through the expedient means of resorting to other matters, such as discussing a different subject or manifesting anger.
There are nine types of verbal transgressions: first, incoherence; second, harshness; third, lack of clarity; fourth, lack of moderation.
The five [faults] are: (1) being contrary to the goal, (2) being untimely, (3) being indeterminate, (4) being obscure, and (5) being incoherent.

Regarding the treatise on departure [from debate], that treatise states: "A proponent of a thesis must first examine the opening of the debate by means of those three types of investigation, and only then engage in the discussion—or refrain from doing so. First, one investigates gain and loss; that is, the proponent..."
First, one should examine whether this treatise will cause harm to oneself, harm to others, or harm to both;
or even if one considers that it should not be established at all. If one knows thus:

"The treatise I have established does not cause harm to myself, and so forth, but is able to lead toward the benefit, purpose, and peace of humans and devas," then one should consider establishing it. This is called "withdrawal."
First, the characteristic of renunciation regarding the discourse on whether [an action] was performed or not performed;

second, when observing the assembly, the proponent of the thesis should carefully examine whether the assembly present is collectively possessed of biased attachments or free from them, whether it consists of the wise and upright or not, and whether it is skillful or not.
