Regarding the seventh proposition, which states that "the presence [of the reason] in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is the correct logical reason" (*saddhetu*), one might ask: if it is present in the similar class, why is it not a non-reason? The intended meaning of the answer is as follows:
what is excluded here is that which possesses the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of being a fault; since it is defined as being definitely present in the similar class, it lacks that fault.
As for the seventh and ninth propositions, because they are excluded by the third characteristic, there is no error. As stated in the *Nyāyamukha*: "As for the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*..."

Regarding "each has three": what are these? There is one [existence], there are two [existences and non-existences], and there are three [existences, non-existences, and both existence and non-existence]. Since there are three in the case of identity, it is likewise so for difference.
As for the phrase "down to nine categories," this single phrase explains that there are nine types within the established tenets (*siddhānta*).
Because there are nine reasons (*hetu*), there are nine propositions (*pakṣa*); this is known from the preceding line of the verse by analogy.

That is to say, in this system of reasoning, the nine propositions and the nine reasons are paired together, such that the first reason is paired with the general proposition, and so on, up to the ninth in sequence.
There is a version of the text that says, "The conclusion arises from nine reasons," but this is incorrect.

In the Vaiśeṣika system, if one establishes that internal sound is impermanent because it is produced by effort (*abhighāta*), there is no fault. However, if one establishes that all sound is produced by effort, then external sound would not be so.
Regarding the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) and the "two": as for the "similar instance," it refers to the second of the nine positions (*navavākya*) and the second [of the two].
This refers to the eighth category: "the second [type] is both existent and non-existent," as clarified in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the phrase "this contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*)," the intent is that among the nine categories, only this one is termed a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*) based on the specific characteristic of the property;
the other eight categories—such as those concerning the specific characteristics of the property, the specific characteristics of the locus (*dharmin*), and so forth—are not included here.
Because it is absent in the middle [category], it is said that [the reason] is not exhaustive.
Regarding the phrase "this has the fallacy of contradiction with what is established" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), I shall now provide an auxiliary explanation:

since this is stated as correct in the *Nyāyamukha*, how could it be a non-Buddhist position? Furthermore, if these nine propositions (*navapada*) belong to the stage of the non-Buddhists, how could they have been established by Dignāga himself? How could a non-Buddhist... [be so]?

Is this also admitted as being the same? If it is not admitted as the same, for what reason must it be said that the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are present within the nine propositions (*navapada*)?

If you say that because the opponent previously raised a challenge based on the nine propositions, [the author] now specifies [this], then even within that very formal argument (*pramāṇa*), it would not be the case that there are only "contradictory and indecisive" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) fallacies;

for within the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself, there are also faults such as the unestablished nature of the specific object of qualification (*svaviśeṣyāsiddha*). Therefore, one should know that the previous formal argument follows [the same logic].
The positions established by both internal and external schools are all flawed.
Regarding the statement that "because the three characteristics are not complete, the cognition of others is not resolved," one asks: which of the three characteristics is lacking? The answer is:

although the proponent claims to fully manifest the three characteristics, because doubt arises regarding all three characteristics from the perspective of the opponent, the three characteristics are deficient.
Furthermore, when the opponent's cognition arises regarding the three characteristics but is indecisive in all cases, it may also be termed "indecisive with respect to all three characteristics.

Moreover, there are two kinds of characteristics: first, the characteristic of the object (*artha*), and second, the characteristic of the cognition (*jñāna*). In the former case, the characteristic of the object is lacking; in the latter, the characteristic of the cognition is lacking.
Regarding the phrase "this reason constitutes contradictory characteristics (*viruddha-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth," this refers to the indeterminate (*anaikāntika*) reasons and others.
As for the "partial correct reasons (*saddhetu*)" in the third clause, this refers to the fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) of reasons;

because it excludes the second and eighth [clauses] and includes only the third, it is called a "small portion" of the third. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: this very third [clause] itself.

Question: Since the "over-qualified" reason (*adhika-hetu*) within the first category is also called a "partial reason" (*aṃśika-hetu*), why is it that this fourth category is also a partial correct reason (*samyag-hetu*), yet only the third is specifically mentioned as such? Answer:

Although the fourth category contains partial correct reasons, when we speak here of a "correct reason," we refer exclusively to the second category, the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) category. Therefore, the correct reason within the fourth category is not included.
This refers to the third characteristic of inclusion (*anvaya*).

Regarding the understanding that "the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) must be of the same category": this means that the similar instance must necessarily resemble the probandum (*sādhya*) in its essential nature;

it must resemble it point by point according to whether the property exists or not. However, while the probandum possesses an essential nature, the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is irrelevant to whether it possesses an essential nature or not.
That which differs from the established subject (*pakṣa*) is called the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

Here, one might ask: "Is it not the case that the category of 'indeterminate' (*aniyata*) is a third [category], since it is neither unwholesome (*akuśala*)—which would be the counter-example—nor wholesome (*kuśala*), which would be the similar example (*sapakṣa*)?
Because it is neither of these two categories, it is called the third. [The response: Suppose there were a third category.
Furthermore, what fault is there? The answer is: there is the fault that one dharma is neither identical nor different; that is, the third dharma becomes indeterminate (*anaikāntika*).

If, however, that fault does not exist—meaning that if the probandum (*sādhya*) simply does not exist, it is called the "absence in the dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*), and thus there is no fault in the middle category (*saṃdigdha*)—then [the reason] is established.

Furthermore, if [the reason] were distinct [from the thesis], such that there would be no definitive correct reason (*saddhetu*), this is the intended meaning of the critique against the ancient masters:

"If your reason is distinct from the thesis, it is then called a 'dissimilar instance' (*vipakṣa*); since the reason is also distinct from the thesis, it should therefore be a dissimilar instance. This is the sense of the critique regarding the thesis.
Because the property (*dharma*) is distinct, one knows that the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) is indeed the reason (*hetu*);

this is because it is the property belonging to the thesis. If it were distinct from the locus (*dharmin*), then the locus upon which the similar property (*sādharmya*) depends would necessarily be different. This refers to the dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*).

If "dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*) were defined merely as being distinct from the locus—such that sound is called the dissimilar class—then the locus upon which the similar property depends, namely jars, basins, and so forth, would be [the locus of] this [similar example].
The jar and the sound to be established are both unreal; they should be called "dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣa*) by virtue of their common property, which is impermanence in the jar.
This is precisely what is meant by "sharing sameness while containing difference."

If that which differs from the property of the subject (dharmin) were all to be called "identical" (sādharmya), this means that what is established as "similarity" (sādharmya-sama) is defined as such because the opponent does not accept it;

for they do not accept that the property to be established (sādhyadharma)—impermanence—exists within the property-possessor (dharmin), nor do they accept its existence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), such as space (ākāśa).
Since both [the proponent and the opponent] do not accept its existence in the property-possessor, it should be called "identical"; this constitutes the objection.
The difference is entirely the same.

This refers only to the "difference" because it clarifies that the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) cites only the permanent (*nitya*) and does not clarify the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); thus it is said, "knowing briefly that [the subject] is established as impermanent (*anitya*)."

According to the underlying principle, this is the same as the preceding case: where the reason exists within the similar instances (sapakṣa), the thesis (pakṣa) necessarily follows; whereas where the thesis is absent in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), the reason is not necessarily present.
Therefore, it is said that "according to the principle, it is the same as the preceding," which first clarifies the similarity of the similar instance (dṛṣṭānta).

Regarding the fact that there are no faults in either the "self-example" (*svadṛṣṭānta*) or the "other-example" (*paradṛṣṭānta*): because they are alike in being "produced" (*kṛtaka*), it is called the "self"; because the other example is not the same [in this respect], it is called the "other.

Although there may be no fault within the current statement, while the other statement contains a fault, what is being clarified here is precisely the "other-example" as being the same [in its logical function].
The "analogy" (dṛṣṭānta) is precisely what is called the "other" (para).

Therefore, as previously stated, when each part is individually analyzed, that which is free from fault in both its own statement and the statement of the other is called a "correct reason" (saddhetu);
all others are designated by names according to their respective faults.
The analogy that "the broad *sthāpanā* [probans] does not establish two categories" means this: since jars, basins, pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth are broad, they are termed "categories" (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) was originally intended to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*); thus, this reason is a property belonging to the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). Because one does not wish to establish an analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is said that the category must necessarily possess a nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "the same dharma, the fundamental establishment of the thesis-meaning," etc., this explains the anticipated objection (*vākchala*). An external objection states: "If the absence of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) allows for the establishment of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), then it should likewise be so [in other cases].
The answer is as can be clearly understood from the commentary (*śāstra*). A thorough examination [of this] should be undertaken.
The three preceding phrases constitute the thesis (pakṣa), the first [member], and the example (dṛṣṭānta) and reason (hetu), the second and third [members].
This means that although the words are not explicitly stated, they are nonetheless present within the three members; "not explicitly stated" refers to the mere absence of the three members.
The "three members" referred to here are precisely the one reason and the two examples.

Since the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*) are meanings rather than entities, the "reason" (*hetu*) and the two "examples" (*dṛṣṭānta*) constitute the two types of probans (*sādhana*). These two examples and the reason are called the "three members" (*trirūpa*).

If one were to take these two separately—meaning if one were to take them as distinct from the subject (*pakṣadharmin*) of the thesis—the reason would have to be equivalent [to the subject]. Therefore, following the present [text], we simply...
One should explain the difference between the thesis (*pakṣa*) and its counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) as appropriate.

Regarding the question: "What is the distinction between this one type consisting of two phrases and the fourth phrase among the four phrases, wherein it is said that 'in three cases there is an omission' and 'in all three cases there is no omission'?
The answer is: the third and fourth [phrases] are simply variations within the four-phrase structure; they exist in relation to one another.

Because their natures are distinct, the third phrase is identical to the four phrases when viewed in mutual relation; however, it differs when not viewed in relation to the four phrases, as it consists of two phrases.
Furthermore, the number of phrases can be understood by this method.

Regarding "non-deficient yet indeterminate" (*anaikāntika*): although the three members [of the syllogism] are complete, because the cognition of another is not produced, it is equivalent to a fallacious proof (*sādhyasama*); therefore, it is called "indeterminate. Question:
If there is a deficiency in the meaning (*artha*) but no deficiency in the substance (*bhāva*), why is this case considered "non-deficient yet indeterminate"?

Answer: In cases where there is a deficiency in substance, the substance itself is merely a non-existent entity. However, in the present case, since there is no deficiency in substance, both [the substance and the meaning] are non-deficient; thus, while they are non-deficient, this does not constitute a fault.

Since the substance of this question is not non-existent, it does not lack a name; yet, because there is a fault regarding the meaning upon the substance, both are termed "indeterminate" (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, regarding that which has a substance but lacks [the required features], there are two kinds: first, the three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) as the means of proof (*sādhana*); second, the reason...

Question: What is the distinction between "deficiency in the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "deficiency in the meaning" (*artha*) regarding the two types of examples used to establish a proof? Answer: Deficiency in the characteristics refers merely to the absence of the three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*).

Deficiency in the meaning refers to the absence of the three characteristics of the reason itself within the example; this constitutes the fallacy of the reason being either "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) or "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

Regarding the two types of examples—the similar (*sādharmya*) and the dissimilar (*vaidharmya*)—although their words may be stated, if they lack the essential meaning of the reason and so forth, the similar example constitutes the fallacy of "non-establishment of both" (*ubhayāsiddha*). The rest can be understood accordingly.

An example of lacking the first characteristic while possessing the latter two is as follows: when a Sāṃkhya teacher, in debate with a Vaiyākaraṇa, establishes that sound is impermanent by using "being visible to the eye" as the reason and "color" as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and "space" as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). This lacks the first characteristic and possesses the latter two;
thus, there is the fault that both [the latter two] are unestablished (*asiddha*).

An example of that which lacks the latter two [characteristics] but not the first characteristic is the Sāṃkhyas’ proof that sound is eternal, where they posit "being produced" as the reason (*hetu*) and use "space" as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), while using "pots and the like" as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). This commits the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svabhāvaviruddha*).

There are cases where the initial characteristic is missing, as well as both [the middle and final characteristics]; for example, when a master of phonetics (śābdika) posits sound as permanent, using "being seen by the eye" as the reason (*hetu*), "space" as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and "form" as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), this is also the fallacy of non-establishment (*asiddha*). The meaning of the case where none of the three are missing can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the "one type of two phrases," it refers to the three cases where all three are missing and the three cases where none are missing.
Regarding these cases where two [reasons] are combined up to three being combined: what constitutes a deficiency in the reason (*hetu*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*)?

These cases of combining two or three can be understood as follows. When there is a deficiency in two or even a deficiency in all three, this clarifies that the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are either deficient in two or deficient in all three;
accordingly, there will be faults such as the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth.

If there is one instance where the reason (*hetu*) is present, there are likewise three types of fourfold permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, regarding the initial fourfold permutation: "The reason is deficient, but the latter [the example] is not"—this refers to the case where the four members are not established.

"The latter two are deficient, but the first is not"—for example, when establishing that sound is eternal, using "lack of material resistance" as the reason, with a jar as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and space as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
In this case, the similar instance is unestablished in both respects, the dissimilar instance is unestablished in both respects, and all three are unestablished.

Regarding "absence" (*vyatireka*): as established in the Vaiśeṣika school, sound is the subject (*pakṣa*) characterized by impermanence; "being visible to the eye" is the logical reason (*hetu*); "space" (*ākāśa*) is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*);

and "color" (*rūpa*) is the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). In this case, all three are present and their textual characteristics are evident. The other two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the statement, "If the reason is present in only one [of the two] and is not excluded from both dissimilar instances," etc., the question is:

Why is it that among the cases where a few characteristics are deficient, the first is called *asiddha* (unestablished), while the latter two are called *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) and *viruddha* (contradictory)? Now, in this case, although a few characteristics are deficient, why are the latter two both called *asiddha* and not termed *anaikāntika*?
The answer is: Because the reason is the same as in the preceding cases, the deficiency of its characteristic of being a reason (*hetulakṣaṇa*) is established above; below, it is discarded.
When there is a thesis that has been established, one may infer from the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) that [the reason] is merely "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) or "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

However, if the example is missing, both [the similar and dissimilar examples] are absent; since it is only when neither is established that it is called a "missing example" (*udāharaṇābhāsa*), one speaks only of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and "not excluded by either" (*ubhayāvyāvṛtta*).
The statement that "one does not say there is a deficiency in the *sādhana* (the means of proof) when establishing a fault" explains the reason for positing a seventh category.

If one were to say that a *sādhana* must necessarily consist of the first two [the thesis and the reason] and that it is only in relation to those two that a deficiency in the *sādhana* is designated, then the seventh category could be dispensed with.
However, since the term "deficiency in the *sādhana*" applies generally to all three types of deficiencies, why would it not be a deficiency? Therefore, the seventh category is established.

The answer, "up to the exhaustion of those not included," intends to say that if the reason directly establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*), then if the first characteristic (*liṅga*) is present, it can successfully establish it;

if it is absent, it cannot. The meaning of the *Nyāyamukha* is that when it speaks of a reason directly establishing the thesis, it refers only to the five types within the category of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the four types of unestablished (*asiddha*) reasons lack the first characteristic and are therefore not mentioned.
Because the three characteristics [of a valid reason] are all lacking in the case of "contradiction with the conclusion" (*viruddha*), it is also not mentioned [here]. Question:

What is the difference between these five types of "indefinite" (*anaikāntika*) reasons—which fail to establish the thesis—and the four types of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reasons? Answer: This is explained as follows:

Because other characteristics are defective and do not conform to the establishment of the thesis, they are not treated as examples [of the unestablished], even though the first characteristic is not lost. In the case of the "inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa*) and "over-exclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*) reasons, the reason is established in relation to both the similar and dissimilar instances.

Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is remote, it indicates that the concordant and discordant [reasons] do not coexist, thereby manifesting that the concordant is the correct reason (*saddhetu*) and the discordant consists of the four types of fallacious reasons (*caturvidha-hetvābhāsa*).
As for these four types of fallacious reasons, the latter two are excluded because they involve logical faults (*doṣa*).

Since the "same" and "different" [reasons] establish the remoteness of the thesis, only their concordance and discordance are indicated. This remoteness exists because they serve as intervening causes (*vyavadhāna-hetu*).

Regarding the concordant [reasons], although there are many, they are briefly explained as two sets of eight; regarding the discordant [reasons], although there are four types of contradiction, they are briefly explained as one:
the contradiction of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon.

To say "each forms its own set" means that within each of the three aforementioned types, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on their respective characteristics; therefore, it is said "each."
The "self-as-a-phrase" (*svayam-pada*) and the three pairs of omissions refer to the mutual application of the three characteristics as phrases.

To take the first characteristic with its three phrases as an example: since the first characteristic necessarily lacks this [property], it is not a universal [reason] and thus fails to be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); therefore, there are only [the remaining cases].
Third: Regarding the statement "there is this property of the thesis (pakṣadharma) up to 'it is not necessarily existent by nature' (*na niyata-sattvādi*)," it is as follows:

when one establishes that "all sound is impermanent because it is produced by immediate effort," using a jar as the example of the reason, this reason—being produced by effort—is present within sound externally.
"Sound possesses [impermanence]"—this thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*) does not exist in the subject; furthermore, it exists in both [the subject and] the example, such as a jar.
To establish this is not correct, for it is not definitively present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). This is precisely what is called "partial non-establishment for both parties. Question:

Since the property to be established (impermanence) can indeed exist in a jar, how can you say it is not a similar class? Answer: The intention here refers to the first characteristic; it is a fault of the first proposition.
Regarding the first phrase of the second characteristic, although it appears later in the analogy, that established entity does not exist;

the remaining [phrases] are all to be understood accordingly. If one does not provide this explanation, the second phrase and so forth will already be established as objects of thought, which can be known by inference.
There are cases where the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) exists but is not necessarily present, reaching some but not all; these are the middle three of the nine positions (*navapada*).

In these three positions, the reason (*hetu*) exists within the subject (*dharmin*) but does not pervade it; this is the fault of the first position of the first characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), namely that the reason is not "present in all similar instances.

Furthermore, for example, when establishing the permanence of sound, using "space" as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is also this [middle] position; although it is called "similar" because it possesses the same property as the permanent thesis (*sādhya*), it is not pervasive.
Since the cause of what is seen by the eye has no name, it is not certain that this exists; this is the ninth fault.

It should be understood that the first phrase of the "non-existence of the property of the subject" (*dharmidharma-abhāva*) is [the basis for this], and the preceding first phrase should also be understood accordingly.

Regarding the thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*) that is not necessarily existent by nature— for example, if one were to establish that "all sounds are eternal" with the reason "because they are produced by effort" and the example "like space"—
it can be understood that there is a fault in the lack of a probans for what is to be established (*sādhyābhāva-asiddha-hetu*).

There are cases where something is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) yet is not non-pervasive (*avyāpin*); this may be a correct reason (*saddhetu*), as it exists in the subject, though it does not fulfill the first characteristic [of the definition of a reason].
Regarding the two types of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) established for the first characteristic, there is one that establishes what is not the first characteristic.
Regarding the four propositions for each of the other two characteristics, this refers to the four propositions of the latter two characteristics combined with the first characteristic;
alternatively, "each having four propositions" means that the three propositions of the first characteristic are each applied to the latter two characteristics to form four propositions.

To examine this further: for instance, establishing the impermanence of sound by using "being visible to the eye" as the reason (*hetu*) and "space" as the similar example (*sapakṣa*) is also an instance of this proposition.
The fallacies can also be understood; since the remaining categories can be explained by analogy with their respective counterparts, they are not set forth here.

First, regarding each being paired with the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*): this refers to taking the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) from among the three characteristics as the statement (*pada*). This constitutes the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), yet it is neither universal (*vyāpin*) nor otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "mutually following without reaching" (*anyonya-anugama-aprāpti*) as a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*): ancient scholars sometimes took the first member as the reason (*hetu*) and the second as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to form the permutations;

modern scholars, however, take only the three characteristics of the reason (*trirūpa-hetu*). As for those who have combined ancient and modern interpretations, there are many such exegeses. Ancient scholars might take the first [member] as the reason and the second as the example to form the permutations, while modern scholars take only the three characteristics of the reason.
Regarding the statement that although the three members [of a syllogism] are complete, it is called "contradictory indecisive" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), there are two interpretations:

first, the fault of the example is termed "contradictory indecisive" according to its respective application; second, when a counter-argument does not arise because the opponents do not mutually agree upon its formulation, this is also termed "contradictory."

There are forty-five types of tetralemmas (*catuṣkoṭi*) in total; forty of these can be understood [from the previous analysis], while the remaining five types consist of the initial presentation and explanation of the similar and dissimilar examples (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Within each of these, the two examples are mutually contrasted to form two sets of four lemmas each.

Furthermore, the aforementioned commentary states that by contrasting the three cases—such as "having an essence" (*savastuka*) and "lacking it" (*avastuka*)—three types of tetralemmas are clarified. When combined with the preceding [analysis], this results in forty-five types of tetralemmas. [...]
Regarding "one kind, two phrases," and so forth: these characteristics are all contained within these four explanations and can be seen by searching carefully.
As for "one kind, three phrases," this refers to the first characteristic mentioned above being paired with itself as a phrase; there are only three.
Since the first phrase alone constitutes the primary [characteristic], it is not included in the count of four, and thus there are only three.

Regarding the "one kind with two phrases," this refers to the cases where three of the [four] phrases are missing from among "essence is deficient" and so forth, or where all three are missing, as well as the case where none of the three are missing.
The Dharma Master said: "If one combines both 'having essence' and 'lacking essence,' there are ninety-four kinds of four-phrased sets;
now, to briefly assist in the explanation, if stated in full, there would be one hundred thirty-five kinds of four-phrased sets."
Since there are two types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), the three phrases and two phrases should also be understood accordingly as being increased [in number].

As for why the three characteristics are not questioned and explained at the beginning: this intention is to say that it is a combined statement asking why the first characteristic is not questioned and why the first characteristic is not explained.

Answer: Regarding the statement that the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) differ based on existence and non-existence, the intended meaning is that wherever the reason exists, it must be the same class as the thesis (*sapakṣa*), and where it does not exist, it is the different class (*vipakṣa*).

Therefore, concerning the uncertainty of whether the thesis and the reason are the same or different, the intended meaning is that the previous question did not address the initial characteristic; rather, the reason and the thesis are distinct.

First, there is no confusion regarding the first [category]; as for why the latter two are questioned, it is because they are indeterminate (*aniyata*). Since identity and difference are indeterminate based on a single [factor], they must be questioned separately.
Regarding the statement that the reason (*hetu*) is defined by its presence or absence in relation to the thesis (*pakṣa*), this clarifies the identity and difference of the thesis:

when the reason exists within the thesis, it is called "identity" (*samāna*); when the reason is absent from the thesis, it is called "difference" (*visama*). The reason is stated as either concordant (*anuloma*) or discordant (*pratiloma*) with respect to the establishment of the thesis.
Regarding "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*): this clarifies that the reason (*hetu*) possesses both sameness and difference.

Because there is a confusion between the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason regarding their shared and distinct characteristics, it is necessary to distinguish them from the first characteristic. Since the reason pertains solely to the property-possessor (*dharmin*), the term "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*) refers precisely to the property-possessor;
it does not mean that the reason itself is named the "property of the thesis. Furthermore, this reason is not [merely] the general [combination of] the thesis and its property.
This Dharma is merely the cause for the existence of dharmas; since the dharma is established within the dharma, there is no confusion, and thus it is not distinguished.

Regarding the statement, "Examining this question, because the two entities are mutually established and manifested," the intended meaning is as follows: in the question, one asks about the identity and difference of the entities;

in the answer, the characteristics of identity and difference are cited to manifest the establishment of the two analogies. There is also a version that reads: "Because they are mutually established and manifested. This is the answer.
Because these two are mutually established and manifested as metaphors, although this explanation has been offered, the reasoning is likely incorrect.

This is because, upon examining the subsequent answer-text, the body of the metaphor is first explicitly presented, and subsequently the phenomena (*dharma*) are specifically pointed out; therefore, one cannot say that they are mutually established in their essence or mutually manifested.
Alternatively, the character "以" (yǐ) may be a scribal error and should be "未" (wèi); for these two essences and characteristics have not yet been manifested.
Therefore, one must inquire and reflect upon this.

Regarding the second point—that it is necessary to provide an authoritative explanation—the intended meaning is as follows: because [the reason] depends upon the *dharmin* (the locus), this *dharmin* is also called the *pakṣa* (the thesis).
This is precisely what the preceding treatise meant when it stated that "the well-established *dharmin*" is a term used for the sake of specific distinction.

If that which is similar to the general thesis (*pakṣa*) being established is precisely the general thesis under dispute— the meaning of "all attributes" (*sarvārtha*) upon the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis—

then if there exists a collection of phenomena (*dharmas*) within that assembly, it is called a "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*). The intention is that if there is a single collection of phenomena [that shares the same properties as the subject], it is named a similar instance.
When the properties under dispute possess even a slight degree of similarity, they may be designated as "similar instances" (*sapakṣa*).

Because the property that serves to differentiate the subject (*pakṣa*)—which is the latter member of the proposition—distinguishes it from other propositions, the subject is termed the "differentiated subject.

The same applies to the "similar instance": when it shares the same thesis, one takes that which exists upon the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as the similar instance. As for the phrase "that which is the similar instance," it refers to the similar instance being the same as the thesis; one takes that which is absent from the example as [the dissimilar instance].
The essential nature [of sound] consists in its inseparability from impermanence; one does not separately apprehend the jar and impermanence.

If that [opponent] does not admit that sound possesses this property (dharma), then for that proponent of the thesis (*sādhana*), the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pakṣa*) would fail to establish a distinction, as the explanation [of the reason] would be rendered impossible.
In short, the meaning is that since he does not admit that sound possesses existence or non-existence...
I maintain that everything other than sound constitutes the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because there is neither a thesis (*sādhya*) nor a probans (*sādhana*) therein.

If one were to establish [the existence of] "existence" and so forth as being accepted by oneself but not accepted by the opponent, it would function as a reason (*hetu*) directed against that opponent.

Because it is established, it is also accepted as the "probandum" (*sādhya*). Apart from the word "accepted," all other instances where there is a selfless locus are considered "similar instances" (*sapakṣa*).
Although this is not explicitly expressed by the words, it is called the "probandum" because it is intended to be accepted; for this reason, there can be four types of contradiction (*viruddha*).
Regarding "contradiction with a qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*): it is like establishing that sound is impermanent and non-self;
here, "sound" itself constitutes the meaning of the qualification, and because it is specifically contested as the subject (*pakṣa*), it is called a "qualification of the subject."
Regarding the faults previously mentioned: since there are phenomena that do not resemble a jar, they should all be non-existent;

to raise a separate objection regarding the "similar class" (sapakṣa) in order to force it to be identical [to the subject] is like claiming that the hair of a tortoise—which lacks that [substance]—is also called impermanent. This contradicts the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), which is immovable and eternally abiding.

The nature [of existence] ought to be impermanent. If one were to claim it is permanent, then even the thesis that "existence is permanent" would fall into the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows:

if one establishes the thesis that "substantial existence is permanent," then because a tortoise's hair lacks substantial existence, it falls into the dissimilar class; however, if one establishes the thesis that "non-substantial existence is permanent," then because a tortoise's hair also lacks substantial existence, it falls into the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "if conditions such as the ear are stilled," first, the original tenets of the two masters are as follows: the Proponent of Origination (Utpatti-vādin) fundamentally holds that there is no manifest sound;

the Proponent of Manifestation (Abhivyakti-vādin) holds that sound exists inherently and, once produced from conditions, remains eternally without perishing. Thus, because the Proponent of Manifestation asserts that the nature of sound is inherently manifest through conditions, it is called "eternal.
When conditions cease and sound is not heard, both masters agree on this point; furthermore, for these two masters, sound does not [arise anew].

Question: Since the hearer only perceives the resonance (*pratiśrutkā*) and does not perceive the sound itself, and since the non-existence of the sound's essence is called "not hearing," what is it that serves as the condition for the resonance?
Answer: It is like a person standing beside a jar who strikes the jar; the resonance arises with the sound as its condition.

Because the resonant sound is tied to the person, the jar possesses the resonance. The internal sound is also like this. Both masters [Vasubandhu and Saṃghabhadra] clarify that the cause is exclusively the production and manifestation.
The binding produces the resonance, and this resonance can produce sound; when this resonance ceases, the sound is no longer heard, whereas if the resonance did not cease, the sound would be audible.

Regarding these two masters, both of whom hold that there is a partial [existence] of all internal and external distinct natures (*bhinnatva*), and so forth, within the arising of sound: [...there is... a middle state.
Regarding these two categories: the first maintains that both internal and external sounds are eternal; the second maintains that internal sounds are eternal while external sounds are impermanent.
This latter category further comprises two sub-types: the first maintains that internal sounds are eternal and their essence is a single unity, like the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Mahāyāna;

the second maintains that internal sounds are eternal but their essence is manifold, such that each individual phenomenon possesses its own distinct sound-essence, as in the case of [the Sāṃkhya] *sattva*.
The Vaibhāṣikas hold that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has multiple entities; thus, these two categories do not both maintain that sound is external.

One [category] holds that sound is impermanent, while the other holds that it is both one and many, as they both maintain that internal sound is both one and many. Among those who hold that sound is manifested (*vyañjaka*), there are likewise four categories;

one follows the position that sound is produced (*utpādaka*) with no distinction. In total, there are eight categories among these teachers who hold such views; therefore, both of these [positions] possess one part [of the truth].
Among these eight views, four are initially produced: first, the view that internal and external sounds are eternal and their substance is one;

second, the view that internal and external sounds are eternal and their substance is manifold; third, the view that internal sounds are eternal while external sounds are impermanent and their substance is one;
fourth, the view that internal sounds are eternal while external sounds are impermanent and their substance is manifold. Once these have arisen...

There are four categories that should be established as such, thus forming eight in total. Question: Regarding the application of the "produced" (*kṛtaka*) reason to sound, there is no dispute over its meaning;
however, when applying the "effortful" (*prayatnaja*) reason to sound to reveal the principle, there appears to be a contradiction. Furthermore, how can external sound possess effort? Answer:
Because it has already been established that all internal sounds are impermanent, one then uses these as the analogy to establish [the same for] external sounds. This should be examined carefully.
Regarding the reason "exertion" (*prayatna*) being unestablished for both parties due to the non-pervasiveness of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma-asiddhi*):

it is called "unestablished for both" because neither the opponent nor the proponent accepts that the external sound is produced by exertion, as they hold it to be impermanent. This constitutes the "partial non-establishment for both" (*ubhayāsiddha-ekadeśa*).

The commentator has omitted the specific identities of the proponent and opponent; however, since [the opponent] does not accept that the external sound is produced by exertion, the reason "exertion" is cited.

Regarding "establishing the same determinate [reason] while the remainder is non-pervasive": when one establishes the impermanence of sound by means of the cause of volitional effort (*prayatna-hetuka*), although it is determinate in its application, it is not pervasive;

for while there are jars as similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there are no lightning bolts. Because jars exist while lightning bolts do not, there is no pervasion. As for the term "the remainder is pervasive," it refers to the mutual pervasion between the initial and final [terms].

Regarding the statement "indeterminate refers to desire, resolve, and so forth": it is like a person who, though exerting diligence in matters such as planting crops, is said to be merely indeterminate;
other types [of volition] involve careful deliberation.
One should consider whether, according to our own school, that which is the Truth of the Path is subsumed under the untainted (anāsrava) Truth of the Path, and so on.

These four types of cognition and so forth examine whether a broad cause or a narrow cause is employed. Through the two causes of "action" (*kṛtaka*) and "volitional effort" (*prayatna*), the narrow thesis of impermanence is established;

likewise, the broad thesis of selflessness (*anātman*) is also established. However, if one employs only the broad cause of "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*), it establishes only the broad thesis of selflessness.

If one establishes the narrow thesis of impermanence by means of the narrow reason of "being produced," and then establishes the broad thesis of selflessness, one takes both the jar and empty space as the common example (*sapakṣa*).
Since the nature of existence is definitively established, even though there is no dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*), the reason is not subject to ambiguity;
thus it is said.
Preface to the Commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, Volume Upper (End) and Volume Middle.
Composed by Puyang Zhizhou.

Regarding "harmonious and correct exposition": when the two components of the proof—the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are in mutual conformity with the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), it is called "harmonious.
When the reason and the example are free from faults, it is called "correct exposition."

It is commonly agreed that "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is called the "property-possessor" (*dharmin*), while that which reaches the status of being "established" is called the "property" (*dharma*).

As for the "property to be established" (*sādhyadharma*), it is not the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself; therefore, it is termed "that which is to be established. In this context, the "produced nature" (*kṛtakatva*) serves as the property to be established. Question:

For what reason does the produced nature receive the name "that which is to be established"? Answer: This meaning of "being produced" is precisely the meaning constructed upon the sound [of the word]; thus, it is called "that which is to be established."

The "distinctions above" referred to in the name established here are the various properties such as suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and so forth, which reside upon the property-bearer (*dharmin*) that is sound.
Suffering is not non-self or emptiness; emptiness is not non-self or suffering; these are mutually distinct.
Now, the reason (*hetu*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) residing in sound is simply one among these distinct properties residing in sound.
Question: For what reason are the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth distinct? Regarding this question, there are three answers below. The meaning of the first answer is as follows:

The essential nature of the thesis in its totality is not a single phenomenon (*dharma*), nor is it the sameness or difference [of phenomena]. This [thesis], which is not a single phenomenon, receives the name "category" (*pakṣa*). The essence of the reason is a single [phenomenon] and thus receives the name "phenomenon" (*dharma*).

One interpretation holds that because the capacity and the object are distinct, the category is named by many phenomena while the phenomenon is named by a single phenomenon; this refers to the thesis.

That which is consistently termed a "dharma" (phenomenon) is so called because it serves as both cause and effect, and because it possesses the nature of being both the subject and the object. Since the cause is the metaphor (the means of illustration) and the dharma is the object (that which is illustrated), one should examine them closely.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the two—cause and thesis—are identical in their commonality and thus termed 'dharmas,'" a dharma is defined as that which produces understanding through its functional efficacy (*laksana*). When these two [cause and thesis] share this commonality, they are both designated as dharmas.
Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is able to produce understanding in others, it is called "Dharma" (*dharma*); this distinguishes it from what preceded.
Next, regarding the similarity and difference of the two subsequent reasons (*hetu*), they refer to the equal categories of meaning established by the proposition (*sādhya*).

Regarding the similarities and differences with the thesis (*pakṣa*) mentioned above: these refer to such criteria as "certainly existing in the similar class" (*sapakṣe sattvam eva*). The underlying intent is this: the reason (*hetu*) can be similar to or different from the thesis;

therefore, it is called a "property" (*dharma*). Because it was previously [discussed] only in relation to the thesis alone, it follows that within the aforementioned similarities and differences with the thesis, only the similarity or difference with the thesis is considered, while the similarity or difference with the reason is not.
This is precisely what is stated in the passage concerning the meaning of "equal classes" (*sādharmya-pakṣa*) in the aforementioned treatise.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent section on the "identity and difference" (sādharmya-vaidharmya) within the reasons (*hetu*), it is stated that among the reasons of identity and difference, only the reason of identity does not [apply to] the thesis of difference. The subsequent treatise says:
"The property of similarity (*sādharmya*) is, for example, like a jar; because the various individual identities and differences are narrow, they are called 'similar instances' (*sapakṣa*).

Now, within these two sentences of the treatise, both the thesis of identity and the thesis of difference, along with their respective reasons, are broad; therefore, they receive the name of "property" (*dharma*).

Regarding the phrase "the remaining text generally reveals," this refers to the general summary provided by this single recitation of the treatise, with the specific dharmas to be pointed out following later.
As for the passage "if there is a dharma or no dharma, it is as previously stated," this text states that one should generally say:
"whether in a locus of a dharma or in a locus of no dharma."
The phrase "the two combined are firm" refers to the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).

Regarding the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), there are three cases where it commits the fault of not excluding the probans: for the third, ninth, and second reasons, the probans is not excluded in part;
for the first and seventh reasons, it is not excluded at all. The question asks: in the fourth line of the section on clarifying the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it says "also the [probandum]..."?
Establishing non-existence is also based on the pervasion of non-existence; thus, it may also be termed "non-establishment in both similar instances" (*sapakṣa*).
Now, why is this "both" category not called the fault of "non-removal in both dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣa*)? The answer is:

in reality, there is indeed the fault of non-removal in both [dissimilar instances], but it is merely omitted as a shadowy abbreviation. Furthermore, if the fourth category of the dissimilar instance is compared with the similar instance, it constitutes non-establishment in both.

Within the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there are no further faults; however, regarding this question, the fourth alternative of the similar class—the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—not only includes cases where neither [the reason nor the probandum] is excluded, but also cases where the entire probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded. It is for this reason that only the non-exclusion of the probans is cited here.

Regarding the statement that "the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) also commits the fault of 'neither being established' (*ubhayāsiddha*)," this is not a fault of the reason (*hetu*), nor is it a fault among the nine types of reasons (*navavidha-hetu*).

This point specifically concerns the faults of the "pseudo-example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) within the section on examples. That the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is not established as the example constitutes the "unestablishedness of the probans" (*sādhanāsiddhi*) within the example;

that its existence is not certain constitutes the "unestablishedness of the probandum" (*sādhyāsiddhi*) within the example. For instance, [if one were to argue] that sound is eternal because it is unimpeded.
Because both the reason (*hetu*)—being a cause—and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—the jar—are absent in the case of that which is eternal and unimpeded, both are unestablished (*asiddha*).

As for the summary statement that combines and concludes [the argument]: simply stating "all produced things" already combines the reason; that they are all impermanent is called the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Thus, the combination of the reason and the conclusion establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*).
That which is "a dharma that possesses a probandum" (*dharmin*) is precisely the jar; this refers to the "probandum" (*dharma*) mentioned above. The *Śāstra-vārttika* states: "If it were so," etc.

This meaning follows from the preceding words and raises this objection: in the formulation of the proof, "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) constitute the probandum (*dharma*).
Since the probandum itself is the reason (*hetu*), one does not need to establish a separate external example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Based on this principle, there is the subsequent passage.

If that which comes to correspond is not of a different category, it should not be established separately from the reason (*hetu*); furthermore, the intention behind the difficulty regarding the meaning of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as being distinct from the reason is as follows.

If the three characteristics of the reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) subsume the two types of examples, and the two examples are identical to the reason, one asks: what is the distinction between the nature of the example and the nature of the reason?

Question: "The two properties—'being produced' (*kṛtaka*) and 'impermanence' (*anitya*)—serve as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); the two properties—'eternal' (*nitya*) and 'not being produced' (*akṛtaka*)—serve as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*);

and the single property 'being produced' serves as the nature of the logical reason (*hetu*). Therefore, the reason and the instance are distinct. Question: Since the essence of the instance consists solely of 'being produced,' and the similarity [of the instance] to the reason is precisely that it is 'produced,' the reason already subsumes the instance.
Now, since the instance also includes 'impermanence,' how can one single reason encompass two properties? Answer: "If one examines the reality [of the matter]..."

Regarding the nature of the treatise on the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): since the "subject" (*pakṣa*) necessarily entails the "probandum" (*sādhya*) along with its cause (*hetu*), and the illustration is spoken of as being concomitant with the "probandum" and "impermanence," it is already subsumed within the "reason" (*hetu*).

Thus, there should be only two members [of the syllogism]. Furthermore, what is called the "illustration" should simply be those two aspects of similarity and difference; why is it necessary to state them separately?
The formulation of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) consists of two aspects, which are called its members (*aṅga*).
Now, regarding the statement "the reason is established" up to "causing the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*) to be accomplished": one might ask, what was Dignāga’s original intention?

Since the two examples are already included within the reason and are not established separately from the reason, why does the treatise state that the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is like a jar, and the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is like [space]?
If emptiness were established apart from causes, it would contradict one’s own school’s treatises, for there are explicit texts [to that effect].

If, on the other hand, you establish an example external to the cause, it would be redundant with the ancient masters; how does this differ from them? Since both approaches involve contradictions, how can you evade them? Answer:

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is stated last, while the reason (*hetu*) functions only to clarify the meaning of the thesis by proceeding forward. It does not, however, further clarify what is "commonly existent" (*sādharmya*) or "differently non-existent" (*vaidharmya*). Since it does not clarify these...
That "the same exists while the different is absent" constitutes the meaning of this reason (*hetu*); it lacks the latter two characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Now, these two examples are cited solely to clarify the latter two characteristics of the reason, so that all three characteristics may be fully manifest and their meaning perfectly clear.

Since the examples are not established as entities separate from the reason, they do not differ from the ancient masters who established them separately for the sake of illustrating the characteristics. Thus, by this principle, there is no contradiction with our own school’s teachings.
There is no error of advancing or retreating.
As for the further objection raised by the opponent, that refers to a specific ancient interpretation of the *nyāyamukha* (Logic Gate).

If the meaning expressed is solely that which is signified by the words "reason" (*hetu*), then because the words signifying the reason are themselves what express it, they are taken as the expression of the signification.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the meaning of the reason that is expressed by the words [stating] the reason. The commentary immediately following states:

"For example, regarding the words 'that which is produced' (*kṛtaka'), the words themselves express the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva'), while the meaning expressed and indicated by those expressive words is the meaning of the reason."
The "expedient means" (upāya) mentioned refers to the two analogies of identity and difference.

Regarding the statement that there are five types of sensory consciousness (*pañcendriya-vijñāna*), the ancient masters cite this intent as follows: "For instance, the five sensory consciousnesses are common to both Buddhists and non-Buddhists;
how could their commonality constitute a fault? Since this is not a fault, even if my two analogies [were to share a similar flaw], it would not matter."
The meaning of the phrase "Furthermore, what fault is there in [the position] that [the effect] exists externally to the cause, which is similar to the non-Buddhists?

is as follows: Because they merely state that it reaches the point of being similar to the property of the subject (*dharmin*), they simply say that the jar possesses the characteristic of being produced (*kṛtaka*), but they do not state that all things produced possess both locations.
The *Sū* (Commentary) says: "It is not stated to be similar to the non-Buddhists; there is a fault in reaching [that conclusion]."
The meaning of the term "hence" (*guo*) is that it does not refer to the failure to state the well-established principle of the five sense-faculties and their consciousnesses as a fault;
rather, it refers to the fault of stating an example that lacks a logical reason (*hetu*) or a property that is not established (*asiddha*).
Regarding the statement, "To illustrate the matter by means of the basis of the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*), the basis of the analogy is itself the matter;

by pointing to this basis of the analogy to establish that sound is impermanent, one avoids the fallacy that everything would be of a similar nature," the meaning is as follows: when the reason (*hetu*) and the analogy are presented, it is said that "all things produced... [are impermanent].
Impermanence serves to distinguish [the subject] from the emptiness, absence of self, and so forth that exist upon sound; it cannot be categorized as being similar to those [properties].

If one were to cite the substance of a jar (*ghaṭa*) alone as the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), would one be citing the jar as a corroborative example because the emptiness, absence of self, and so forth existing upon the substance of the jar are similar to the emptiness, absence of self, and so forth existing upon sound?
That is to say, is it the emptiness, absence of self, and so forth that exist upon the very same substance [as the jar] that are being cited? Indeed, they are.
This type of fallacy does not exist here, nor is there the fallacy of "seeing the same as being burned," because the jar is not taken as the essential body (*svarūpa*) of the example.
It is not necessary for the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the meaning of the thesis (*sādhya*) to be identical;

rather, if—as I say—one holds that "whatever is produced is impermanent," then the fact that the produced nature and impermanence residing in the jar are concomitant with the sound clearly constitutes the essential body of the example, wherein the class-characteristic of being produced and being impermanent [is established].

If one were to claim that what is produced by sound is also impermanent, then if one cites only a jar as an example, the body [of the example] would lack the sense of being a "concordant class" (sajātīya).

Therefore, regarding the point that the analogy of the empty jar— which was not considered a valid reason— should also become a valid reason, this is the Master’s present critique of the ancient view.

In the ancient [tradition], only the pervasive nature (*vyāpti*) was taken as the reason (*hetu*), while the other two were merely pointed out as the essence (*svabhāva*). Since the reason is applied toward both [the similar and dissimilar instances], it should also establish the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, he concludes," this refers to the *Nyāyamukha* concluding that the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) serve solely to manifest the reason.

However, when only one part is provisionally designated as the "reason" (*hetu*), that one part is precisely the property of being present in the entirety of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); thus it is said to be "one part.

Furthermore, because it is definitively expressed by the word "only" (*eva*), the term "definitive" (*niyata*) indicates the three characteristics of the reason. The "reason" (*hetu*) refers to the name and the phrase.

The phrase "the sound of the words" refers to the reason (*hetu*). The four characters "only for the purpose of manifesting the reason" constitute the summary of the meaning of the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) within the section on the gate of reasoning (*yukti-mukha*);
here, they are explained again to clarify the intent of those four characters.

"What is the need for such protracted deliberation as to why we should alter the views of former masters? This statement means: what is the point of laboring over the meaning of "other" or "protracted"?
This argument seems erroneous and should be treated simply.
The phrase "because the dharmas are different" serves as a general heading for the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

"Because both are different" clarifies that the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) differs from the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). One should understand the meaning of the aforementioned "similarity" (*sādharmya*) solely by understanding this "difference.

[The passage] beginning with "There is an interpretation" up to "furthermore, he raises a difficulty himself" is indeed a question-and-answer section composed within Master Fashi’s own commentary (*śāstra*).

If it is argued that [the opponent's position] such as "sound is impermanent" is subject to this same critique, the phrase "if it were so" (yadi tarhi) applies to the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself; thus, this objection equally targets both the opponent and oneself.

Consequently, one should state that [the reason] "because it is not different" applies to the non-difference [of sound from its nature]; this equally asserts one's own position, while the opponent mistakenly takes the reason (*hetu*) as the primary point.

The "different school" (*anyatīrthika*) serves as an auxiliary, while the "different commentator" (*anyavyākhyātṛ*) correctly takes the "school" (*tīrtha*) as the primary [subject]; the "different reason" (*anyahetu*) is thus an auxiliary to the "different school. Now, examining the meaning of the text:
if it were so, then up to the point where the "school" follows, there would be no such passages as these. If one intends to challenge the commentator, one should examine that question:
why is it that what is established (*sādhya*) is not stated to be "universally non-existent"? This proponent’s statement says: "In this place, it is said that what is..."
When establishing [a thesis] such as "non-existence," why is it not stated that [the property] is "pervasive"? This can be understood from the following question.

Regarding the property (*dharma*) established in a thesis (*pakṣa*), its scope may be extremely broad; for example, when one establishes that "sound is impermanent," this sound possesses qualities such as suffering, emptiness, and selflessness—this is what constitutes its broadness.
If, regarding the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), one says it is "pervasive" or "pervasively non-existent," then there would be no dissimilar instance at all.

In this chapter, when [the opponent] posits "emptiness" and so forth as being different from this [subject], they are immediately refuted by the fact that there is no self; thus, it is said that there is no dissimilar example.

Now, when we speak of "difference," we mean only that [the subject] differs in one respect from impermanence—that is, it is something produced—rather than differing from all such qualities as emptiness, selflessness, and suffering.
Regarding the fault in the other [opponent's] positions, the fifth member [of the syllogism] is faulty because the similar example (*sapakṣa*) does not necessarily possess that nature;

thus, it fails to establish a valid reason (*hetu*). As for the term "other" (*para*), it refers to the similar example being "other" [than the subject], and since we are now precisely clarifying what is "different" (*anya*), it is called "other."
Regarding the fourth category, "partially correct" (*kiṃcit-samyak*): although it is not entirely correct, it is called "partial" because it is not fully correct. Why is it called "partial"?
For instance, when five [reasons] are unestablished (*asiddha*), two or eight are established, and only one remains unestablished, it is also called "partially correct.
Because it is not completely established, it is termed "partial."

To reverse this and establish that what is originally non-contentious emptiness is eternally abiding: if one takes "separation" (*li*) as the category for "contention," then while "emptiness" (*kong*) is above "contention," "eternally abiding" (*changzhu*) is not above "sound" (*sheng*).
That which is originally eternally abiding is precisely that which is "sparse" (*shu*) upon sound;
thus, emptiness and so forth—including *nirvāṇa*—are all equally eternal.
