The intended meaning is that since the fault of the subject's property being contradictory (*dharmasvarūpaviruddha*) already exists within [the opponent's] own argument, it cannot render the preceding inference of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only) indeterminate.
The phrase "at that time, for the sake of Śīla" refers to Dharma Master Cien’s commentary on the work of Dharma Master Jing.
If one must likewise proceed from autonomous inference (*svārthānumāna*) to the stage of opposition (*parārthānumāna*), this intention generally clarifies the method of establishing inference:

when opposing through common inference (*sādhāraṇānumāna*), one must employ common reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) to refute or establish a thesis; as for the case of another’s inference (*parārthānumāna*)...
The opponent uses the principles of another school to raise an objection against him; if he does the same for himself, [the following must be addressed]:

When stating that the reason depends upon a "thoroughly established" (*prasiddha*) subject, the word "thoroughly established" is used to exclude what is not so established. Now, regarding the color admitted by oneself, upon what does it depend?

Is this not a fallacy of the "one-part reason" (*ekadeśāśraya*), wherein the reason lacks a basis? Furthermore, if one employs a cognition that qualifies the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣaṇa-pramāṇa*), [upon what does it depend?]

If one were to establish [the thesis] together [with the opponent], it would not be "unestablished" (*asiddha*) because it relies on one's own school; yet, by using it to refute oneself, how could it possibly support the correct principle?
As for the response that the thesis is unestablished, this excludes cases where neither party accepts it. The intention of "admitted by oneself" is contained within the reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, even if another Buddha’s form-realm (*rūpadhātu*) depends upon that [other world-system], there is no contradiction, as it is admitted by oneself. Moreover, since it is only one part of the reason that is "self-accepted," there is no impediment.

Because, when examining the fault [in their position], there is no characteristic [of such a thing]; furthermore, one understands that the opponent’s original position does not establish the form of a Buddha in another world-system.
To speak of the form of a Buddha in another world-system is a transformation of consciousness, just like the category of "tortoise hair":

although it lacks a substantial entity, when one speaks of "tortoise hair," it is a transformation of consciousness that does not depart from consciousness. For one who establishes [a position] independently, this meaning of "not departing" is decisively established as being other [than consciousness].
If one does not establish the principle that [the object] is not separate from consciousness, it must necessarily be established as being like a tortoise’s hair and so forth.

If one follows the latter explanation, there would be no harm even in not employing the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*). Furthermore, it is difficult to conceive how Master Jing could have used the term "admitted by oneself";

his intention was to exclude the inference that contradicts the specific characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-viśeṣa*) within the Mahāyāna, for such an inference would contradict the Mahāyāna. This is because [the object] is truly existent and ultimate.
Visible form is not separate from visual consciousness because it is included within the first three [elements] of the eye-consciousness complex yet is not itself included by the eye.

Regarding this proof, the Hīnayāna schools raise an inconclusive objection (*anaikāntika*): "Is it the case that visible form is not separate from consciousness because it is included within the first three elements of the eye-consciousness complex yet is not contacted by the eye—just like the eye-consciousness itself?

Or is it the case that it is not separate from consciousness because it is included within the first three elements of the eye-consciousness complex yet is not contacted by the eye—just like the unwholesome visible form admitted by the Bodhisattvas themselves?"
Because it is not included [in the category of the object], one is free from eye-consciousness and form;
if one does not state "by one's own admission" (*svavacanena*), then one cannot take the unwholesome form of a Bodhisattva as an "undetermined" (*aniyata*) case. Now, we say this is not so.

In the method of logic (*hetuvidyā*), when establishing a position, one may employ the phrase "by one's own admission," but the opponent must necessarily refute that position based on the previously stated thesis (*pakṣa*). The unwholesome form of a Bodhisattva is not a [valid] great [thesis].

How could it be permissible to treat this as an inconclusive reason? Since we have not seen such a statement in the text, one cannot take one’s own interpretation and point out a fault within another’s formal argument (pramāṇa); for that would necessarily mean that all formal arguments would lack validity.

Furthermore, regarding the fallacy of being "only for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*): because the Mahāyāna does not accept that form (*rūpa*) is separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*), whereas the Hīnayāna itself accepts that form is separate from consciousness, this reason is "only for one party.

As for the reason applying to that form, it refers to the reason consisting of the inclusion within the first three [elements] as accepted by the Hīnayāna itself, applied to the form that is established through consensus (*prasiddha*).
Because [the opponent] asserts transformation, they speak of "commonality with matter" (*sādharmya-rūpa*);

however, this is not accepted by the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, regarding the example of similarity (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is also the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāsiddha*). This is because the Mahāyāna does not accept that the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is necessarily distinct from consciousness;
thus, as an example of similarity, it lacks the probandum.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "in the case of a cognition of an accomplished object (*niṣpanna-vastu-jñāna*), there is a fixed characteristic of separation," the intended meaning of this teaching is to demonstrate that the sense faculty (*indriya*) and its corresponding consciousness (*vijñāna*) are not separated from one another.

This is because the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object can, in turn, take that very faculty as its objective support; thus, the perceiving consciousness and the perceived faculty are not fixedly separated.

When one speaks of a "remote objective condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*), it is intended to distinguish it from the "proximate objective condition" (*sannikṛṣṭa-ālambana*); that is to say, it refers to that which is not separate from consciousness.

One cannot say that there is no fixed [relationship], yet claim that there is a fixed state of separation; for if the meaning were that the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is distantly separated from the cognizing consciousness (*vijñāna*), how could there be a fixed state of separation?
(Alternatively, if the original text contains the character "況" [kàng] instead of "定" [dìng], both versions are acceptable.

What is called the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done) is that which, after the attainment of Buddhahood, these very five consciousnesses turn back to take the eye-faculty as their object, thereby illuminating and manifesting it.

Because it is able to discern all matters within the five sensory realms of the entire world such that nothing remains uncomprehended, it is called the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Regarding the term "proponent's own admission" (*svavacana*), this refers to the statements of the three preceding [scriptural] collections (*piṭaka*); as for the term "admission by the opponent," this refers to...
Dharma Master Jing’s argument is based on inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the thesis that "the true nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is empty": the reason is that they are dependently originated;
the example is that they are like illusions. Regarding the thesis that "the true nature of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) is not truly existent": the reason is that it does not arise.
The concordant example is said to be like a flower in the sky.
If that which relies on the teaching is called "one's own words" (*svavacana*), then one's own words are identical to one's own teaching.
If that which relies on the teaching is called "one's own words," this should give rise to the four subsequent propositions. There may be two sets of four propositions based on the teaching.

Therefore, it is clear that their claim that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) must not be without reality contradicts their own words; for the Lokāyatas themselves reckon the four great elements to be real, yet now they say they are not real.
Thus, they violate their own speech.
This refers to those who contradict the teachings; because the number of their propositions is no different from that [of the Sāṃkhya], they are included therein.
Furthermore, "those who compose it" refers to the proponents of the Sāṃkhya school; "it" refers to that treatise itself.

That which is about to become the "Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth is also called *pradhāna* (the Primal Nature); when it has not yet transformed into the twenty-three principles (*tattva*), it is merely named *svabhāva* (Self-Nature).
When it is about to transform, it is then named the "Great One" and so forth.

Regarding the eleven faculties: the five faculties such as the eye are the five cognitive faculties (*buddhindriya*), while the five functional faculties (*karmendriya*) are the [organs for] excreting urine and feces, and so on.
These are the skin-faculties of the hands and feet; the faculty of mental equanimity is the eleventh.

"Great" (*mahat*) refers to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as it gradually increases; this is called the Great One (*mahat*). As for the ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*), it perceives that which belongs to the spiritual self (*puruṣa*).
All objects are brought forth by means of this ego-grasping, which causes the primordial nature to transform and arise. Apart from the essence of the spiritual self, there exists something distinct.

Because the ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*) and the *puruṣa* act as the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*), it is said that they grasp the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which are the five objects of the senses (*viṣaya*).

How can these be considered both the source and subject to transformation? Because the Great Principle (*mahat*) is capable of producing the objects of the senses through successive transformations, it is both the source and that which undergoes transformation.
Each of the *sattvas* and so forth possesses three qualities: yellow corresponds to greed, joy, and pleasure; red to hatred, anger, and suffering; and black to delusion and equanimity.
As for "the darkness of dullness," this refers to dullness itself and not to the light of clarity.

Regarding the "intermediate" [category]: the first is *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and the last is the *puruṣa* (spiritual self); all others are collectively termed "intermediate. As for the statement that their "function may exist or not exist":
it is because when these very *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* exercise their function, they are able to transform into the twenty-three principles (*tattva*), at which time they exist;
and when they do not transform, they do not exist. Therefore, it is said that their function may exist or not exist.
The *Saptati* (Seventy Verses) on Gold was composed by a follower of the Sāṃkhya school.

After this disciple had completed his studies in the Sāṃkhya system, he traveled to other countries carrying a fire-bowl upon his head and wearing an iron-plate garment; with a protruding belly, he sought out debates.

When he engaged in debate according to the [Sāṃkhya] treatises, he spoke of the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as being inverted. Consequently, the king of that country and all the non-Buddhists fell into ruin.
Having gained victory through this, he composed seventy verses; the King bestowed gold upon him, and because of this, he took it as his own title.
That which has no separate basis is called "inseparable nature" (*avinirbhāga*). When the general [characteristic] is not established, it is called the *anāśraya-śāstra* (treatise without a basis).

When the particularized [object] is not established, it reaches the point of explaining the self (*ātman*) as being the thinker (*cetanā*). Question: In all methods of logic (*hetuvidyā*), do the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) not both...?

Regarding the present analysis: the term "self" (*ātman*) applies to both the ultimate and the conventional. Since even the Buddha’s teachings admit the existence of a conventional self, how could it be that the "object to be distinguished" (*viśeṣya*) is unestablished?
In response to the opponent: When one speaks of the "self," if it refers to the actual self, then if it were merely a conventional self, it would simply be a designation (*saṃjñā*).

Therefore, by employing the term "self," one knows it refers to the ultimate self; thus, the "object to be distinguished" is established. This also applies to [the term] "space" (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

According to this principle, if one were to employ concise language, there would be no fault. [Objection: Since it is stated below that "there is a nature" (*svabhāva*), why is this not a case of the "unestablished nature of the qualificand" (*viśeṣyāsiddha*)?

[Response: Although "identity" (*tādātmya*) and "difference" (*anyatva*) are distinct, both are substantially existent (*dravyasat*). Therefore, when the word "existence" (*sattā*) is used, there is no fault of lacking a qualificand; this is not the same as my position. [Objection:
If that is so, it is still untenable, because although identity and difference are distinct, the word "existence" is common to both. Thus, the [qualificand] remains unestablished.

Although the "separate attainment" (prāpti) differs in being either provisional or real, because the term "self" (ātman) is used identically for both, the object qualified [by that term] should likewise be established as such. To this, the response briefly indicates: according to the actual nature of phenomena, all instances should be expressed with the word "is";
however, this word has been omitted for the sake of brevity—one should reflect upon this.
Question: If it is argued that the "self" (*ātman*) cannot be established as that which is distinguished by volition (*cetanā*), the intent of this question is as follows:

In the Mahāyāna, the substantial entity of a self is not posited; since the entity of a self is non-existent, if one were to negate it by saying "the self is not the self," the "self" presented as the subject (*pūrvapakṣa*) would fail to be established, resulting in the fallacy of the non-establishment of that which is to be distinguished. Such is the meaning of the question. Below, in the response, if there is something to be distinguished...
If one refutes another by saying, "Your position that the self is non-self" and thus distinguishes between them, there is no such fault.

How can it be established that the "self" and so forth exist? The intention is to inquire: how can the non-Buddhists establish that the essence of the self exists, or how can they establish it as an existent phenomenon (*dharma*)? Consider this carefully.
Whatever expressive speech there is must have that which it refers to; this is the case with the statement "I am non-self. The opponent refutes this, saying:

"If you maintain that 'I' must be non-self, then this very non-self is the principle being referred to. If the expression were not qualified by the word [non-self], there would be the fault of failing to establish a distinct referent."

If it were not so, it would result in [the fallacy of] "becoming established" (*prasajyate*). If one does not make a distinction, it results in the fault of the previously distinguished [position] being unestablished (*asiddha*).

There is a version where the character "becoming established" (*chéng*) is written as "contradiction" (*wéi*); if that were the case, it would result in the fault of contradicting [the intended meaning].

Regarding the phrase "because [the reason] exists within the particular (viśeṣya) among the two aforementioned fallacies": this refers to the fact that in the previously stated thesis (*pakṣa*), the established subject (*dharmin*) and the established predicate (*dharma*) are presented in their respective order;
thus, the subject is taken as the first. As for why it receives the name of a "fallacy," this is said in terms of its being unestablished (*aprasiddha*);
it is also called a "non-establishment of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*). The meaning of this is that even if the subject itself is unestablished, it may likewise be so designated.
Regarding the term "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*): it is not established here because it is contrasted with the subsequent member [the predicate];
rather, it is called "unestablished particular" (*viśeṣyāsiddha*). It cannot be designated by the name "unestablished basis. The same applies to the subsequent member:

when it is contrasted with the preceding member [the subject], it is called "unestablished qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), and cannot be designated by the name "unestablished substratum" (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Regarding the phrase "the first fault is called 'unestablished basis' because there exists a distinct qualifier": the "first fault" refers to the fault pertaining to the *dharmin* (the subject), as it occurs at the beginning of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
This fault of the *dharmin* may also be termed "unestablished basis. It is called "existent" because there exists a distinct qualifier that is not itself a fault;
thus, the absence of a fault in the qualifier is designated as "existence. One must examine this carefully.

The first fault is also called "the inability to establish the existence of another based on itself," because that which possesses the fault is incapable of relying upon another to establish its own existence;
this precisely indicates the nature of the fault, as may be understood from the subsequent passages. A careful examination [is required].
"Commonality" (sāmānya) refers to both identity and difference; because it consists of this identity and difference, it is called "commonality.

"Generality and particularity" (sāmānyaviśeṣa) means that among the three categories of substance, quality, and action, each does not overlap with the others, which is termed "generality and particularity.

"Identity" (sāmānya) refers to the fact that within the twenty-four qualities and the actions, there are five [qualities] and nine [substances] respectively, each having its own distinct name, which constitutes their common identity. "Particular identity" (viśeṣasāmānya) refers to the twenty-four qualities.

Regarding the identity and difference between the name "quality" (guṇa) and the name "quality": within the qualities and within the stages (bhūmi), if one takes any single quality, its atoms (paramāṇu) are each distinct;
furthermore, because there are also atoms within water, they are called "different."

That which has "the arising of wisdom" as its characteristic refers to the essential characteristic common to both the two characteristics and the eight characteristics. "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) means discernment (*prajñā*).
It is by way of conjunction that wisdom arises;

that is, it is through the nature of conjunction that wisdom is attained. If it were otherwise, it would not be possible. This meaning explains that [wisdom] is the conjunction and the awakening to conjunction.

When dharmas such as pleasure unite with the self, by what means is that conjunction achieved? It is through the self acting as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) that conjunction first becomes possible;
only then can qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth unite with the self. If the self did not act as the cause, cognition and the rest would ultimately never be able to conjoin.
Question: By what cause, then, does this self itself come into existence? Answer: It exists through the conjunction of cognition and the other factors.

When combined they arise, just as in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) where the Great Producer (mahājāti) produces the Small, and the Small produces the Small; and the Small again produces the Great Producer, such that they necessarily transform and produce one another—this is also like that.

If it were spoken of in a general sense, saying that phenomena arise through the combination of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*), then even in the Buddha-dharma there would be a combination according to the Mahāyāna that would not be subsumed [by the opponent's position]. Since I am now speaking of "I" (*ātman*) as the cause of combination, both faults are established.
That which is the causal condition for their conjunction is none other than myself.

Of these eight statements, this single phrase alone is the aforementioned partial statement; while the preceding seven among these eight statements both involve the distinction between subject and object and thus fall under the fault of being partial, this eighth statement—being half-true and half-false—is likewise subsumed under the category of partial faults, and is therefore identical to the aforementioned.

The "partial" clause refers to the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). As for the "entirely non-existent" clause, it refers to the "both" clause within the aforementioned qualifier, wherein both the self and the other—the qualifier—are unestablished.
"All are this fault" means that, excluding the eighth clause, the remaining seven all share the fault of being unestablished in the third sense (*aprasiddha*). This is certain.

"By this" means that because there are faults regarding the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and their co-presence (*ubhaya-asiddhi*) as mentioned above, these same faults should also apply here.

These include the faults of being unestablished for oneself (*svataḥ-asiddha*), for the other (*parataḥ-asiddha*), for both, or partially; as well as the fault of doubt (*saṃśaya*). Regarding "the four great elements" (*mahābhūta*):

this is the subject (*dharmin*), which the Vaiśeṣikas themselves accept as being included within the category of substance (*dravya-pada*), yet the Mahāyāna does not accept it as such; this is the distinction.

Regarding the claim that "it can transform color and so forth," the Sāṃkhya school only admits that the mind’s *sāmānya-vijñāna* (universal consciousness) can transform color, whereas the Mahāyāna does not admit this;

and the Mahāyāna admits the *ālaya-vijñāna*, whereas the Sāṃkhya does not. Because they do not mutually admit these [positions], it is called "mutual non-establishment of the particular" (*ubhaya-āsiddha-viśeṣya*) and "mutual non-establishment of the qualifier" (*ubhaya-āsiddha-viśeṣaṇa*). The subsequent search for the meaning will be clear.

When both [the opponent's position and one's own] are inconsistent, this constitutes the fault of "non-establishment of both" (*ubhayāsiddha*). Since the Sāṃkhya school itself does not admit that karma exists as a distinct entity, and Buddhism likewise does not admit that it has a separate substantial nature, these are all instances of this same fault;
that is, the fault of "conformity" (*samāna-doṣa*).

Alternatively, for those who contemplate according to principle up to the point of the True School (Shingon), this meaning is explained as follows: the fundamental intention of establishing a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is to oppose the opponent and conform to oneself;
thus, when it accords with one's own tenet, it is not a fault. Conversely, that which does not accord with one's own [tenet] is entirely considered a fault.

This is why the word "or" is used, and the rest should be understood by analogy. Furthermore, it is explained that when establishing a thesis through formal inference, it must be mutually accepted; if it only conforms...
If one does not distinguish [the object] from itself, it results in faults such as the unestablished nature of the "other" (*parakīya*) and so forth; therefore, the word "or" (*vā*) is employed.

As for the statement that there is contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), since all objects of a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) are objects of direct perception, and while the various forms (*rūpa*) of the sense-bases of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) are [usually] perceived, the claim that a concentrated mind cannot perceive them now constitutes a contradiction with direct and inferential cognition. To establish this, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is set forth: [The sense-base of tangibles...].

Because all states of meditative concentration on form (rūpa-dhyāna) are subsumed under one or another of the five sense objects, it follows that [the claim] that color, fragrance, and so forth are contradictory to inference is refuted by direct perception. Furthermore,

there are cases where something contradicts direct perception yet is not non-learned or worldly, such as when the Vaiśeṣika masters establish the "five categories" (pañca-padārtha) in opposition to the Buddha's Dharma.

The meaning is not that I have personally attained [this realization], nor is it as the Mahāyāna claims—that color is not an object of the eye and so forth—but rather that it merely contradicts one's own direct perception while not contradicting the "hare-in-the-moon" [convention].

Regarding those who contradict direct perception, the "ultimates" (*paramāṇu*), and the "simultaneous" [causality], where the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*) cannot be established: for instance, how does the Vaiśeṣika school contradict its own direct perception?

If [you argue that] identity, difference, and so forth are not apprehended by the five sense faculties, does this mean that the Buddha’s Dharma does not allow for the existence of the five sense faculties?
If you say that it does not rely on the Vaiśeṣika system but contradicts your own doctrine, what is the characteristic of the "other" (anya) in your formulation? The answer is:

it contradicts one's own perception, the cognition of others, and the specific [characteristic], and so forth; this is possible, as it corresponds to the second of the four propositions that contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa-viruddha*).

The method of argumentation is as follows: In contrast to the Buddhist teachings, the Vaiśeṣika school asserts that phenomena such as cognition (*buddhi*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are not objects manifest to the self (*ātman*).

They maintain that cognition, pleasure, and so forth are indeed objects manifest to the self. Now, to claim otherwise would contradict their own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the Buddhist teachings do not admit a self.

Moreover, the character "other" (*tā*) in the phrase "the fault of being distinguished by another" (*tānyena bhedadoṣa*) should have been "he" (*ta*); the current commentary has corrected this to the character "he" (*ta*) in its explanation.
If a property contradicts what is commonly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) and must necessarily be established as distinct, it is like establishing that sound is not audible;
this is indeed an establishment because both the proponent and the opponent agree that sound exists.

For example, if one contradicts what is manifest to oneself such that it cannot be established for both oneself and others— just as when the Vaiśeṣika school posits the five categories of the self (*ātman*) against the Buddhist Dharma,

and the self is not something manifest to them; this is a contradiction with what is manifest to oneself for the Vaiśeṣika, and because the Buddhist Dharma does not accept it, it is "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*).

For example, if one contradicts what is manifest to oneself while conforming to the meaning accepted by others—such as when one perceives that pleasure is not the object of the self—that contradicts what is manifest to oneself;

yet if it conforms to the tenets of others which the Buddha’s teachings do not permit, this is indeed a case of conformity to others. There are also cases where both [the proponent's and the opponent's positions] are unestablished (*ubhayāsiddha*) and yet conform to each other; for instance, when the Buddhist school posits against the Sāṃkhya school that the self (*ātman*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) truly exist.
This is because it contradicts the tenets of others and lacks [proof] within one's own school; thus, this is a fault.

Regarding the "method of proof" (*vidhi*) among these nine faults, the methods of proof employed by the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Sarvāstivāda, Sautrāntika, and various Mahāyāna schools can be understood by reflecting upon their respective philosophical positions.
Regarding the seven [types of] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) combined with three sets of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*): the first alternative is admitted as being in agreement;

the second alternative excludes that which is not established for both parties, taking only that which is in agreement; the third alternative excludes inference (*anumāna*), as inference is the primary subject of the first set of four alternatives.

Thus, these eight combinations conclude the aforementioned rationale. As for the four sets of four alternatives, they take the seven types of direct perception combined with the three sets of four alternatives.
Taking the statement and inference as the primary [categories], each of the four-line sets constitutes four groups of four lines.

Regarding the four types of contradictions with worldly convention, first, the contradiction with inference is as follows: one might claim that there must be a rabbit in the moon because it possesses a Buddha, just like a doe when she is pregnant;
this is because non-Buddhist teachings themselves state that the moon has a rabbit, which is a contradiction of one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*). This is easily understood.
To claim that performing an inference for others (parārthānumāna) in all such cases is not a fault is as stated in the treatise:

when one employs an inference that contradicts the teachings of another—such as the doctrine that sound is subject to destruction—it is an instance of contradicting another while conforming to oneself; therefore, faults such as "contradicting the teachings of another" do not apply. The rest may be understood through reflection.

Furthermore, regarding what is not the word of another: this constitutes a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) in itself and does not involve admitting the faults of another, nor is it an inference based on another's speech.
As for the statement, "The remaining seven pairs up to the four-line [tetralemma] are also like this," it means that by taking the first line as the subject and comparing it with the eight lines,
one performs eight sets of four-line tetralemmas; then, excluding the first line, one takes the second line as the subject and compares it with the eight lines, and so on, until...

The application of the eighth proposition to the eight phrases is likewise; its application to other [propositions] is also thus. Regarding "phrases" and "non-phrases," that which is faultless is called a phrase, while that which possesses faults is called a non-phrase.

As for designating the proofs and cognitions of the proponent and opponent as "gates," this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound, referring to the gates of their respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Next...
The phrase "the lower [category] is the gate of identity of self-characteristics" (*sva-lakṣaṇa-samānādhikaraṇya*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
If it were not a meaning that ought to be established in the current debate, this intention would clarify that what "ought to be" follows one's own inclination;
that is, it can only be established once the opponent has previously failed to understand it. If one has already granted it, even if it were one's own position...
To commit the fault of "concordance with another" (*parasaṃmata*) is precisely to establish what is concordant for the other.
If one does not state the meaning accepted by oneself when formulating a formal argument (*pramāṇa*), and instead establishes the position of the other, this is indeed concordance with another.
Regarding the exclusion of the "concordant" (*samāna*) fallacy from among the remaining eight faults: simply stating that it prevents others from understanding encompasses all eight faults.
To establish a thesis (*pakṣa*) is to cause others to produce understanding; thus, it is called a "true thesis. If another does not understand, it is not subsumed under a true thesis;
therefore, it is said to "encompass the eight. Since the concordant fallacy has already been granted by the other party, it must be excluded.

Regarding "it should be known by analogy with the reason": since there is already a reason that causes doubt within the reason (*hetu*), it also causes a thesis that is subject to doubt within the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Therefore, by saying "by analogy," one understands that the previously mentioned [reason] which causes another to comprehend includes the thesis that is subject to doubt. Here, however, only the thesis is included, not the proof (*sādhana*).

Regarding the phrase "the fifth category is partially absent herein": in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the fifth category consists of three parts—causing another to understand, lacking a proof (*sādhana*), and having a thesis (*pakṣa*) that is subject to doubt. All three of these are subsumed under the fifth category of that treatise.
However, because this [present work] subsumes only the thesis and does not subsume the proof, it is said that the fifth category is absent herein.
If that which is established as the probandum is identical to or different from the thesis (*pakṣa*), this is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
It has no distinct superior function [to differentiate it] from what is termed "unestablished" (*asiddha*). There are some texts that state the name "unestablished thesis," but this is incorrect;
because it lacks a superior function, it cannot receive other names and is thus merely designated by the term "unestablished."

If [it is argued that] "the reason is unestablished for oneself" (*svataḥ-asiddha*) refers only to cases where someone accepts a reason as unestablished for themselves and thus calls it an "unestablished reason," we shall now refute this;
the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) accepts it in its broader sense.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the text, "The meaning of 'unestablished' and so forth is explained," this refers to the four types of unestablished reasons (*caturvidhāsiddha*) discussed in this treatise, all of which are defined in relation to the [opponent's] lack of acceptance.
That which is capable of establishing a thesis is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
The two cases where both [proponent and opponent] lack a reason, up to the case where there is no basis, correspond respectively to the four types of unestablished reasons.

A reason that lacks an entity (*avastuka*) based on a subject (*dharmin*) that lacks an entity refers to the refutation of the category of "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), stating: "Great Existence exists."
Because that which is established as non-existent is subsumed under one of the six [categories], it is like the preceding five propositions; that is, it is a non-entity.

Regarding the reason for being a non-entity based on an entity or a factual phenomenon: the sound is an entity, and "being devoid of self" is the property to be proven (the predicate). The reason is "because of being an object of cognition.
This is what is meant.

Question: There is also a commentary by the Master Fǎguǐ which states: "As for the 'nature of being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) mentioned in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, it is explained in accordance with that [other] commentary.

This [position] incurs the fallacy of "one or the other" (*anyatara-āpatti*) when compared to other schools, because by not employing the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*svābhyupagama*), one fails to exclude the positions of others; thus, the fallacy of "one or the other" arises.
The first error:
The *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* and other treatises were spoken by Śrāvaka Arhats of the Hīnayāna. The term "and others" includes other Hīnayāna treatises. Question:

Furthermore, do you admit that Mahāyāna sūtras exist within the Hīnayāna? If you admit they exist, then establishing them [as non-existent] now would constitute the fault of contradicting what is accepted (*abhyupagama-virodha*).

If it is universally established [as a tenet], yet you do not allow for its inclusion within the thesis (*pakṣa*) without qualification, would this not constitute the fallacy of the unestablished subject (*āśrayāsiddha*)? Answer:
Although the opponent accepts that there is a Mahāyāna, they do not accept it as being the word of the Buddha; therefore, there is no harm in establishing it here.

The establishment of a single *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition) over forty years refers to the fact that it was only after the masters such as Saṃghabhadra had worked on this single *pramāṇa* for forty years that it was finally completed.
*Āgama* is a Sanskrit term; it means "instruction" or alternatively, "transmission."
Regarding the statement that "the Sarvāstivādins themselves claim these were spoken by the Buddha," the meaning is this: within the Sarvāstivāda school there are two positions.

Those who accept [these texts] as being spoken by the Buddha can be understood accordingly. However, those who do not accept them as being spoken by the Buddha hold that when Kātyāyanīputra composed the treatise, he cited what appeared to be the Buddha’s words to establish his principles;
in reality, they were originally not spoken by the Buddha.

Furthermore, among those of other Hīnayāna schools who accept that the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* was spoken by the Buddha, it should be understood that for those who do not accept it as the Buddha’s word,
the name "Prakaraṇapāda" is applied to what is otherwise known as the *Jñānaprasthāna*.

Regarding the point that "the Mahāyāna is not included among those things not accepted as the word of the Buddha," the meaning is this: the Mahāyāna accepts that the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* is not included among those things accepted as the word of the Buddha, yet the Hīnayāna itself does not accept it;
conversely, the Hīnayāna accepts that the Mahāyāna is not included among those things accepted as the word of the Buddha, yet the Mahāyāna itself does not accept it.
Because they do not mutually accept one another's positions, it cannot be established as a definitive consensus that [the Mahāyāna] is not the word of the Buddha.

To summarize the current point: both parties agree that it is merely a property (*dharma*) residing upon the cause of pleasure. As for what this [cause] is, it refers to all the treatises of the six *pādas* within the non-Buddhist (Hīnayāna) teachings.
When one asks, "Does your Mahāyāna accept that these were spoken by the Buddha?"—this is precisely the intended meaning; it is not a case of a single opponent’s unique consensus.
"Since the Buddha’s words are not included [in your definition], do you perhaps accept that the Mahāyāna was spoken by the Buddha? Furthermore, he presses him again:
"And who accepts that the Mahāyāna is not the word of the Buddha and thus not included? This intention is now for the sake of not distinguishing within the reason (*hetu*).

If one says that both the proponent and the opponent agree, then one can exclude a portion of the Śrāvakas who do not accept that the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* was spoken by the Buddha, as well as the various outsiders."
The "path" (mārga) here consists of two types when contrasted with the Śrāvaka-vehicle and the non-Buddhists (tīrthika); this is why the treatise states it briefly as "both.
If one were to say merely "both," then when contrasting the Śrāvaka-vehicle and the non-Buddhists, the Mahāyāna teaching would be admitted by them not to be included within the Buddha's word;
this would constitute the fault of "following the other" (parānuvāda), because while the Mahāyāna admits it for itself, the other party does not admit it.
If the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* were also included within the [Mahāyāna] tenet system, it would contradict the Mahāyāna’s own scripture.
Regarding the phrase "one part is unestablished for both," "one part" refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna* in relation to the Mahāyāna;
"unestablished for both" refers to the fact that neither the Mahāyāna nor those who do not accept the *Jñānaprasthāna* as the word of the Buddha acknowledge it—this is what is meant by "common."
It is granted that this is not included among the Buddha’s words because the reason for it does not exist within the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
When the Hīnayāna school makes an indeterminate statement, they say, "Is it as you yourselves admit regarding the *Jñānaprasthāna*? This refers to what your own Mahāyāna admits;
it does not mean that the Hīnayāna admits it.
If one were to establish a thesis such as that of the Sarvāstivāda and so forth, it would contradict one's own school;
the meaning of this is that while the Sarvāstivāda themselves admit that these were spoken by the Buddha, when they are confronted by the Mahāyāna, their own admissions contradict their own school.

However, if one simply states that [the subject] is like the *Jñānaprasthāna*, which is universally established for both parties and is not subsumed under what was spoken by the Buddha, then it contradicts one's own school.

By this, the Great Master correctly identifies their reason as "admitted by oneself" (*svābhyupagata*) and "established for both parties" (*prasiddha*), thereby exhausting all possible fallacies. [Question: It is not yet known what kind of inference (*anumāna*) this is.
[Answer: There are nine types of inference—those of others, those of oneself, and those common to both—and this is an inference based on what is established for both parties (*sādhāraṇa-anumāna*).

Regarding the statement that "Vijñaptimātra is also subsumed under the authority of the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*)," the intention here is to accept it as being spoken by the Buddha, who is the authority of scripture.

Since those who delight in the Mahāyāna accept it as being subsumed within the sūtras, the phrase "delighting in the Mahāyāna" is included in the reason (*hetu*) precisely to exclude those who do not delight in the Mahāyāna;
therefore, the term "accepted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*) must be included in the reason.
Regarding the phrase "blazing heat, surging flames, and so forth," this refers to six characteristics that manifest and establish the fire of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-vahni*):
first, having flames; second, having the nature of heat; third, surging flames—"surging" meaning to fly upward; fourth, having smoke; fifth, having illumination;

and sixth, flying smoke—"flying smoke" meaning causing the smoke to fly upward. Because it possesses these six characteristics, it is called the "flame of the fire of conditioned phenomena," consisting of flames, surging flames, and smoke.
These four, including flying flames, differ in terms of their height and depth.

Regarding the statement that "the earth element serves as the substance" and so forth: fire takes charcoal as its substance, which is the earth element; the movement of the flames is the wind element;

the flowing of the flames and the molten metal are both moisture, which is the water element; and the nature of heat is the fire element. Thus, these are the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Regarding the statement, "Because it is established, it is called a synthesis; it is certain with respect to the horn," etc., this clarifies that there is doubt concerning both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), as well as their combination.
There is certainty regarding the horn as the qualifier, and doubt regarding fire as the qualified; by combining these two, the point can be understood through careful examination.
However, as for the six causes, what are they? Furthermore, regarding the specific distinctions, there are two types of doubt:
doubt concerning both the whole and a part, and doubt concerning both the self and another. Since there is also a whole-part [doubt] within the other, the meaning of the six causes is established.
By analogy, there are also cases where there is doubt regarding existence and substance, yet neither is fully established; this was previously because the thesis was entirely without substance.

Now, in both cases, there is exclusively the existence of a substance; both the basis (*āśraya*) and that which depends upon it (*āśrita*) possess substantial reality, as will be explained below regarding the bases for doubt.

As for "independent phenomena" (*kevaladharma*) and "conjoined phenomena" (*sahitadharma*), these refer respectively to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), each of which is individually unestablished; this is what is meant by "independent phenomena" and "conjoined phenomena."

This means that [the reason] is not established for both parties. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "for both," it refers to the fact that this very [reason], whether as a solitary phenomenon (*kevaladharma*) or a concomitant phenomenon (*sahitadharma*), is subject to doubt for both parties—namely, doubt regarding either one of them, doubt regarding their conformity, and so forth; thus, the proponent and the opponent are designated as "both.
The phrases "because they are contradictory" and "because they conform to that" conclude the aforementioned faults. The initial statement "appearing like a flame" is then followed by:

It is certain that there is a fire of actual things; this contradicts one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*). To conform to the opponent’s doubt, he further states, "because it resembles a flame," thereby conforming to that [doubt].
Furthermore, as for "all causes," this refers to the very essence of the cause. The intention here is that when establishing an *upamāna* (analogy) thesis, it is like employing a reason (*hetu*).
Since Chengzong was unable to distinguish between the locus (*āśraya*) and the located (*āśrita*), his reason was flawed due to the fault of lacking a qualification regarding the locus;

how much more so now, when he does not even admit that emptiness exists? Furthermore, since he does not admit either the qualities (*guṇa*) or their locus, how could his reason not incur the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*)?
Question: Regarding the aforementioned point concerning the fault of having no basis (*anāśraya*), the intent of this question is as follows:
Previously, it was stated that since the thesis (*pakṣa*) consists of a non-existent entity (*avastu-dharma*), one must likewise employ a non-existent reason (*hetu*) which is itself without a cause.

Now, if this reason is likewise non-existent in accordance with [the thesis], it would still rely upon a non-existent emptiness-thesis; thus, the reason would incur the fault of having no basis (*anāśraya-doṣa*). As for the statement "Now, since this reason... [it continues as follows].

"Following one [of two] while lacking a basis" means that the other follows one while lacking a basis. To say "there is no property-possessor (dharmin) following one" means that the statement of a property-possessor is itself the lack of following one.

How much more so when both are not established (ubhayāprasiddha), meaning that neither the property-possessor nor the reason (hetu) is accepted by the opponent; therefore, they are called "both unestablished."
Furthermore,

if the specific property (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the subject (*pakṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), yet the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), how can this be? For example,

when establishing against the Sāṃkhya that sound is impermanent because it perishes, the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is unestablished as a specific property of the subject according to the opponent's own tenets.

The fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) consists in the reason establishing that the specific characteristic of the property (*dharma*) does not belong to the subject. To exclude this, [the text] states that "transformational impermanence" is established;

since the reason exists elsewhere as well—namely, in all things other than sound taken collectively as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—it is said that the probans (*sādhana*) does not exclude [the property from the subject]. Regarding the phrase "contradicting the specific characteristic of the subject," it means that the reason establishes that the specific characteristic of the property is not present in the subject.
Regarding the statement that "the cause upon which [the property] depends is indeterminate as to existence or non-existence," this means that the cause applies to both existence and non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "because the two types of non-entities [lack] the full portion [of the property] and thus constitute the basis for the supreme virtue":

one might ask, if the substratum (āśraya) does not exist, would it not incur the fallacy of the "unestablished locus" (āśrayāsiddha)? Since the self (ātman) is accepted as an existent entity by the Sāṃkhya school, how could it be considered an unestablished locus?
This refers to the fact that the "self" (ātman), which is the basis for one part [of the argument] and is not established as the probandum, is not accepted by our own Buddhist school.
To answer: first, we shall examine the two reasons (*hetu*) which lack a real basis; this refers only to one part [of the subject]. Now, to assist in forming this single phrase:

when the Sarvāstivāda school posits the self as substantially existent (*dravyasat*) in opposition to the Mahāyāna, the reason cited—"because it is the locus of attributes" (*guṇāśraya*)—is what remains of this [argument]. All other points should be considered accordingly.
[Objection:

It is the same. Furthermore, regarding that which is stated in this treatise—that "the self (ātman) is volition" according to the Sāṃkhya school—if one were to establish such a thesis, the basis (*āśraya*) of this treatise would not be established.

Regarding the statement "because it is not accepted that the great element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*) produces the great fruit": the Mahāyāna does not accept that the great element of space has a substantial entity (*dravya-sattva*) capable of producing a fruit, nor does it hold that the cause [of production] functions within space.

Nevertheless, all [positions] are definitively established by taking the existence or non-existence of the substratum (*āśrayin*) as the basis for the various propositions; this refers precisely to these two cases—both together and individually.
The first [type], "non-establishment of the basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*), necessarily consists only of the formulation of propositions based on the presence or absence of the reason.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "hesitation regarding non-establishment" extends to "not distinguishing between existence and non-existence," the meaning is this: where there is an entity, establishment is possible;
where there is no entity, as in the case of hesitation, establishment is impossible. It is for this reason that it is not distinguished [from the former].
Regarding the statement that "the two together following one basis does not constitute a proposition," there should actually be one such proposition here.
The question is: for what reason do four [of these] fail to constitute a basis? Why is there a distinction in the number of propositions, which differs from others? There is a specific reason.

If this question were not raised to introduce the subsequent text, it would be difficult to fully comprehend upon a first reading. Thus, [the author] proceeds by answering all at once with "both together are unestablished" (*ubhayāsiddha*) and so forth.
This explains why, in the first two cases, the "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*) is formulated as a sentence regarding the existence of an entity;

furthermore, from "hesitant unestablished" up to "not distinguishing between existence and non-existence," this explains why, in the third case, it is formulated as a sentence not distinguishing between existence and non-existence;
furthermore, from "the basis of the object" up to "the unestablished basis," this explains the general unestablished basis.
One can establish the reason for the distinction between the number of terms and the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) regarding oneself and others.

If one admits that "self" and "other" extend to the point where the locus (*āśraya*) is not established, this constitutes a fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddha*). This is the correct explanation of the fourth point:

the reason why one does not distinguish between self and other in terms of their lack of intrinsic nature. The intended meaning is that if one admits that even a small portion of the reason exists within the thesis (*pakṣa*), then it is [only] half-...
Because it exists partially and lacks [the other part], it necessarily cannot be the basis; thus, it is "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Since it is entirely absent [in one case], one cannot take either "self" or "other" as a single term in the proposition.
"Furthermore, there is no hesitation because [the mind] has reached the state of being without hesitation"—this explains the basis [of hesitation].

"If it did not exist, the statement 'there is hesitation' could not exist, because existence and non-existence are distinct"—this means that "existence" refers to hesitation and "non-existence" refers to the basis, as doubt and certainty are definitively different.
"Doubt is predetermined by its basis."

Regarding the statement "there are nine propositions concerning the non-establishment of both," this master maintains that since "both" already includes the non-establishment of the basis for doubt, it is as in the aforementioned fault.
Among those that are "both," they all belong to this category. Fundamentally, there are four propositions for the non-establishment of both;
these apply to both existence and non-existence. There are two propositions for the non-establishment of doubt. What, then, constitutes "both"? It refers to the complete non-establishment of both.

Regarding the three propositions in which the locus of one [of the two parties] is unestablished (*ekadeśāśrayāsiddha*), these refer to the cases where both have an existent entity, both have a non-existent entity, and both have an existent entity in one part;
these constitute the aforementioned "both" propositions.

As for the eighteen propositions resulting from adding those in which one [party] is unestablished, there are eight such propositions for the "one" case alone, which may be understood through deliberation.
Among these, there are four propositions regarding the "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*); within this, each individual [proposition] contains six propositions.

All those above are instances of a single proposition. Altogether, these comprise twenty-seven propositions, both complete and partial. Furthermore, one should understand that these twenty-seven propositions correspond to the twenty-seven positions combined within the aforementioned four types of "unestablished basis," which should be applied to both the "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*) and the "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*).
Regarding the twelve propositions consisting of one category of dharma that is not universally pervasive and is joined by conjunction:
there are two propositions within both [the disputant and the opponent], four propositions within either one, three propositions within the state of doubt, and three propositions within the locus;
these together constitute the twelve propositions.

Regarding the cases where [the reason] is neither a universal property nor a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), up to those involving fifteen permutations: within the "two-fold" category there are two permutations;

within the "either-one" category there are four permutations; within the "doubtful" category there are three permutations; within the "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddha*) there are six permutations; and within the "synthetic" category there are five permutations.

Question: If the reason (*hetu*) does not exist in the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) does not exist in either [the thesis or the reason], what is the intended meaning? Will the example establish the thesis through the reason?
If the example cannot establish the thesis and the reason, it is termed "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Question: If, in this case, you intend for all faults of the reason (*hetu*) to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*), then your intention is to establish this thesis as being faultless;
it is not that the name "intention" refers to establishing the thesis by means of the reason.

Although the reason possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*), everything else should be understood by analogy. This is answered by citing an example based on the first characteristic of the reason.

Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established, it is called "non-establishment of the thesis" (*pakṣāsiddha*); the three types of non-establishment are likewise so named. As for the three [types of] non-establishment:

they are so called because both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are unestablished. Why are there only three types of non-establishment? It is because the reason (*hetu*) is absent in the thesis, and it is absent in both [the similar and dissimilar instances] of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*);
thus, although there are two [kinds of absence], they are treated as three. Regarding this question: "If that is so, then it is identical to what was previously stated by the Master [Dignāga]."

Regarding the meaning of the response to the question below: although all three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) involve fallacies of the reason (*hetu*), only the first is designated as the "fallacy of the unestablished thesis" (*asiddha-pakṣa*).

Although there are many different types of unestablished reasons, what prevents the designation of "unestablished" from applying exclusively to this one? As for the other cases, they are all included within the category of the "contradictory thesis" (*viruddha-pakṣa*), which refers to both the similar and dissimilar examples (*sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*).

The inquiry immediately preceding this stated: "Is it the case that while it is a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), it is not universally applicable across the four types of unestablished reasons? One.
Question: How is it that what was previously called the "cause" (hetu) is now referred to as the "initial characteristic" (ādi-lakṣaṇa), and why is the collective name "unestablished" (asiddha) used?

Answer: It is not so. There are three phrases regarding the initial characteristic; the first phrase mentioned previously is the third phrase, which immediately follows the four "exhaustions" (kṣaya).

What is now called the "initial characteristic" refers to all three phrases of the initial characteristic as being the "initial characteristic," rather than taking only the first phrase of the initial characteristic. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the statement, "Because the reason [‘being an object of cognition’] can establish only the proponent’s own thesis (*pakṣa*) for Kuan," it is as follows:

For instance, when the Buddhist doctrine establishes the thesis that "sound is non-self" because it is "an object of cognition," the reason—excluding sound itself—all phenomena that are non-self serve as the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, all permanent and impermanent phenomena are taken as similar instances; there is not a single phenomenon that is a self which could serve as a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

An example is not called a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) unless it functions as a reason; however, if a narrow reason can establish a narrow thesis—such as establishing sound as impermanent by citing the two reasons of being produced (*kṛtaka*) and being dependent on volitional effort (*prayatnāntarīyaka*)—both are valid. But if one were to use these two reasons to establish that sound is non-self (*anātman*), this would be a case of a narrow reason establishing a broad thesis, wherein all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) would become the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) consists of both that which is the fruit of karma (*karmaphala*) and that which is not the fruit of karma (*akarmaphala*).

The six types of neutral consciousness (*avyākṛta-vijñāna*) are the fruit of karma, whereas the six types of wholesome and unwholesome consciousness are not the fruit of karma. Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the five sense faculties such as the eye are common to both being the fruit of karma and not being the fruit of karma;
those obtained in the present life due to past habitual tendencies (*pūrva-śīla*) are termed the fruit of karma. As for food and sleep, they are not [the fruit of karma].

Regarding the contradiction of karmic results: that which is definitively contradictory and causes a definitive contradiction refers to the reason "being produced by volition" (*kāryatva*) when the thesis is "eternal"—

"That which definitely causes contradiction" means that by means of the reason of being produced (*kṛtaka*), the thesis is made to become contradictory.
What is the reason of being produced? It establishes that sound is impermanent. What is the reason of being audible? It establishes that sound is eternal.
This definitively establishes the contradiction. The sixth and third [categories] correspond respectively to the two types of contradiction;

Furthermore, regarding that external objection, "that" refers to the *nyāyamukha* (Entrance to Reasoning).

The former is an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), while the latter must be an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)—this indicates that the aforementioned Mahāyāna is the initial opponent, who serves as the basis for the subsequent [inference].

It is said that self and other can be known; furthermore, it is stated that if one establishes a *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself) only in contrast to a *parārthānumāna* (inference for others), it is difficult to establish a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for oneself.
When confronting an opponent, since the inference for oneself is itself the opponent's "other," there are no two [categories of] self and other.
This means that if one designates something as "self," the adversary is designated as "other"; if both were "self," there would be no such thing as establishing an adversary.

The self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*) and the opponent-established (*parataḥ-siddha*) constitute the two [types of establishment]. Other meanings may be understood accordingly. To examine this: if the name "opponent" is established as self-established, then it is called "other";

there is no such thing as both the proponent and the opponent being self-established, nor both being other-established. If both were self-established, it would be a true *sādhana* (proof); if both were other-established, it would be a true *dūṣaṇa* (refutation).

The method for these cases and their fallacies are as explained in the Commentary (*Vṛtti*). As for the claim that the result of meditation is a determinate form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), [it is refuted as follows]:...
As for the Bodhisattva’s actual body being the "fish-rice" color, this color arises from meditative concentration and is called "concentration-resultant form" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
Its substance is substantially existent (*dravyasat*).

That [category] is broad while this is narrow; as in the nine fallacies regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*), this is a fallacy of the thesis itself, which is termed a "similarity to inference" (*anumāna-sama*).

To deviate [from a rule] while not possessing all three characteristics is called "broad" (*viśāla*). Why is it called broad? Because it is so named by virtue of not being subsumed under "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
However, that which is contradictory certainty is itself a contradiction with inference (*anumānaviruddha*). What is this?
It is that among the six types of "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) reasons, such as when the Vaiśeṣikas and others oppose the argument regarding the production of sound.

If one does not rectify the four types of contradictions with one's own tenets (*svavacanavirodha*) regarding the previously stated reason based on what is heard in the *Śabdanaya*, what are these four? They are:
contradiction regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), and so forth, up to contradiction regarding the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*).
The subsequent fault of contradiction is precisely the four types of contradiction; it receives the designation "subsequent" because the contradictions are determined to exist first.

As for the objection that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is refuted by the claim that sound should not be sound because the word [“sound”] does not distinguish [its specific nature] within its own statement—this constitutes a contradiction with one's own tenet (*siddhānta*).

Furthermore, one may formulate another inference as a "contradiction regarding the qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*) for the fault of one's own prior thesis. The inference would be:

"Sound, which is impermanent, ought not to be an impermanent sound. This commits the fallacy of failing to establish the subject (*dharmin*), because it restates both the property (*dharma*) and the subject together.
Moreover, the term "impermanent" is the very point of contention; it is what is intended here, yet now [the opponent] says...
Furthermore, this would result in yet another fallacy. Therefore,
the statement "this means of valid cognition is not subsumed under a fallacy"— where "this means of valid cognition" refers to the aforementioned Vaiśeṣika claim that sound is impermanent—

if one were to apply this to both the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) mentioned previously and the qualification (*viśeṣa*) of the subject, these two [would be excluded].
These faults are all illogical and cannot cause the aforementioned *pramāṇa* of the Vaiśeṣika school to incur these faults.

Regarding the statement "this [determination] also has four kinds," the meaning is as follows: while the previous [case of] contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*) involved one reason contradicting four [factors], this determination also contradicts four; that is, this very contradiction of determination also contradicts four. Therefore...

Question: According to what was stated previously, it should be understood that within the *vitaṇḍā* (destructive debate), both the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*) possess various distinctions.

Why, then, does this present treatise speak only of the fault of violating the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property? Answer: This present treatise speaks only of the property as it is presented in words; furthermore, since this is the "predicate" (*viśeṣya*) within the thesis (*pakṣa*), it is the very property that is the primary object of dispute. Therefore, there must be a dispute regarding the property.
Although the locus is also presented in words, it does not cause the characteristic of the thesis to extend to the other two [the reason and the example].

Although it is admitted within the context of specific distinctions that [a reason] is not verbally expressed, in the case of one’s own inference (*svārthānumāna*), it is not a fault for another to be uncertain.

For instance, when a proponent establishes their own inference, the reason they themselves have established flows over to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of the other’s inference; yet, from the perspective of that other person, this reason remains indeterminate.

The fallacy of uncertainty (*anaikāntika*) in one's own inference is precisely the fallacy of "uncertainty for the other" (*parānaikāntika*) within the other's inference; and that which is "uncertainty for oneself" (*svānaikāntika*) within the other's inference is as follows:

when establishing the tenet of another's position with the primary intent of refuting them, the probative reason (*hetu*) they employ migrates to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) within one's own inference.
This probative reason of theirs commits the fallacy of "uncertainty for oneself," which is itself the "uncertainty for the other" in their own inference.

Within the categories of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) is itself indeterminate. In this treatise, for the time being, we shall explain the six types of "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) by subsuming them under the category of the "unestablished" as recognized by both parties.

Within each of these, there are four kinds of unestablished reasons. Furthermore, in this treatise, we shall clarify the principle of the six inconclusives primarily by way of those that are unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*).
The statement "In reality, both possess one analogy, though they are equal" explains the reason why the three [types of] *asiddha* (unestablished reasons) are not established.

Regarding the phrase "the twenty-seven and the fifty-eight types," the question is: according to logic, it would also be appropriate to take two hundred and sixteen types in relation to the twenty-seven as the constituent terms (*pada*); why then are only fifty-four paired with the twenty-seven?

Yeta [argues that] in reality it should indeed be so; however, the Master of the Commentary (Soshu) has merely provided a brief indication regarding the dharmas and has not exhausted the full reasoning.

Now, Dharma Master Zizhou takes the two hundred and other types of indeterminate [reasons] and correlates them with the twenty-seven general categories, totaling five hundred and eighty-three hundred and thirty-two kinds of indeterminate reasons.
Upon further careful calculation, these fifty-four indeterminate reasons are assigned to the four types of unestablished (*asiddha*) reasons, which together total two hundred.
[Question: Regarding the sixteen [cases] where four are not established, twenty-seven are assigned to fifty-four, which together total one thousand four hundred and fifty-eight propositions.

One asks: since the first characteristic of the previously mentioned "common indeterminate" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) gate was missing, and the third "uncommon indeterminate" (*asādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) gate lacked the second characteristic while the others lacked two characteristics—why are these further paired with the "not established" (*asiddha*) to form these propositions? [Answer: It is in relation to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that...

Furthermore, there is no fault in the analogy regarding the question: "How can it be said that the latter two characteristics do not exist? The answer is: even when speaking in relation to the basis of the analogy, there is likewise no fault.
(From the *Yinming ruzhengli lun shu qianji*, middle volume)
*Commentary on the Nyāyapraveśa*, Fascicle Lower, Preface. Composed by Zhizhou.

Regarding the meaning of "contradiction" (*viruddha*), it refers to two tenets being mutually opposed. Question: Now, these four fallacies primarily clarify the fallacies of the reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*).
Question: Since it is called a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*) because it contradicts the thesis (*pakṣa*), how does this relate to the matter of the reason contradicting the thesis?
Answer: The reason receives its name through a possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*). It is also called a "reason that contradicts the thesis.
Here, the "subject" (*adhikaraṇa*) is the contradictory thesis; because this is the reason for that contradictory thesis, it is therefore called a "contradictory reason."

Since the subject (*pakṣa*) itself contradicts the thesis (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*) may also be designated as "contradicting the thesis. However, it is not the case that a reason is called "contradictory" simply because it contradicts the thesis.
Question: Now, since the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) contradicts the original thesis that sound is eternal, why can you say that this reason does not contradict the thesis?

Answer: These four reasons do not all equally contradict the *dharmin* (the property-bearer) of the original thesis; rather, they contradict the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that *dharmin*.
There are cases where, although these two reasons contradict the specific distinctions of the thesis, they do not contradict the original thesis itself;

thus, neither of these two reasons is called a "reason that contradicts the thesis. Regarding "contradiction of the thesis" (*pratijñā-virodha*), when four types of contradictions occur within the thesis itself, all of them are termed "contradiction of the thesis" because they contradict the original thesis that was established.

"Not altering the other's reason" means that when the opponent uses the proponent’s own established reason to commit the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*), it is called "not altering the other's reason.

Therefore, regarding the objection that even in the absence of a thesis (*pakṣa*) there is a contradiction with the example of the reason: if one names a reason that contradicts the thesis as "contradiction," [then the objection holds].

Regarding this, there is an objection: since the reason contradicts the thesis, it is called a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*); yet the thesis itself should also be called "contradictory to the thesis" (*viruddha-pakṣa*).

Because of this objection, it is said that because the word [of the thesis] serves as a reason for a property contrary [to itself], the objection is established by taking the absence of the thesis as the example.
"That which is non-contradictory is likewise contradictory" refers to the *Nyāyamukha*. Now, according to the commentary on the *Nyāyamukha*, how is this so? It is as follows:
the Vaiśeṣikas establish that the eyes and other sense organs must exist for the sake of another because they possess the nature of an aggregate, just like bedding and the like.
This is the intended meaning of the Vaiśeṣikas; however, when considering them from the perspective of "another," this formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is invalid.
If [the reason] is "contrary" (*viruddha*), it is defined as that which the opponent does not accept as a real self (*ātman*), yet accepts as a conventional self (*prajñapti-ātman*);

this is likewise called "contradictory. Furthermore, when the proponent himself accepts that there is no contradiction, yet the opponent uses that very same reason to establish a contradiction—this is also the case.
The *Nyāyamukha* merely points to a specific distinction regarding the property (*dharma*).

Regarding the claim that there is no contradiction when considering the opponent's position from the perspective of another: if one asks how the probans (*hetu*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and the probans of "having a single real entity" (*ekadravyavattva*) can be established as non-contradictory for the proponent, the Master [Dharmakīrti] states they are established as non-contradictory.

If one asks how the probans of "being produced" can be established as non-contradictory when considered in relation to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), which is not different from the subject (*pakṣa*), one must reflect further on this.
Regarding the phrase "because the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) is neither determinate nor existent": what is this?

For example, when one establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) that sound is impermanent, using "emptiness" as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and "being produced" as the reason (*hetu*), since the property to be proven—impermanence—and the reason—the state of being produced—do not definitely exist upon that similar instance of emptiness, it is said that "the property to be proven is neither determinate nor existent. As for the phrase "because it does not exist": [it refers to the non-existence of those two].

It is certain that there is no [valid] reason (*hetu*), because he stated that the reason for sound being eternal is "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*); since it was stated in this way, the reason is indeed rendered non-existent.

Regarding the point that the first instance modifies the example while the latter three follow the original: the intention here is that when there are four contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*), one must necessarily employ the original [example].
It is also acceptable to illustrate this by changing only the first [member] while leaving the latter three unchanged.
Question: There are cases where a reason contradicts the thesis; should such a case not be termed "contradiction" (*viruddha*)? Answer: This was already explained previously:

it serves as a cause for a property contradictory to the thesis, yet lacks the fault of the reason being similar to the thesis (*sādhya-sama*). Since the reason contradicts the thesis, it is named "contradiction."
Now, for what reason is this again taken up as an objection? Although it was briefly mentioned previously, the underlying reasons were not yet explicitly set forth;

therefore, at this time, the matter is further interrogated to reveal that this syllogism likewise possesses four fallacies. The question is the same as before, but the answer differs from the previous one.
Furthermore, regarding the passage from "contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dharma by name" up to "contradiction with inference based on mere names":
this answers the previous question in two parts. The preceding text constitutes the first answer, while this present text is the second answer.

Within this second answer, the response to the thesis (*pakṣa*) is also called a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*), which simultaneously addresses a latent objection (*āśaṅkā*). The latent objection asks: "Does the thesis not contradict the reason?"

Question: "There are four ways of opening [the argument] that contradict the thesis; does this mean there are four [types of contradiction]? Answer: This can be understood from the commentary (*śāstra*).

It is not so. Why?
