Because if it were otherwise, these contradictions of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-viruddha*) would apply only to cases where the statement is made by way of synthesis (*saṃgraha*), namely the contradiction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viruddha*), and would not apply to cases where the other three types of contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*) are explained by way of analysis (*vibhāga*).

Regarding the statement "this school’s doctrine of dharmas": this refers to the school of *hetuvidyā* (logic) known as "this school," which distinguishes itself from the doctrines in the sūtras concerning self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth.

As for the phrase "because that which is to be established is either existent or non-existent": this "existent" or "non-existent" does not refer to the distinctions between my own [Buddhist] categories of phenomena.

Regarding the meaning of the term "generally" (*fan'er*)—as for the doubt concerning whether the two self-natures of person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) exist or do not exist, and so forth—it is because the two self-natures of person and phenomena are each distinct.
This means that the self-natures of person and phenomena are mutually distinct.
Regarding "emptiness and so forth are pervasive": suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so on, universally pervade all things such as form (*rūpa*). Regarding "not pervasive":

these phenomena such as form do not extend to other higher categories and are thus called non-pervasive; yet they are termed "pervasive" in the sense that, for example, regarding form, all forms are [included therein].

Regarding the statement, "Although this is identical to what preceded, it is divided into two gates": although this is identical to what preceded, the former was presented first and the latter is explained now;

thus, there is no distinction between the preceding specific [treatment] and the general one. However, as for the slight difference in the teaching, this refers to the two distinct types: the *Abhidharma* and the *Buddhabhūmi*.

Furthermore, as for the fact that their meanings are also different, the *Abhidharma* is termed "specific," whereas within this [present context], the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is distinguished as "general."

Regarding the statement that "the categories are distinct because their meanings are also distinct": this refers, for the time being, to the distinctions between the pervasive and the limited, and between the prior and the subsequent.

As for why, among these three, one accepts [the pervasive] yet does not take the prior and subsequent [but rather takes the limited and pervasive], the answer is: because in the case of the limited and the pervasive, a fixed rule is established;
whereas in the case of the prior and subsequent, there is no such fixed rule, and thus they are not accepted.
Regarding the preceding [subject] and the common [predicate]: these are both the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and the distinction (*viśeṣa*), all of which are presented within the words.
That is to say, because the preceding and succeeding [terms] are collectively intended as a "distinction," both the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) possess a self-nature.
Now, what is intended here is that which is accepted within the mind as the object to be established; this is called the "distinction," and it does not refer to everything.
That which is not expressed by words is all termed "distinctions.
As for the meaning being as previously stated, it refers only to what is established by the intended sense; therefore, it is said that not everything is included.
To cause the statement of a reason such that these four types result in a contradiction is this one reason that contradicts the four.
This is the thesis.

Regarding the first two [points], which individually contradict one cause: this refers to the fact that within this context, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena and the specific attributes (*viśeṣa*) of phenomena can each individually contradict one cause.
Regarding the statement "the latter two both contradict the two reasons": these latter two contradictory reasons are so called because they contradict the reasons of two types of proponents;
thus, it is said that "the latter two both contradict the two reasons," as one reason contradicts two propositions, and this is termed "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) with respect to those propositions.

Regarding the statement that these three types, along with the other twelve, constitute the two kinds of causes— the intrinsic characteristic of phenomena (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa*) and the differentiation of phenomena (*dharma-viśe�șa*)—

as explained in the treatise: since each of these two causes is distinct, yet both the intrinsic characteristic of subsequent existence and the differentiation of subsequent existence share a single cause, they are referred to as "three types."
Regarding that which was first stated by him among the three faults of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*):

the fault of the thesis being contradicted by inference (*anumāna-viruddha*) at its initial statement is precisely the fault of the contradiction of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*) within the thesis, as well as the fault of the counter-balanced reason (*pratibādhita*). Now, this first fault here is likewise the fault of the contradiction of the specific characteristic of the property;
since it is identical to that [previous case], it is therefore called the "contradiction of the specific characteristic of the property" when stated at the outset. From that...

Regarding the initial statement: since the aforementioned inference and the contradiction with certainty both concern the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dharma, this [present argument] follows from that;
therefore, it is precisely at the outset that the contradiction regarding the specific characteristic of the dharma is stated. This is certain.
Regarding the second position: among the four causes, it refers to the "produced cause" (*kṛtaka-hetu*) and the "exertion cause" (*prayatna-hetu*).
The exertion cause is the second cause. It is called the "second position" because it is designated as the second based on its cause;
the exertion cause is the second. The cause that arises from exertion, when inverted, becomes its opposite; this is the sixth of the nine propositions. This is in contrast to [the first].
The fourth phrase receives the second name.

This "pseudo-reason" (hetvābhāsa) is precisely that which, among these four types of contradiction, is the "contradiction regarding the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddha-hetu*);
it is the "reason of being produced" (*kṛtaka-hetu*).

Question: Since one continues to employ the old [reason] up to the point of "arbitrarily changing the similarity" (*yathā-saṃmata*), if the first [of the four types of contradictory reasons] is not changed, it must fail to establish the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) [of the reason], resulting in a contradiction;

yet if the latter three are changed, they must also fail to establish the latter three characteristics, resulting in contradictions. How, then, can it be said that "one may arbitrarily change the similarity"?

Answer: To say that "one may arbitrarily change the similarity" is a general clarification that among all four types of contradictory reasons, those that can be corrected or made similar are permissible.
Regardless of whether these four [reasons] may be modified or made identical, among these four fallacies, the first must necessarily be modified while the latter three need not be.
If these four are left as they are, whether modified or identical, they would no longer constitute the four fallacies. Question: If they are not modified or made identical, what fault is there?
Answer: If they are not modified or made identical, then there would be no single reason that contradicts two, three, or four [of the others], and so forth.

The fifteenth [type of fallacy] is the "contradiction through the mere labor of positing" (*śūnyatā-vyarthāpatti*). Regarding the others, when combined with any one [of the three types of reasons], they may constitute a contradiction of two reasons.

As for "any one," once the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is modified, it becomes a reason based on the specific characteristic of the property (*dharmasvalakṣaṇahetu*); then, by combining this reason with any one of the latter three [reasons], it constitutes a contradiction of either two or three [reasons].
Because they are equal, it is said that "one [of them] follows.
To claim that the first example is altered while the latter three are not altered is a definitive explanation of why a single reason contradicts two systems;

for if these four common characteristics were contradictory such that the examples could not be altered to achieve parity, there would necessarily never be a case where a single reason contradicts two systems.
This refers to the four types of fallacies regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*).
"Dissimilar" (*vaidharmya*) may be either present or absent; that is, it exists within the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) or does not exist there, hence it is called "both.

According to this, the intention of the sub-commentary below is that a potential objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) should be raised here: among the examples in this treatise, the first example is modified, whereas the latter three are not.
The treatise itself clearly explains this; why then can it be said that "the analogy may be changed at will"? Does this not contradict the teaching?

Because there is this anticipated objection (*pūrvapakṣa*), the meaning of the objection in the commentary (*śāstra*) is recorded here. The objection in the commentary is the objection raised by the proponent (*vādī*);

the response is the answer given by the opponent (*prativādī*). Now, taking the intention of the opponent’s answer, it says: "The latter three [characteristics] are contradictory, as determined by reason."
Although one may rely on the treatise without altering the metaphor, how can a contradiction be established? The opponent replies:
The proponent originally lacks skillful means and, through deceptive calculation, falsely takes a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) as if it were a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The opponent then seizes upon this "pseudo-similar example" presented by the proponent and treats it as a true similar example. For the proponent, however, this "true similar example" [as perceived by the opponent] is not actually a dissimilar example.
To illustrate this principle: although the latter three fallacies do not alter the analogy, they establish the contradiction of the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, the opponent objects: "Since you have established the contradiction of the three characteristics through reasoning based on the latter three [fallacies] even without altering the analogy, I too shall establish the contradiction of the three characteristics through reasoning based on the latter three points of the treatise, even without altering the analogy, by means of a modified analogy."

It results in a contradiction with the first statement; although the metaphor was changed there, even if it were not changed according to the underlying logic, it would still constitute a contradiction.

If one follows what was said, this implies that if one follows the opponent’s words, then according to this treatise, if the first of the four statements changes the metaphor while the latter three do not, then the subsequent three will fail to establish the three characteristics of contradiction, resulting in the fault of non-contradiction.
Regarding the statement in the *Nyāyamukha* that "the 'reaching' [of the reason] remains as it was in the old version," this answers the previous objection.
Since the *Nyāyamukha* does not state that the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) must also be changed, it follows that the similar instance may be either modified or left as it was.

It is clear that one cannot rely on the initial position of changing every single instance nor on the final position of never changing any of the last three; rather, the similar instance is subject to either modification or retention.
The intention of the statement, "To cause the student to know that the reason is definitely not the fault [of the example] prior to the example," is as follows:

although the first [reason] is modified after the example is presented while the latter three are not modified, both the modification and non-modification result in contradiction; this clarifies that it is not a fault of the example, but rather a fault of the reason.
Regarding the latter three reasons, although they appear established when examined, the intention of the initial proponent was to establish their own fundamental measure (*pramāṇa*), and so forth.

When the [opponent] departs from [the proponent's] intended meaning and reformulates it so that it does not constitute a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*), although the proponent’s original intent was to take a dissimilar example as a similar one,
the latter three reasons (*hetu*) are nonetheless established relative to the proponent’s original intent.

To "jointly state the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*)" means that in the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) regarding this sound, both the preceding [inferential] elements are taken together as the property and the property-bearer.
The dharma and its *dharmin* constitute this measure; the dharma and its *dharmin* are taken together to form the subject (*kartṛ*).

Alternatively, according to the Grammarians (*Śabdikāḥ*), the former measure—the dharma and its *dharmin*—is taken together to form the subject for this subsequent measure, because the *dharmin* of that [former] dharma is itself the *dharmin* of this [latter] dharma. Thus, it is said to be the *dharmin* of the dharma. This is the examination of the *dharmin* of the dharma.
Regarding the question: "Since both parties are subject to one of the faults [of the reason], how is this subsumed under 'pseudo-faults' (jāti)?

The answer is: To falsely point out a fault where the other party has established no fault is called a "pseudo-refutation" (dūṣaṇābhāsa); since one now merely returns the same fault to the opponent, it is called a "pseudo-reason" (hetvābhāsa).

Regarding the "non-establishment for both parties due to a fault": when the two properties—sound and impermanence—are taken as the subject (*dharmin*), and the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is posited, it is non-established for both the proponent and the opponent because it does not reside in one part of the subject, namely impermanence. This is what is meant by "non-establishment for both parties regarding one part."
If it is granted that the proponent also commits one of the faults of the *anuyoga* (consequent) fallacies by relying on [the reason], this is another fault of the *anuyoga* for the opponent;

for that which the opponent does not grant as the basis for the thesis—namely, the impermanence established by the proponent—is precisely what the proponent himself accepts as the basis for the opponent. Thus, the proponent becomes his own opponent.
Furthermore, regarding the point that impermanence fails to establish its locus (*āśraya*): the meaning of this statement is that all reasons (*hetu*) must depend upon a factual subject (*dharmin*).
Since the factual subject "impermanence" does not exist as a substantial entity, the reason—which depends upon it—lacks a locus.
To claim there is no such dependent [reason] is incorrect; this is clearly established.

Suppose an objection is raised: "When one establishes [a thesis] regarding the various non-similar instances (*avisadṛśa*), this opponent incurs the fault of 'contradiction with the specific characteristic of the reason' (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddha*) as previously stated.

Since that fault is not established, the proponent further attempts a defense, saying: "I do not incur the fault of 'contradiction with the specific characteristic of the reason' because my previous formal argument (*pramāṇa*) does not alter its original reason (*hetu*).
Now, if the reason is altered, is that not indeed his fault? The alteration of the reason is expressed as: "It is admitted that there is none."
Because it is constant, the following does not say: "This too is not a fallacy," for among all pseudo-fallacies (*asad-uttara*), this is established as the characteristic of a fallacy;

and because among all responses that point out fallacies, there is none that resembles this one. Thus, it is said: "Among all pseudo-fallacies, the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*) of the thesis-proposition (*pakṣa*) necessarily does not alter the reason (*hetu*).

Since the reason has already been altered, the previously stated "unestablished" (*asiddha*) fallacy is subsequently rectified. He then offers a defense, saying: "I have altered the previous reason, intending to..."

Regarding the fault of the distinction between dharmas (*dharma-viśeṣa*), one cannot take both "sound" and "impermanence" together; therefore, it is said that "sound" is not the original subject of dispute.
This is the intended meaning of the subsequent commentary (*vṛtti*). As for the phrase "all pseudo-propositions" (*sarva-pratijñābhāsa*), this wording is inverted;
it should rather be stated as "the absence of all pseudo-propositions. Consider this carefully.
Regarding that which acts as a condition for it and that which does not act as a condition for it, the sequence of whether the constant sound is audible or inaudible should be understood accordingly;
this is further questioned for the sake of careful examination.
As for the meaning explained here, the intention of this passage is to provide the reason for its use for the benefit of others.

Regarding the reason of "being an accumulation," it is unestablished for both [proponent and opponent]. If one were to establish the self as an existent entity, neither the proponent nor the opponent would admit the existence of a reason based on accumulation;
since the Buddhist doctrine does not admit a true self, how could there be a reason for its existence?
Regarding the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of being an aggregate (*saṃghātatva*), it is as follows:
"The self (*ātman*) must not be the self, because it is an aggregate, just like a bed or a chair. It should further be stated: "All things that are aggregates are not the self."
That which is established as a provisional self based on the eye and so forth is precisely this [self] viewed from the perspective of its functional activity;
since the essence of this provisional self is impermanent, it is called "provisional."

Regarding the statement that "the self (ātman) experiences the five subtle elements (tanmātra) through these [senses]": Question: According to the fundamental tenets of Sāṃkhya, the five subtle elements are experienced by the real self (puruṣa).
Why, then, is it said here that the self experiences them through the eyes and other senses, and that the eyes and other senses experience the five subtle elements? Answer: There is no fault in this.
Taking the sense organs as a provisional gateway, the self experiences the five subtle elements; the self and the eyes experience the five subtle elements simultaneously.
It is not only that the eye experiences while the self does not;
if one considers the real self to be superior by virtue of its being the thinker, this intention is explained as follows:

if one regards the thinking subject and the object thought as superior or inferior, then the real self is indeed superior, because it is the real self that is capable of thinking. The rest is explained according to the commentary.
Regarding the phrase "because it contradicts one's own tenet": it contradicts the tenets of the Buddha-dharma because [the Buddha] does not admit a self (*ātman*).

As for the statement "there is no negation," you should carefully consider my words. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "To hold that the self is volition (*cetanā*) is precisely the view of the Sāṃkhya school; the essential substance of the real self is itself volition."
"That which is capable of reflection is the self.
This passage, stating that one should not regard even bedding as merely something used provisionally,
is cited by Master Kuī to establish his refutation.
The *Seventy Verses on Ultimate Truth* was composed by the Bodhisattva [Aryadeva]. As for the *Seventy Verses on Gold*, it has already been explained above.
Regarding the statement that "each has its own generality, particularity, and so forth," there are two types of generality and particularity:

first, general generality and particularity; second, specific generality and particularity. Within the first, general generality and particularity, there are again two: first, general generality; second, general particularity. First, general...

Regarding "commonality" (*sāmānya*): although the essential natures (*dharmatā*) within the category of real entities (*dravya*) are ninefold, they are all equally real; therefore, this is termed "universal commonality. Subsequently, regarding "universal difference" (*viśeṣa*):

among the nine factors within the real, the qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karma*) are collectively different; thus, it is termed "universal difference. Within these two [categories], universal commonality and the difference of qualities follow the same principle as explained for the real entities;
their meaning is easy to understand. Following this, within "particular commonality and difference," there are also two divisions: first, the particular...
Regarding "identity-in-difference" (*ekatva-viśeṣa*), first, as for "identity-in-difference": among earth, water, fire, and so forth, each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) is distinct from the others;

this is called "difference. Yet, because they are all equally real (*dravya*), it is called "identity-in-difference. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound where the "difference" itself is the "identity. Second, as for "distinct difference":
among the nine categories of real entities (*navadharma*), each is distinct from the others; this is called "difference. This "difference" [is further analyzed].
"Because they are distinct, they are 'distinctly different' (*bhinna-bheda*); this is also a *karmadhāraya* compound. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation 'understanding the distinction':

now, within each of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are many atoms (*paramāṇu*) that are not identical; these are termed 'distinct. Because being distinct is itself difference, it is called 'distinctly different,' which is likewise a *karmadhāraya*.
The same applies to time, space, and so forth. Between the two categories of quality (*guṇa*) and activity (*karman*), the distinction and identity are to be understood accordingly."
The distinction between the one and the many, as explained according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) based on the aspect of dependence upon others, is understandable.

Furthermore, regarding that which is eternal and possesses the nature of being able to harmonize and combine: why is it that the "same" and the "different," the "many" that can be the same and the many that can be different, receive the name "many";
and why do the "harmonized" and the "combined," the "many" that can harmonize and the many that can combine, receive the name "many"?

If it is asked whether the term "conjunction" (saṃyoga) refers to only one thing, the answer is as follows: This conjunction of identity and difference arises based on names to produce the understanding of meaning.
While we speak of "identity and difference," identity and difference are not one; they are many. As for the word "conjunction," its essence is not different [from its constituents];
it is called "conjunction" precisely because it is one.

Question: Although the qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*) are conjoined with and depend upon the substance (*dravya*), why do you not say that the substance is their cause, but instead say they are "without substance"?
Answer: Qualities and activities depend solely upon the substance, yet the substance itself is not their cause.
It is like a person who dwells depending on the great earth; the earth is not the cause of that person.

Regarding the statement, "The Great Universal (mahāsāmānya) and the Particulars (sāmānyaviśeṣa) both exist in each individual substance": Question: Since the essence of the Great Universal is existent, it can be said to exist in each individual substance;
however, since the essence of the Particulars is non-existent, how can it also be said to exist in each individual substance? Answer:

That the Particulars are said to "exist" does not mean they are named "existent" because their essence is existent. Rather, they are designated as "existent" based on their capacity to function as the commonality and particularity of substances and so forth.

The three phrases "causing [them] to be real," etc., share both commonalities and distinctions; it is in reference to this aspect of having both commonality and difference that the nature of sameness and difference acquires the designation "existence.
Therefore, it is stated below: "Causing the three categories to be distinct, they are named 'one' and 'real'."

Regarding the phrase "there are many substantial entities such as 'existence' and 'non-existence'": this means that the capacity to possess [an entity] is termed "existence," while the absence of such capacity is termed "non-existence.

To speak of "existence" and "non-existence" refers to the capacity to possess atoms and so forth, which is "existence," and the incapacity to combine with existing things and so forth, which is "non-existence."

Regarding the statement that "dharmas have greatness and ultimacy" and that "dharmas have identity and difference," these two phrases concerning dharmas both refer to the three dharmas of reality (*satya*), equality (*samatā*), and so forth.

Within these three dharmas of reality, equality, and so forth, there exists greatness; within these three dharmas of reality, equality, and so forth, there exists the nature of identity and difference.
The statement that "there is one who possesses virtuous karma and yet there is also one who does not" contains within it a profound principle;
however, if one were to say "it exists extensively," as in the commentary, one would commit the fallacy of contradicting a point not admitted by the opponent.

"Similarity and difference are not examples" means that others do not admit that "great existence" (mahāsattā) possesses the cause of being a single real entity; nor do they admit that similarity and difference constitute great existence.

Therefore, it is said they are "not examples. Furthermore, if there were a reason (hetu) consisting of a single real entity within great existence, since others do not admit that great existence possesses a single real entity, how could it serve as an example for existence? Thus, it is said that "the probans is unestablished" (asiddha).

Regarding the statement in the Buddha’s teachings that "there is form" or "there is the outflowing," this is a general indication that there exists the Great Existence (*mahāsattā*), as well as the three entities such as "existence-in-reality" (*sadbhāva*) and so forth;
these three entities are not non-existent. Just as the existence of the outflowing is "existence," so too the existence of form is "form.

Furthermore, just as the existence of emptiness is "emptiness," so too the existence of sound is "sound. Thus, because form exists, it is form; and because emptiness exists, it is emptiness. The same applies to sound.
Therefore, this is an illustration: that which possesses form (rūpin) has a correlate; because there is a great [cause], there is a correlate. The subject (dharmin) is "that which possesses form.
"Possessing form" means that upon the substance of form (rūpa-svabhāva), there is the quality of resistance (sapratighatva); because form is resistant, it is called "possessing form.
It is not that apart from form there is a separate possessor, as in the case where space possesses sound—sound adheres to space and is thus named after it.
Regarding "emptiness exists," it is not that there is an emptiness distinct from sound; the same applies to the three categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*).

Because their essence is not non-existent, they are termed "existent. This existence is not something separate from these three that possesses them; rather, it is the very existence admitted by our opponents.

As for "existence with outflows" (*sāsrava*), the essence of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) is not itself the outflow; it is [the outflow] belonging to another.

Because the outflows (āsrava) cause the mind-king and its associates to become possessed of outflows, they receive the designation "outflowing" (sāsrava). The afflictions (kleśa) are the agents that outflow, while the mind-king and its associates are the objects that are outflowed.
The afflictions are likened to a great vessel, and the mind-king and its associates are likened to the contents such as grain.

Regarding the phrase "the existence that is capable of possessing": this explains that the essence of the outflows (*āsrava*) of the afflictions is that which is capable of leaking, and the phenomena that are leaked are likewise great existents.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the existence that is capable of possessing and that which is possessed":

there is no need for a subtle [existence]; rather, it is an existence that is distinct from substantial reality. This is an existence within the reason (*hetu*), not an existence within the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

It exists; moreover, as for the various causes that should not be conceptually differentiated, this meaning is precisely that these causes are not non-existent and possess great existence (*mahāsattā*).

Is it not because one does not permit such differentiation? Furthermore, if each individual subtle hair-part of the various causes were to be conceptually differentiated, then among all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no correct cause (*saddhetu*).
If it is as you say that the dyad (dvyaṇuka) possesses two or more real entities, how so?
The dyad possesses two or more real entities because this very dyad is produced from two kinds of ultimate atoms (paramāṇu), namely its father and mother;
it is not that the dyad can produce the father and mother ultimate atoms that it is said to possess two or more real entities.
If one says that there is a real entity (vastu), it falls into the fault of both [theses] being unestablished; herein there are two types of "both unestablished":
first, "both unestablished" in its entirety, and second, "both unestablished" in part. Regarding the former, how is it that there are twelve real entities?

These are earth, water, fire, and so forth, up to space, self, and mind—these nine are collectively termed "real entities" (dravya)—along with qualities (guṇa) and activities (karma), which together constitute the composite whole (samavāya).
These three factors, together with the preceding nine, constitute twelve. As for the establishment [of the categories], there are primarily only the first eleven;

the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is also called "unreal" (*avastuka*), and is therefore established as a "partial" [category]. Both the proponent and the opponent agree that conjunction does not exist.

Since "similarity and difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) cannot serve as an example—because there is no difference between similarity and difference within conjunction—it is said that both parties agree on this point.
Regarding the first point, "both parties fail to establish it in one respect," and the second, "both parties fail to establish it in both respects and in one respect":

both the proponent and the opponent agree that the substance (*dravya*) of real entities (*sat*) and so forth is not non-existent, and thus they call it "existent. Within this phrase "existent," one part—namely, the parents and the atoms—is non-substantial (*adravya*), and thus they call it "non-substantial.
Because of this one part, which is both existent and non-substantial, the argument proceeds; this is agreed upon by both the proponent and the opponent.

Since neither the proponent nor the opponent admits that there is a real entity such as "substance" (*dravya*) that is not non-existent in its own-being, yet they do admit a single non-real entity consisting of a composite whole, it is said that both reasons are unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), or unestablished for one part of both (*anyatarāsiddha*).

These two reasons are unestablished for both parties with respect to the first characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*). If those [composite] entities were real, they would immediately become fathers and mothers.

An atom (*paramāṇu*) is likewise without substantial reality. Now, if one speaks of "that which lacks substantial reality" while taking only those parent atoms as the referent, one cannot take the "son" atoms;
for the proponent and opponent both agree that these "son" atoms and so forth are not without substantial reality. Thus it is examined.
Regarding the statement "substance and so forth can possess [existence]," etc.:
substance and so forth can possess that which exists, namely "Great Existence" (mahāsattā). This "Great Existence" category...
It cannot be established that there is the capacity for the non-substantiality of the "synthesized" (*saṃghāta*) category.

Since there is no capacity for substantiality and so forth in the absence of substantiality, this very substantiality and so forth—which are not non-existent in their own-being—possess the capacity for their own-being;

thus, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) which are the parents of that [substantiality] are designated as "non-substantial. This reason is not admitted by either the proponent or the opponent regarding substantiality.

Because there is an existence that is not non-existent within the phrase "conjunction," it is said that both [positions] are established; because both are not established as a single part, it is said that there is no real non-existence.

As for the example, it also commits the fallacy of the unestablished probans (*asiddha-hetu*); that is to say, taking "existence and non-existence" as the reason is identical to "sameness and difference."

The analogy cannot establish identity or difference; as for the statement that the probans (*hetu*) is unestablished and also non-pervasive—meaning it does not pervade the term "conjunction" (the *samudāya*)—if one were to propose "because [it] lacks real existence" as the probans, at first glance this seems to refer only to the absence of reality in the term "substance" (*dravya*), and thus it does not encompass qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*karman*). Therefore, one must examine it closely.
At first glance, it seems that [the term] "non-substantiality" can only apply to the category of substantiality;

if one says there is non-substantiality because of the existence of non-substantiality, this would be like saying there is "great existence" (mahāsattā). It can only apply to the category of substantiality as a semblance of non-substantiality, for since there is no non-substantiality within qualities and activities, one does not say they are "non-substantial."

Question: Regarding the statement "the existence of existence and the existence of the dharma" up to "non-establishment for both," the intent here is to clarify that the existence of existence (*mahāsattā*) is called the "dharma of existence.

When there is a real reason (*hetu*)—that is, a real entity that is not non-existent—it constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). Since the existence of the great universal (*mahāsattā*) is established, its reason is precisely this non-non-existence.
Both the proponent and the opponent agree that the reason exists and that the dharma of the thesis exists; thus, the reason and the dharma of the thesis [are established].

Since the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*) are not mutually related, and since the reason (*hetu*) does not exist upon the locus, why is this not a case of "non-establishment for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*)?

Here, "both" refers to the proponent and the opponent. Answer: The meaning of the previous question is that while "existence" (*sattā*) and "the existent" (*sad-dharma*) are not non-existent upon [the categories of] "reality" (*sat*), etc., there is also a single reality; likewise, the reason is also not non-existent upon "reality," etc.
Because it is their very nature, [the universal] can pervade all existing entities (*dharmin*).

Regarding the statement that "there is no need for further words because there is no distinction among qualities and activities," this precisely explains the previous question. Furthermore, the three reasons share a single analogy, just as with the "nature of similarity" (*sāmānyatva*):
namely, that it possesses a single reality (*dravya*), possesses qualities (*guṇa*), and possesses activities (*karman*). Thus, these three reasons are all based upon...
Because "sameness" and "difference" serve as the analogies, it is said that the three reasons share a single analogy.

Among qualities (*guṇa*), activities (*karma*), and so forth, there is no confusion regarding one quality, two qualities, or many qualities; therefore, it does not say "there is one quality" and so on.

Regarding the statement that "each of these three reasons is present in each of the first three [theses]," this means that these three reasons are all present upon each of the preceding theses, such as "non-real" and so forth.
Based on these three reasons, each one individually forms three types of theses; when combined, there should be nine.
As for how this is so, it is because the syntactic structures are mutually modified.

Regarding the explanation of the reason for this, it says: "As for reaching the point where both are determined," one asks: "If there is a single real cause that can establish another [property] and also attain determination, how can it be that it does not contradict itself?
The answer is: A single real cause establishes the existence of a thing (*sattva*), but it is not [the property of] being real (*vastutva*) and so forth.
Although that [existence] is determined, it can establish existence, yet it is not "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), because it is absent from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) of "great existence" (*mahāsattā*) is what is being established, the fault of contradiction (*viruddha*) is incurred; this is specifically the fault of "contradiction with the certainty" (*niścita-viruddha*).

Although the reason (*hetu*) is present in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), namely that this "common nature" (*sāmānya*) can exist as each individual real entity, yet the substance of the reason is not "great existence"—it lacks the "great existence" which constitutes the similar class of the thesis—and since the common nature differs from great existence, they are not similar.
This refers to that which serves as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) for the thesis (*sādhya*) being established.

Question: If that is so, then up to the point where there are no similar instances (*sapakṣa*) at all—this question intends to follow from the preceding textual meaning. The meaning of the text is as follows:

you have posited that "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) is a real entity, while "sameness and difference" (*tādātmyatadutpatti*) are not real entities, yet you take these as the similar examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). You then state that [these] are sameness and difference.
Although the nature [of existence] is neither real nor a "great existence" (*mahāsattā*), it is treated as a "great existence" for the sake of providing a counter-example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).

If that is the case, when establishing that sound is impermanent, since sound possesses audibility while a jar lacks audibility, the jar should serve as the counter-example; such is the intent of the question.

Regarding the subsequent statement, "Furthermore, in all propositions there is no dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)," this objection has two meanings: first, it suggests that if you say one must [provide a counter-example] with respect to the subject (*dharmin*)...

Regarding the first point, concerning similarity with the similar class (*sapakṣa*): for instance, the property-possessor "sound" being impermanent is similar to the property-possessor "space" being devoid of self and so forth, which is permanent;
thus, this permanent space should become a similar class. If one accepts it as a similar class, there would be no dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
Second, as for the pot being seen to be subject to combustion, since it is distinct from sound, it can serve as the impermanent sound [of the example].
If all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) were considered similar instances (*sapakṣa*), then there would be no dissimilar instances at all, which would render the purpose of the critique meaningless.
Accordingly, a commentary states: "Furthermore, it should be understood even better that for every thesis (*pakṣa*), there would be no similar instances.
One should examine other versions to verify this.

Since it has already been established that there is a "reality" that is equally present [in both], why does the preceding text merely state that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is equally present and not say that the locus (*dharmin*) is equally present?
How can it be said that there is a contradiction with the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the locus? Answer:

What I have now formulated as this "contradiction with the self-characteristic of the locus" is also a case where the property to be proven is equally present. How so? It is because "existence" (*sattā*) is the property to be proven.
The thesis is that "this existent nature (bhāva-svabhāva) must be non-existent," and the reason is "because it possesses a single reality.
This is like the case of "sameness" and "difference," which possess a single reality of sameness and difference; yet, sameness and difference themselves are not the existent nature.

Since the existent nature possesses a single reality, it should—like sameness and difference—not be the existent nature. Thus, by taking the absence of a real existent nature as the similar instance (sapakṣa), etc. [the following applies].
If this fault were applicable to the "existence" (*sattā*) established by the Vaiśeṣikas, one might object that it applies equally to the "existent entity" (*dharmin*);

however, what is now stated is that even apart from the existence of a real substance, there is still a dharma. It is not being said that apart from the existence of a real substance, the existent entity itself reverts to non-existence; this is certain.

Question: Since "existence" (*sattā*) is a property of an entity (*dharmin*) characterized by its own specific marks (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, this question arises from the intention of the previous response.
You previously established a thesis (*pakṣa*) that equally takes "existence apart from real entities" as the probandum (*sādhya*).

Now, since this "existence apart from real entities" is intended to have the meaning of a particularity (*viśeṣa*), the reason (*hetu*) "being a single real entity" contradicts this particularity of the property of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣa-hetu*).

How can it be said that there is a self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon as its cause? Such is the intent of the question. In the following answer, the point is that this statement is not being asserted here;
for if one were to follow the words immediately and raise an objection, it would be termed the fallacy of contradicting one's own characteristic (*svabhāva-viruddha-doṣa*).
If it were not so—if this "intention" (*manas*) did not seek out the words—it would be difficult to refute the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

This [refutation] would implicitly entail a refutation of the existence of the "Great" (*mahat*). Regarding that which is to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*), the word "subject" (*dharmin*) must be something already established (*prasiddha*).

If it is already established, then there is no fault regarding the specific characteristic of the subject. Now, to say that it "exists" while having the nature of non-existence—is this not a contradiction of one's own position?
If this were not the case, then all the subjects (*viśeṣya*) that are universally established would be subject to the fault of non-existence.

If one does not take the words as expressing the existence of a nature, but instead takes the intended implication to be an existence distinct from substance (*dravya*), then the subject itself becomes unestablished.

Since this is so, all universally established subjects would lack this [existence], resulting in the fault that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of this dharma (the subject) is absent. Therefore, it is known that these faults are all...

[Objection: "Since this [subject] is not established as the distinct object (*viśeṣya*)—because it does not rely on what is intended in the mind, but merely states a commonality in words based on the existence of something apart from a real entity—the subject is unestablished (*asiddha*), which is also a fault regarding the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the locus (*dharmin*). What fault is there in this? [Response:

Since the reason has not yet been stated, the fault has already been manifested; how then could there be a fault of the reason? Furthermore, this is not a case of a non-differentiating reason (*aviśeṣaka-hetu*). This...
However, there is a factor that serves as the cause for the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon, but not as the cause for its specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

If one does not rely on words but grasps the intended meaning, then what is accepted as established becomes the "qualified" (*viśeṣya*), and thus this fault does not arise. Furthermore, this will be examined below.

Furthermore, there is the fallacy of "contradicting one's own tenet" (*siddhānta-virodha*) and "one-sided unestablishedness" (*anyatara-asiddha*). Regarding "contradicting one's own tenet": within one's own school’s tenets, there is no such thing as a "real entity" (*dravya-sat*) that exists apart from [the categories];

yet now you speak of a "real entity existing apart [from them]," which thus contradicts your own tenet. Regarding "one-sided unestablishedness": one [of the two parties] holds that it has an essential nature (*svabhāva*), while the other holds that it lacks an essential nature.

If [you argue that] real entities and so forth are not non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then the existence of even one real entity constitutes the "one-sided establishedness" of having an essential nature. If [you] take...

Regarding "Great Functioning" (*mahāvyāpāra*), there is one real cause which is precisely the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Whichever of these two [realities or absence of nature] is taken individually, both are self-corroborative (*svataḥ-prasiddha*) and not corroborated by another (*parataḥ-prasiddha*).

As for the fact that the opponent first stated this collectively and now likewise refutes it collectively, the intention is that the proponent merely spoke in a general or inclusive manner, yet it is actually [the case].
Regarding the opponent’s objection that "existence" (svabhāva) is also subsumed within "non-existence," [the author] replies:

because we do not speak of "non-existence apart from real existence" (na pṛthagbhūtam asad vastu), there is no fault of contradicting our own tenets (*siddhānta*) based on whether it is non-existent or not non-existent in relation to real existence;

nor is there the fault of the "equivalence of the point at issue" (*prasaṅgasama*) based on whether it is existent apart from real existence. Therefore, it is said that there are no such faults. As for what follows below, where it says "the words are the same but the meanings differ":
There is a statement that although the meanings are the same, the difficulty lies in the fact that "non-real existence" (asat) is distinct [from real existence].
This is because the three—real substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and activity (karman)—reside within this very substance;

when these three essences are in a state of conjunction, they serve as the objective referent for the expressive words, and thus it is said that they arise simultaneously with the words that express them.

Regarding "taking the three as the cause for existence": this means that when the expressive words that designate [substance], [quality], and [action] have these as their referents, they are dharmas possessing substantial reality (*dravya*).

Since their substance is existent, they also serve as the objects of the cognitions that take them as conditions. How so? It is because through the Great Existence (*mahāsattā*), substance, quality, and action first become established as existent, whereby the expressive words and the cognitions that take them as conditions are then able to arise.

This refers to that which is conjoined with substance (*dravya*) and so forth; this "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) is a statement regarding conjunction and non-conjunction with substance and so forth. Regarding the phrase "apprehended by all faculties":
one might ask, why is it said only that they are "apprehended by the faculties" and not "apprehended by the mind (*citta*) and so forth"?

The answer is: for the time being, we discuss this based on the presence of an object. It is because the faculties can apprehend objects, and by means of the faculties, the resultant consciousness (*vijñāna*) is induced; that which is induced is the consciousness itself.

This refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). Since these mental factors abide by depending upon the sense faculties, and speaking from the perspective of what is predominant, the faculties—which are the objects of apprehension—are mentioned first.
Regarding the phrase "certainly not produced, eternal, and so forth," this is the formal explanation of existence (*sattā*); the essence of existence is eternal and is not something produced.

Regarding "lacking qualities" (*nirguṇa*), the intended meaning is as follows: "qualities" refers to the qualities of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), not the qualities of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Thus, it is called "lacking qualities. Furthermore, regarding "having no subtle divisions," this means that while there are no subtle distinctions of degree or difference, they are equal in their reality and so forth, yet there are nine such categories.

Regarding "eternal," "without qualities" (*nirguṇa*), "without activity" (*niṣkriya*), and "without parts" (*niraṃśa*), when analyzed according to various categories, these four gates are definitively not produced and so forth.
As for the ten-fold analysis of the meaning of these ten phrases in the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*, it states:

"In this regard, concerning the categories of 'having existence,' 'produced,' and 'unproduced,' [the eternal] is exclusively unproduced; the same applies to 'eternal' and 'non-eternal. 'Without qualities' refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*)."
Regarding the phrase "possessing qualities": this phrase is called "without qualities" because it is devoid of movement;
the phrase "possessing action" is not a phrase [referring to] action because it lacks subtle divisions—it is a single phrase of existence without manifold distinctions.

Because there are nine kinds such as "not-as-it-is" (ayathārtha) and so forth, that which possesses real qualities and action is this phrase of existence; although it lacks qualities, action, or movement, it is nonetheless capable of [existence].
Substantiality, quality, and activity; "substantiality" refers to the lower [category] of examination.
The term "different" (*anya*) excludes that which is identical; although this interpretation exists, it does not accord with the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*.

Regarding "that which is different from what is conjoined" (*anyasamaveta*): "different" means distinct; "from what is conjoined" means from that which possesses the property of being conjoined; "one" means great (*mahat*).
That which "exists" is called "one existence" (*ekabhava*). Although the Master of the *Shigui* (Time-Track) Commentary likewise makes this judgment, doubt has not yet been entirely dispelled;
one should reflect upon this further later.
Regarding the identity or difference of the nature of existence (*bhāva-svabhāva*), although these two types are both of the nature of existence, [the former] is not accepted by him.

Regarding the statement that [the *mahāsāmānya*] possesses the nature of having an object (*sālambanatva*) while not grasping the "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), nor grasping the "existence of commonality" (*sāmānyasattā*)—and thus does not grasp up to the nature of being a cognizer (*ālambakatva*)—there are two interpretations. One says: this is based on the coarseness and superficiality of the objects.

The faculties (*indriya*) are able to illuminate [objects] first; therefore, they are mentioned first. As for the mental factors (*caitta*) apprehended by them, their objects of cognition are profound and subtle;

thus, they are not mentioned. Judging from what is presently manifest, the mind (*citta*) is also able to take objects as its conditions. This is evidenced by the following passage which asks: "If there were no substance, how could the mind arise?
Thus, it is known that [the faculties] serve as objects for the apprehending mind, and this also applies to the mind taking [them] as its conditions. Furthermore, another interpretation is provided.

The Vaiśeṣika school maintains that mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), such as cognition (*buddhi*) and pleasure (*sukha*), are admitted to exist; yet since these lack substantial entity (*svabhāva*), how can they function as objects for a perceiving subject?

In response: I now establish them as being of the nature of a perceiving subject (*ālambaka*) by taking their capacity to act as such, rather than by taking them as the objects (*ālambana*) of perception.
Therefore, those [mental factors] do not take other mental factors as their own perceiving subjects.
Because there is no cause, that which lacks conditions does not arise; if "Greatness" (mahat) and so forth do not yet exist as real entities, these three likewise do not arise.
Therefore, the aforementioned reason—that it is a reason for the qualification of an existent phenomenon—is precisely this: the reason that [the subject] possesses a real entity.

Although the wording here is brief—meaning that although this treatise does not fully set forth the formal procedure, one should follow it from here—the commentators of the present day raise this objection against the principle of "not being separate from the real existence" (*dravyasat*).
However, their objection regarding the principle of "not being separate from the real existence" is not valid;
the logic is clearly evident.

Regarding the statement, "Now, this brief [explanation] is sufficient and thus poses no difficulty": the meaning of this is that if one were to take only the latter member of the compound as the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), then this reason would constitute the fallacy of being a self-characteristic of the property (*dharmasvalakṣaṇa-doṣa*) rather than the fallacy of being a qualification of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣaṇa-doṣa*).

However, since we now universally accept the intended implication as the qualification, this difficulty does not arise; thus, there is no obstacle to the objection raised by the opponent. This is how the external objection is resolved.
The opponent says: "Those that establish a distinction are all the predicate (the *dharma*), so how can they constitute a distinction within the subject (*dharmin*)?

Therefore, it is said that what is merely the predicate is called the 'specific characteristic' (*svalakṣaṇa*), while that which is intended by the mind is called the 'distinction. Since we are now looking at what is intended by the mind, it obtains the name 'distinction';
thus, there is no fault or contradiction. This is indeed a careful examination.

The response to the charge that this contradicts one’s own tenets is as follows: Within this very *Śabdika* (Grammarian) school, it is asserted that sound is indeed sound, and it is further admitted that there exists a mind capable of cognizing that sound within the sound itself.
Now, to first state that it is "not sound" and subsequently claim that "there is no mind that cognizes sound" and so forth—does this not constitute a confusion of one's own tenets?

Furthermore, since the original argument did not dispute the existence of sound, but rather the fact that sound possesses the nature of being an object of cognition, this [objection] is categorized as a "pseudo-refutation."

Regarding the statement that "all [reasons] enter into the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and thus lack the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)," this means that, with the exception of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), all existent phenomena (*dharma*) enter into the similar instance.

Question: Why is it necessary to state "with the exception of the four great elements"? Answer: If one were to say merely that "the essence is not non-existent," and did not exclude the four great elements, there would be an inconclusive fallacy.
This inconclusiveness would consist in the following: that the nature of the great elements is like color and sound, in that their essence is not non-existent.
Therefore, it is not the case that [the elements] are the four great primary elements (mahābhūta), because the essence of the four great primary elements is not non-existent;
since there would be this fault [if they were], the reason states "excluding the four great primary elements."
"Tangxing" refers to Tangxing Temple in Fen Prefecture. As for Master Jun, his name is also written with the character "Jùn";

both are pronounced with the second tone. He was truly a pivotal figure in the Buddhist community: "pivotal" (*shu*) refers to the socket of a door hinge, while "knot" (*niu*) refers to a fastening knot on clothing.
"The age of *qi*" refers to those under fifteen, so called because they wear *qi* (brocade) garments; "extraordinary" (*qi*) refers to extraordinary talent.

"Also, 'floating on the boat of universal compassion' (*fan ci zhōu*): 'floating' (*fan*) refers to principle (*lǐ*). It is like a skilled helmsman; furthermore, 'floating' (*fan*) means crossing directly across.
The 'admiration for Dharma Master Juàn' who 'pilot a boat to ferry living beings' is a metaphor. 'Śrāmaṇeras saving ants'—'to rescue' (*jiù*) means to cross over by cutting through the water.
Some write it as *sì*; this should be examined."
"Tiāo nián" (tied-up hair) refers to the time when one is like a young snail; "yǐng" (tip) means to pull out; "biàn" (discernment) refers to the seven types of discernment.
"Chéng qīú" (pure crane)—some write it as "chéng," for the characters "chéng" and "chéng" are similar; "yīng" (hero) refers to one whose wisdom surpasses a thousand people;
"chī" (unfurl) means to spread or to extend; "zhì" (substance) refers to physical form; "ruì" (clarity) comes from "shèng" (sage); "lán" (orchid) refers to fragrance.
The general title of the "Cao" (Grass) section is "Yi" (Easy). It says, "When two people are of one heart, their sharpness can cut through metal; its fragrance is like that of the orchid.
This refers to those who accord with medicinal stones. "Fu" means mutual conformity; "yao-shi" (medicinal stones) refers to everything that corresponds to pain.
"Xiang" means to lift up; "yuan" means to belong to; and "sai" means to lift up.
"Zǎo" refers to the finest grade of *zǎo* grass. A "thousand-jūn" consists of thirty *jīn* per *jūn*.
Now, as for the characteristic of the correct cause (*yīng zhèng yīn xiàng*), since it has never contradicted the ultimate principle, the previous two sections have not yet been answered;

therefore, I shall briefly explain the identity and difference of the thesis (*zhòng*), the examples (*yù*), and the section on logical consistency. Through the property of the reason (*yīn fǎ*), one establishes the property of the subsequent term (*hòu chén fǎ*), rather than establishing the subject (*yǒu fǎ*).

Regarding the statement that "the thesis established by means of the reason can achieve four meanings," this implies that if the reason exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa) and is absent from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), it will enable another person to produce a definitive cognition; thus, the correct reason can achieve these four types.

If that were so, there would be no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). For example, if one establishes that sound is impermanent, then this very fact of its possessing such qualities as suffering, emptiness, and selflessness—along with its permanence—would constitute the dissimilar instance.
Since these qualities of suffering, emptiness, and selflessness likewise exist within that permanent sound, they would be similar [to the subject], and thus there would be no dissimilar instance.
If this logic holds, there would also be no similar instance (*sapakṣa*); how, then, could it be permanent?
If impermanence is dissimilar, it cannot serve as a valid similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Although the intent of the objection is to reach that point, when one objects to its specific distinction, the question arises: "What is meant by 'adding words' (*sopaskāra*) versus 'not adding words' (*nirupaskāra*)?

When another establishes a statement asserting existence—claiming it is neither a substance (*dravya*), nor a quality (*guṇa*), nor an action (*karman*)—one immediately objects to this statement by calling it "not adding words. This is the intended meaning of the term "not adding words."

Since it was granted that [the reason] is distinct from "real existence" (*mahāsattā*), yet was not mentioned in the opponent's statement, the word "existence" (*sattva*) is added, such as "having the nature of being an object-condition" (*sālambanatva*).

Therefore, the treatise states: "When this very reason is stated in this manner regarding the aforementioned thesis concerning 'having the nature of being an object-condition,' all of this constitutes the 'addition' (*adhika*) which points out a fault."

Now, regarding the statement that expressing the words and presenting the ultimate principle do not contradict one another: this refers to the intention behind this treatise, which—based on the expression of words and the intended meaning—accepts that four positions are established.
In the *Nyāyamukha*, it relies solely upon what is intended; since the verbal expression is merely concealed, it is said that "the dharma is established by words."
The following section, beginning with "the specific characteristics of the phenomena taught in this treatise" and continuing with "the causes," explains the first gate.
Thus, regarding the term "manifesting the cause": one asks why the latter three [causes] do not mention "manifesting," while the very first is immediately called "manifesting the cause.
The answer is that the first instance uses the term "manifesting" because, based on both similar and dissimilar examples, it truly and without artifice clearly manifests [the meaning].

Therefore, it is said that the latter three are presented as "counter-examples" (*vipakṣa*) by way of a door; this serves as a gateway to implicitly include the meaning of the formal proof (*sādhana*), yet it is not explicitly clear and thus is not given the name "explicit.

This means that when the remaining three [reasons] are applied to the thesis (*pakṣa*) under dispute by both parties and investigated through reasoning, none of them possess a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). This is the intended explanation.

Regarding the three types [of fallacious reasons] mentioned subsequently, it should be understood upon reflection that they all lack both the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

As for the "inconclusive reason" (*anaikāntika-hetu*) and so forth, the question is: why does this passage appear? The answer is that it refers back to the previously mentioned "contrary application" (*viruddha-viniścaya*) using the old terminology.

Because the fault of contradiction has already been pointed out, it is termed "contradictory-undetermined" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*); furthermore, since the reason itself has not been altered, it should be called "contradictory. This passage is introduced for that reason.

To establish a valid reason (*saddhetu*), one must show that the thesis (*pakṣa*) applies to the property of the subject (*dharmin*). When the opponent attempts to refute this by claiming it is contradictory, the proponent presents the reason to establish the thesis;
thus, the fault has not yet arisen. The opponent does not alter the reason or the example, but instead points out a fault in order to render the meaning indeterminate (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding the statement that "the two types of refutation do not produce definitive knowledge," this refers for now to the first four; in reality, all six types involve the non-production of definitive knowledge.

One might ask: since both are equally invalidating by establishing a contradiction with the uncertain [reason], why is one called "producing definitive knowledge" while the other is "not producing definitive knowledge"?

Answer: This distinction between "producing" and "not producing" definitive knowledge arises because there is a difference between the two types of refutation in the way they formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to expose the fault.
Therefore, that which differs from the former is precisely this contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), whereas the former was the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
If the reason established is correct—that is, if the proponent's reason exists in both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—then it is called a correct refutation;
however, if the opponent points out the fault of inconclusiveness within that [context], it is indeed a contradiction.

If one establishes a reason (*hetu*) that is truly valid, how could it not be non-erroneous (*anaikāntika*)? This correctly explains that what is contradictory (*viruddha*) is not called "non-erroneous.

The reason why the contradictory is cited as a reason is that it renders the thesis (*pakṣa*) faulty; it is not a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), but rather the reason itself constitutes a fault. Since both [the contradictory and the non-erroneous] are equally absent in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and equally present in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), they manifest no contradiction.
If a non-erroneous reason reveals its fault only after [the debate has proceeded], it applies to both sides; how then could it not be non-erroneous? By virtue of this...

Therefore, it is known that these are not called "indeterminate. As for the indeterminate causes mentioned below, they are explained as collateral responses to objections (*paryanuyoga*) rather than direct answers to the preceding question.
Thus, these four characteristics do not contradict the four or six [characteristics]. This concludes the previous response to the objection; the latter three causes are likewise identical.

There is no difference between existence and non-existence. Furthermore, the following section provides the formal explanation for the second question, beginning with: "Moreover, since the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena arise from causes that are not different.

Now, regarding the point that the latter three [categories] are treated as identical to the first by taking difference as identity: if one were to discuss this according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), the nature of identity and difference...
The proponent establishes "difference" as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) and treats it as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Now, this [reason] constitutes a contradiction with the third, fourth, and so on, because while the first [reason] takes a different instance as a similar one, the latter three also take a different instance as a similar one; thus, those that are contradictory can establish the third and fourth.

That which takes difference as similarity is precisely this nature of similarity-and-difference (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-svabhāva*), which the proponent employs as a dissimilar instance to establish [the thesis] as a similar one.

Because it is a metaphor, it is said that "the different is treated as the same. Regarding the first instance of treating the different as the same: the initial property (*dharma*) and its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) are the same as the corroborative example (*upamāna*).

Even if one changes [the example], because it is established by changing what is different, it is called "treating the different as the same. Now, examining the latter three cases where there is an application (*upanaya*):
this refers precisely to the combination of those two or three, and so forth. This is the examination.

At first glance, this reason appears to be a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) one; however, it is actually a "non-existent" (*asat*) reason because the Vaiśeṣikas assert that existence (*sattā*) is distinct from substantiality (*dravyatva*).

In this context, "substance and so forth" serves as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), while "the nature of generality and particularity" (*sāmānya-viśeṣatva*)—which, though distinct from substantiality, is not [itself] existence—is falsely taken as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Thus, the reason "because it is asserted not to be non-existent" exists within the dissimilar instances of substance and so forth, where the nature of generality and particularity is present.
Regarding the phrase "at first glance" (*chà*) in the statement "at first glance they seem identical, yet upon careful investigation they are in fact different categories":

the word "at first glance" is used because, when one examines the three or four reasons mentioned previously, the Master [Sthiramati] had earlier clarified that the single reason contradicts the three; since he admitted that it is not the case that [the other reasons] are absent, the single reason thus contradicts the four. As for the term "previously" (*xiàng*), it refers to what was stated before concerning the three or four reasons. It clarifies that while the single reason contradicts the three, it does not contradict the four.

"Contradicting one's own [position]" (*svaviruddha*) and so forth: the Vaiśeṣikas establish their own inference (*svānumāna*), whereas the Buddha’s Dharma contradicts others; therefore, it is called "contradicting one's own" and "contradicting others.

Regarding inference by others (*parānumāna*): when one does not establish an inference for others, yet within that inference for others one commits these four faults, this is called "contradicting others.
Because one contradicts this inference for others, it is called "contradicting others."
Since it is admitted that a single cause can contradict all four types, we know that these four are not necessarily mutually exclusive.
This means that while it is clear a single cause can contradict all four types, it does not follow that each of these four causes must individually contradict all four other causes.
It is not denied that they might contradict two, three, or four; in reality, there are cases where they contradict two, and there are also cases where they contradict [more].
Regarding the third, fourth, and so forth:

since it is granted that a single cause reaching [multiple effects] is not necessarily contradictory, the meaning of this statement is as follows: when the opponent previously challenged [the position], the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon was taken as the basis;

taking the real entity of another as "similar" and the similarity of another as "different," the three subsequent [characteristics] are contradictory. Taking the similarity of another as "similarity" and the difference of another as [difference]...
If their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are thus different, how can there be the combination of two with two, or three with three, and so forth?
This is the intent of the opponent’s objection, which challenges the treatise by claiming that such differing modes of activity constitute a contradiction in the tenets.

Now, since it is already admitted that a single cause can contradict four [other causes], there is no contradiction even when the phrase "the intrinsic nature of phenomena" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇa*) is combined with the latter three. Thus, the sentence is not inconsistent.

Answer: At first glance, regarding the two reasons mentioned in the textual flow—namely, the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reason which possesses both the "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "volitional effort" (*prayatnāntarīyaka*) reasons, and which is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent—it is precisely these four aforementioned contradictory reasons that constitute being unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent.
Question: Is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) the fault of the first characteristic, while "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is the fault of the latter two characteristics? Each [fault] is distinct.
Question: How is it that these [reasons] do not constitute a "contradictory" (*viruddha*) logical mark? Answer:

They are not stated with reference to the actual entity (*tattva*), but rather with reference to the name (*nāman*); thus, there is no fault. This contradictory reason is established as a fault of the latter two characteristics.

Since the original reason was intended to correctly establish the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the reason lacks the [required] characteristic and thus cannot establish the thesis, this contradictory reason is so named.

Regarding "not being unestablished as a reason" (*asiddha-hetu*) and so forth: if there were nothing contradictory or subverting [the thesis], this would be a logical method; however, the meaning of this is not yet clear.

When that reason is established as correct, it is called a "correct reason" (*saddhetu*) because it occurs within the subject (*dharmin*) of the proponent's thesis; if it functions as such a reason, it is contradictory.
When the opponent uses this reason to produce a fallacy, it is called "contradiction" (*viruddha*).
That which is correct must contradict this, and that which contradicts this must be correct; this clearly explains the reason for the "indefinite" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy.
As for "this contradiction must," the one who can refute it finds the fallacy of the indefinite within the proponent's proof.
It is called "truly capable of refutation" (sat-pratipakṣa); therefore it is said that "this contradiction must be correct," for "correct" refers to being truly capable of refutation.

"According to what is appropriate" means that one follows what the proponent has established; by employing the reason (*hetu*) established by the proponent to create a contradiction, one speaks of "according to what is appropriate.
If this contradiction lacks correctness, it is simply the thesis (*pakṣa*) of the proponent. If that [thesis] lacks contradiction, it is the capability of the opponent (*prativādin*).
"Refuting [the opponent] and establishing [one's own position] correctly.
If there is a passage stating that "if the latter three [reasons] are not established, one may say they exist," this constitutes a single textual unit.

The meaning of this is that the latter three, even if not established, can apply to both the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*); thus, there is at least one instance of the inconclusive and so forth.

While it is possible for this meaning to apply to any one [of the three types]—such as the indeterminate (*anaikāntika*) or the contradictory (*viruddha*)—it is not the case that all indeterminate or contradictory reasons possess the latter three types of unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, the commentary states: "There may be the indeterminate, etc.

Regarding the phrase "with respect to any one of the three," this means that among the latter three types of unestablished, each can be found to exist individually in relation to either the indeterminate or the contradictory.

Furthermore, regarding the "indefinite" (anaikāntika): there is the indefinite by reason of one [aspect] being indefinite, the indefinite by reason of doubt regarding one [aspect], the indefinite by reason of the basis of one [aspect] being indefinite;

there is the contradictory by reason of one [aspect] being contradictory, the contradictory by reason of doubt regarding one [aspect], and the contradictory by reason of the basis of one [aspect] being contradictory.
If, in the case of the latter three types of "unestablished" (asiddha), there could be the indefinite and the contradictory, [one might ask: does the unestablished lack its first characteristic?

Consider how the faults of the latter two characteristics— namely, the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) and the "contradictory" (*viruddha*)— are established as such. Regarding the phrase "inference for oneself, for others,
and for both," among the four types of contradiction, there are three each based on inference for oneself, for others, and for both, totaling nine.
Furthermore, if one takes these ten causes that can contradict [the thesis] and applies them to each of these thirty-six [points], there are fifteen [contradictions] for each;
in total, this amounts to five hundred and thirty-four contradictions.
Regarding the distinction between existence and non-existence based on the relative breadth or narrowness of similar causes (*sādharmya-hetu*):

that which is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), yet not contradictory (*viruddha*), is termed "broad" (*viśāla*). That which is both unestablished and inconclusive, but neither contradictory nor [the other two], is next "broader.

That which is unestablished but is merely unestablished—neither inconclusive nor contradictory—is termed "narrow" (*saṃkucita*). The formulation for the inconclusive and the contradictory follows the same principle.

This [point] contradicts what was stated regarding "common" (sādhāraṇa) [reasons]. If one says that the four types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*) lack only the first characteristic [of being common], then why are the indeterminate (*anaikāntika*) and contradictory (*viruddha*) reasons not included among these four unestablished reasons?
